raw_record.support_text: The paper describes thiabendazole-induced jaundice characterized as drug-induced cholestasis of the idiosyncratic type, with cholestasis, slight or absent hepatocellular necrosis, modest inflammatory infiltrate, and a high proportion of eosinophils. Onset of jaundice after first exposure varied from 2 days to 4 wk, and the course, though potentially prolonged (7 mo in one case), was invariably self-limited; two reported deaths were not caused by hepatic failure.

Treatment was supportive; steroids gave no improvement in one patient, phenobarbital reportedly benefited another.

raw_record.support_text: The paper describes phenprocoumon-induced liver damage (phenprocoumoninduzierter Leberschaden), first described in 1963. According to a BfArM analysis based on spontaneous reports it constitutes ~2% of all phenprocoumon side effects and ~1% of all hepatopathies are phenprocoumon-induced. The clinical picture is extremely variable, ranging from simple hepatitis to (sub)acute liver failure with fatal outcome, as in the presented case. Hepatopathy typically occurs 3-9 months after starting phenprocoumon, with latencies up to 7 years reported; in the presented case the patient had taken Marcumar (phenprocoumon) for 6 years.
raw_record.extra_details: Sold as Marcumar; anticoagulation indication. Latency typically 3-9 months, up to 7 years; present patient used phenprocoumon for 6 years. Clinical spectrum from simple hepatitis to (sub)acute liver failure with death. BfArM spontaneous-report analysis: ~2% of phenprocoumon side effects and ~1% of hepatopathies attributed to phenprocoumon. Four cases of this complication occurred in the authors' patient population during 2006-2008, two fatal; a Mainz case series illustrates the broad clinical spectrum. An immunologic genesis is considered likely (borderline ANA titer, exacerbation upon re-exposure, 'drug-allergic' course); cross-sensitization with other coumarins noted. Steroid therapy attempted without influence on outcome. Histology showed portal inflammatory infiltrate, group necrosis with cholestasis, collapse zone with clearing, and focal fiber increase; the course evolved into rapidly developing liver cirrhosis with subacute liver failure.

raw_record.support_text: In a CCSG randomized study of childhood leukemia patients free of disease for 2.5–3 years, those continued on chemotherapy developed serious chronic toxicity. Among 7 children continued, a child on daily methotrexate for 255 days developed hepatosplenomegaly, elevated liver enzymes, bony osteoporosis, and severe scoliosis; a percutaneous liver biopsy demonstrated cirrhotic changes, and liver function tests returned to normal after methotrexate was discontinued. Two other patients had clinical evidence of liver disease with altered liver function and hepatosplenomegaly after 461 and 1211 days of methotrexate maintenance, both improving after discontinuation.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric childhood leukemia patients on chronic maintenance therapy; one patient also received methotrexate plus four other drugs cyclically as an unresolved co-exposure.
raw_record.extra_details: Chronic methotrexate toxicity. CCSG randomized study (1966): 7 children continued treatment, 3 developed serious chronic toxicity. Daily methotrexate for 255 days led to hepatosplenomegaly, elevated liver enzymes, osteoporosis and scoliosis, with cirrhotic changes on biopsy; liver function normalized after discontinuation. Two further children on methotrexate maintenance for 461 and 1211 days had liver disease with altered liver function and hepatosplenomegaly, improving on discontinuation. Minnesota series: hepatic fibrosis in 12 children, usually asymptomatic despite abnormal BSP excretion and transiently elevated OCT/SGOT immediately after methotrexate. CCSG 903 maintenance methotrexate (30 mg/m² twice weekly p.o.): predominant clinical toxicity hepatic; of 216 patients on study >4 months, 80 had elevated liver enzymes (median time to definite elevation 167 days); liver biopsy showed significant cirrhosis in 5 and fibrosis in 9 (moderate fibrosis mean 389 days, cirrhosis mean 530 days on MTX); 9 of 11 with fibrosis/cirrhosis had prior acute methotrexate toxicity. Pathologic findings in MTX-induced liver disease (12 patients): portal fibrosis 10/12, enlarged/double-nucleated hepatic cells 9/12, portal inflammation 7/12, periportal fat 4/12, cholestasis 1/12, hepatic necrosis 1/12.

raw_record.support_text: In this phase I trial, intoplicine was given as a 72-h continuous i.v. infusion, escalated to a maximum tolerated dose of 336 mg/m²/day, where grade 3 and 4 granulocytopenia and elevations in hepatic transaminases associated with nausea and vomiting were noted. The paper states that a prior intoplicine trial (Abigerges et al., 1-h i.v. infusion) ceased dose escalation because hepatocellular damage, indicated by rising liver enzyme levels, resulted in death in one patient, and that in the van Gijn et al. study (24-h continuous i.v. infusion) liver toxicity was also dose limiting, with death in one patient due to liver failure associated with intoplicine treatment. An increase in hepatic transaminases was evident at 336 mg/m²/day, prompting a halt to dose escalation at 440 mg/m²/day, and the authors conclude liver toxicity appears independent of infusion duration.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Phase I trial in advanced cancer patients; drug administered as 72-h continuous i.v. infusion with dose escalation to a maximum tolerated dose of 336 mg/m²/day; escalation to 440 mg/m²/day halted because of transaminase increases. Deaths from liver failure were reported in prior intoplicine studies using shorter (1-h and 24-h) i.v. infusion schedules.
raw_record.extra_details: Dose-limiting liver toxicity. Grade 3/4 transaminase increases observed at 56, 224, 336, and 420 mg/m²/day dose levels (1 each; one grade 4 at 224 mg/m²/day) and another at 420 mg/m²/day. At 336 mg/m²/day transaminase elevation was associated with nausea and vomiting. Prior trial (Abigerges et al., 1-h infusion) stopped because hepatocellular damage from rising liver enzymes caused death in one patient; van Gijn et al. study (24-h infusion) reported dose-limiting liver toxicity and one death from liver failure associated with treatment. Intoplicine is an inhibitor of topoisomerase I and II. Authors conclude liver toxicity is independent of infusion duration.

raw_record.support_text: A number of reports have suggested an association between azathioprine therapy and veno-occlusive disease, especially in renal-transplant recipients. Of 16 reported cases, 10 presented with jaundice as a predominant symptom, 5 had hepatomegaly, 3 ascites, and 1 splenomegaly. All patients became symptomatic 6 months to 9 years after renal transplantation; 8 had hepatic failure, 3 had progressive portal hypertension, 3 died of nonhepatic causes, 1 improved after azathioprine withdrawal, and 1 improved after a portacaval shunt.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Renal-transplant recipients on continuous azathioprine therapy.
raw_record.extra_details: Veno-occlusive disease characterized by non-thrombotic concentric luminal narrowing of sublobular hepatic veins without large hepatic vein obstruction. 16 reported cases; symptoms 6 months to 9 years after renal transplantation (11 between 12-24 months); among 16: 8 hepatic failure, 3 progressive portal hypertension, 3 died of nonhepatic causes, 1 improved on withdrawal, 1 improved after portacaval shunt. Some acute, some insidious progression to chronic liver disease.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report a patient who developed nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and fatigue 2 weeks after starting rosiglitazone therapy, and state that they believe the most likely cause of his symptoms and elevated liver enzyme levels was rosiglitazone-associated hepatotoxicity. Rosiglitazone was discontinued on admission, symptoms immediately improved, and liver enzyme levels returned to normal over ensuing weeks. Because the patient had no fever, rash, or eosinophilia, the authors concluded the liver injury caused by rosiglitazone seemed to be idiosyncratic rather than a classic immune mechanism.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report: patient was an icteric, obese male with prior acetaminophen use (up to 4 g/d for 2 years, 3-4 tablets daily 3 months before admission) and prior brief exposures to troglitazone (discontinued after 1 week for nausea) and repaglinide (discontinued for nausea/dizziness); acetaminophen level on admission was 3.2 µg/mL (normal 10-30). Symptoms appeared ~2 weeks after starting rosiglitazone; rosiglitazone was discontinued on admission; symptoms resolved and liver enzymes returned to normal 7 weeks after discontinuation. No signs of hepatic failure at any time; aspartate aminotransferase fell rapidly while ALT remained elevated during 8 days of hospitalization. No fever, rash, or eosinophilia (peripheral eosinophil count 90 x 10^6/L). Abdominal CT consistent with fatty liver.

raw_record.support_text: Six cases of hepatotoxicity secondary to trazodone have been well described, one confirmed by inadvertent drug rechallenge. Three cases occurred within 9 weeks of starting treatment with a mixed cholestatic and hepatocellular histological pattern; two other cases developed jaundice after 7-8 months of use with liver function tests increased until 6 months after withdrawal (one showing a chronic active hepatitis pattern on histology); and one occurred after 18 months of use while on low-dose steroids. Liver injury was self-limited upon discontinuation. The mechanism seems immunoallergic/hypersensitivity given associated exanthema/rash or leukonychia, positive antimitochondrial antibody, eosinophils in liver specimens, and a rapid response on rechallenge.
raw_record.extra_details: Six well-described cases; one confirmed by inadvertent drug rechallenge. Latency 9 weeks to 18 months. Histology mixed cholestatic and hepatocellular; one case chronic active hepatitis (jaundice after 7-8 months, LFTs elevated up to 6 months post-withdrawal); one case after 18 months of use on low-dose steroids. Immunoallergic/hypersensitivity mechanism (exanthema, leukonychia, antimitochondrial antibody, eosinophils, rapid response on rechallenge). Liver injury self-limited on discontinuation. p49: main psychoactive metabolite is mCPP via CYP3A3/4 hydroxylation, further metabolized by polymorphic CYP2D6; poor metabolizers have higher mCPP steady-state concentrations; thioridazine (CYP2D6 inhibitor) increased mCPP plasma concentrations ~50%; the only fatal liver failure case involved combined trazodone and trifluoperazine (neuroleptic) treatment.

raw_record.support_text: A patient developed liver disease after beginning trazodone; liver tests returned to normal after she stopped the drug, and no other etiology was evident, which the authors state strongly suggests drug-induced hepatotoxicity. The authors also attribute her leukonychia to trazodone based on timing of onset and resolution, but this is not a liver-injury claim.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report: liver disease developed after starting trazodone, resolved on dechallenge, with no other evident etiology. Two previously reported cases of trazodone-induced hepatotoxicity are noted: one patient developed a rash and elevated hepatic enzymes without jaundice 3 weeks after starting the drug, and the other became jaundiced 2 weeks after starting trazodone; both recovered within several weeks of stopping the drug. Leukonychia was also attributed to the drug but is not a liver-injury finding. Authors advise that physicians be aware that hepatotoxicity can be caused by trazodone.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report a 67-yr-old man with primary Sjögren's syndrome who developed acute hepatitis 2 yr after a total cumulative dose of 40.5 g of cyclophosphamide (CYC), given as continuous low-dose oral therapy (100 mg/day reduced to 50 mg/day). They note that although hepatotoxicity is not uncommon during high-dose CYC therapy, hepatitis induced by low-dose treatment has rarely been described, and that in such cases hepatotoxicity occurs within the first 2-8 wk at 50-180 mg/day, whereas this case represents a cumulative low-dose hepatotoxic effect.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patient with primary Sjögren's syndrome; co-medicated with prednisolone 5 mg daily; continuous low-dose oral administration (100 mg/day for 6 months, then 50 mg/day, then 50 mg alternate days) with a total cumulative dose of 40.5 g; acute hepatitis developed after approximately 2 years of therapy.
raw_record.extra_details: Presented with progressive jaundice for 3 wk; deeply jaundiced on examination with no hepatomegaly. Labs: albumin 28 g/dl, alkaline phosphatase 213 U/L, SGOT 408 U/L, SGPT 269 U/L, gamma-GT 430 U/L, total bilirubin 506 umol/L with direct bilirubin 366 umol/L; normal clotting, no eosinophilia. Liver biopsy showed distorted acinar architecture, marked hepatocyte balloon degeneration, confluent zone 3 loss of hepatocytes, moderate cytoplasmic and canalicular cholestasis, and mixed acute/chronic portal inflammatory infiltrate, compatible with drug-induced acute hepatitis. ERCP and ultrasound normal; HAV/HBV/HCV and CMV/EBV/HSV serologies negative, AMA negative. Liver function normalized 6 wk after stopping CYC (dechallenge with resolution, no rechallenge reported).

Serum paracetamol concentrations were elevated in both mother and baby nine hours after ingestion, but the mother's liver enzymes and coagulation profile were normal.

raw_record.extra_details: Serum paracetamol 133 mg/l at 9 h post-ingestion falling to <0.1 mg/l by 32 h in the infant; INR 3 at admission, normalised at 48 h; hypoglycaemia blood glucose 2 mmol/l; bilirubin up to 99 mmol/l; AST up to 86 U/l; treated with intravenous N-acetylcysteine (150 mg/kg over 30 min, 50 mg/kg over 4 h, then 100 mg/kg/24 h until INR normal); infant mildly jaundiced on day 1, discharged well on day 7; mother had normal liver enzymes and coagulation.

raw_record.support_text: Benzbromarone is no longer commercially available in the USA and was withdrawn from the European market in 2003 due to the risk of severe hepatotoxicity. Case reports describe fulminant hepatitis associated with the use of standard doses of benzbromarone (100 mg/day) over short periods (three months). raw_record.extra_details: Withdrawn from the European market in 2003 and no longer commercially available in the USA due to risk of severe hepatotoxicity. Case reports of fulminant hepatitis at standard therapeutic dose of 100 mg/day over about three months. In Brazil sales are permitted by ANVISA and benzbromarone is reported to have a safety profile identical to sulfinpyrazone. Benzbromarone is metabolized in the liver by cytochrome P450 and should be used with caution in patients with hepatobiliary diseases.

raw_record.support_text: Benzbromarone (BBR) was withdrawn from many countries in 2003 as a result of 11 unexplained cases of hepatotoxicity, of which nine patients died of fulminant hepatic necrosis. Subsequent analysis effectively excluded other causes of liver failure, and all patients who were re-challenged with BBR developed hepatotoxicity within weeks of restarting the drug.
raw_record.extra_details: Benzbromarone (BBR) and its metabolite 6-hydroxybenzbromarone block renal uric acid reabsorption by inhibiting URAT1; used for gout, particularly in renal impairment. Withdrawn in many countries in 2003 after 11 unexplained hepatotoxicity cases (refs 50-53); nine of 11 patients died of fulminant hepatic necrosis; other causes of liver failure effectively excluded; all rechallenged patients developed hepatotoxicity within weeks of restarting.

raw_record.support_text: Benzbromarone is a powerful uricosuric drug; after reports of several serious hepatotoxicities, benzbromarone was withdrawn by Sanofi in 2003. It is mainly used in Japan, China, Singapore and other Asian countries for gout and hyperuricemia.
raw_record.extra_details: Benzbromarone is a uricosuric agent used at ~50-200 mg/d for gout/hyperuricemia. Withdrawn by Sanofi in 2003 after reports of several serious hepatotoxicities. raw_record.extra_details: Hepatic necrosis was widespread centrilobular involving zones 2 and 3 with macro- and micro-vesicular fatty change; timescale of 5 days from exposure to jaundice; pyrexia was prominent; initial mild rise in aspartate aminotransferase followed by delayed grossly elevated aminotransferases, elevated bilirubin, and prolonged prothrombin time; pattern associated with halothane hepatitis. Injury is very rare; the authors conclude isoflurane is not free of the hepatotoxic effects of halothane, occurring much less frequently.

raw_record.support_text: Paracetamol is frequently taken as an overdose in suicidal attempts, and hepatic damage of all grades of severity, from minor to fulminant hepatic failure, may result, with bleeding often being a major problem and not infrequently the direct cause of death. Low clotting factor levels were attributed in part to impaired hepatic synthesis and increased consumption from intravascular coagulation.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose (including suicidal overdose) in adults.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatic damage of all grades from minor to fulminant hepatic failure. In 66 patients, early coagulation changes included low clotting factors II, V and VII within 24 hours; prothrombin time ratio exceeded 2.2 within 30 hours of overdose in all patients who eventually died (9 deaths in the series), and the ratio was less than this in those developing only moderate hepatic damage. Severe hepatic damage was defined as plasma bilirubin >69 umol/l and was the group from which all 9 deaths occurred. A controlled trial of fresh frozen plasma (300 ml every 6 hr) in 20 patients with prothrombin time ratio >2.2 reduced the maximum prothrombin time ratio abnormality but did not reduce morbidity or mortality. Coagulation disturbance was of short duration, with prothrombin time ratio returning to normal within one week of overdose.

raw_record.support_text: Paracetamol is the commonest drug ingested in overdose in the UK. In the early stage of poisoning paracetamol rarely results in specific clinical features, and the risk of liver damage can only be predicted from the plasma paracetamol concentration, so estimation of plasma paracetamol concentrations is important in all patients presenting with a history of a paracetamol overdose.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose setting; in the case series, three patients with a staggered overdose presented more than 24 hours after ingestion.
raw_record.extra_details: Risk of liver damage is dose/concentration-related and predicted from plasma paracetamol concentration; three of 26 patients presenting after a staggered overdose developed severe hepatotoxicity and were treated with NAC on arrival, though presentation at >24 h after ingestion reduces NAC efficacy. In 11 of 99 patients presenting within four hours of ingestion with paracetamol levels 150-200 mg/l at four hours, liver function tests, renal function and INR were normal at discharge.

After onset of toxicity, valproate was stopped after a median of 7 days in the L-carnitine group and 8 days in the untreated group. raw_record.extra_details: Cohort of 92 children with valproate-induced hepatotoxicity collected from US, German, and other centers; valproate median dose 39 mg/kg/d (treated) and 43 mg/kg/d (untreated), duration median 81 vs 72 days. raw_record.support_text: Valproate-induced hepatotoxicity is described as rare, but often fatal, and is attributed to direct disruption of mitochondrial processes. It is heralded by nonspecific symptoms such as lethargy, nausea/vomiting, or worsening seizures, and occurs more frequently in at-risk populations such as mentally retarded individuals, young children, and those taking multiple drugs. One proposed mechanism is drug-induced carnitine deficiency.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Reported more frequently in at-risk populations including mentally retarded individuals, young children, and patients taking multiple drugs; most children appeared malnourished (69% <25th percentile for weight, 38% <5th percentile).
raw_record.extra_details: Retrospective inception cohort from the International Registry for Adverse Reactions to Valproate; 92 patients with severe, symptomatic, valproate-induced hepatotoxicity (90 with epilepsy, 2 with bipolar disorder); outcome was hepatic survival (deceased and liver transplant combined as terminal hepatic failure). Valproate stopped after a median of 7 days in L-carnitine-treated and 8 days in untreated patients. 48% of 42 L-carnitine-treated patients survived vs 10% of 50 treated with supportive care only (p < 0.001).

raw_record.support_text: The authors report the first biopsy-proven case of efavirenz-induced hepatitis. Hepatitis and hepatic laboratory abnormalities resolved after the entire antiretroviral regimen was stopped, and although dechallenge was not with efavirenz alone, the authors state that the causal role of efavirenz is obvious because zidovudine and lamivudine had been taken for 2 years without problems and efavirenz was the only new drug. They concluded that HCV infection played a limited role because HCV RNA remained negative throughout the course of hepatitis and no HCV-related abnormalities were found on liver biopsy.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Concomitant HIV and HCV (serotype 1) infection; continued co-treatment with zidovudine and lamivudine; dechallenge involved stopping the entire antiretroviral regimen rather than efavirenz alone; initial supratherapeutic intake of 1200 mg/day for the first 3 days before settling at the prescribed 600 mg/day.
raw_record.extra_details: 45-year-old man with HIV infection; hepatitis and cutaneous rash developed within 4 weeks of switching indinavir to efavirenz (600 mg/day). Symptoms: nausea, right upper quadrant pain, rash, fever (38°C). Laboratory: ALT 718 IU/l (normal <38), AST 336 IU/l, GGT 1180 IU/l rising to 1611, ALP 684 IU/l rising to 928, eosinophilia (460 to 1110/mm3), bilirubin 18 µmol/l (no jaundice). Biopsy showed dense portal infiltrate of histiocytes, lymphocytes and eosinophilic polymorphonuclears with some apoptotic bodies; no interlobular bile duct damage and no microvesicular steatosis. Liver tests and eosinophilia returned to normal within 1 month after stopping antiretroviral treatment. Autoantibodies (antimitochondrial, anti-smooth muscle, anti-endoplasmic reticulum, anti-LKM, anti-nuclear) negative; HCV RNA negative throughout. No rechallenge attempted because of possible immuno-allergic mechanism. Efavirenz is a non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (1,4-dihydro-2H-3,1-benzoxazin-2-one), extensively metabolized by P450 cytochromes to 8-hydroxylated metabolites then conjugated as glucuronides.

raw_record.extra_details: Acute hepatic failure occurred as a severe TACE complication attributed to high-dose CDDP. Reduced tumor growth was seen but no overall survival benefit in the cited randomized trials.

raw_record.support_text: Four patients are described in whom anicteric hepatitis appeared to be related to the use of nitrofurantoin. All had increased serum transaminase levels, hypergammaglobulinaemia, and liver biopsies suggestive of chronic active hepatitis; three showed cirrhotic features and two had circulating albumin-IgG-complexes ('tailing-albumin'). Serum transaminases became normal within weeks of drug withdrawal, while hypergammaglobulinaemia and biopsy findings persisted during 2-6 months of observation. One patient was re-challenged with nitrofurantoin, which resulted in recurrence of elevated serum transaminases after nine weeks of medication.

raw_record.support_text: The authors conclude that long-term use of nitrofurantoin in moderate doses in patients with normal kidney function may cause or trigger chronic hepatitis. They cite a challenge (rechallenge) with the drug in patient no. 1 and rapid normalization of serum transaminases in all patients after withdrawal, together with no elevated transaminase levels in a well-matched control group, as strong evidence. Liver biopsies in all four patients showed chronic aggressive hepatitis with piecemeal necrosis and mononuclear/eosinophilic infiltration, with signs of developing cirrhosis in three patients; none were jaundiced and alkaline phosphatase was normal.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Long-term (chronic) use in moderate doses in patients with normal kidney function; exact dose not specified; none of the patients were jaundiced and clinical picture was not severe.
raw_record.extra_details: Four patients; biopsies taken at maximal transaminase increase; first biopsies showed enlarged portal tracts with mononuclear and eosinophilic polymorphonuclear infiltration, piecemeal necrosis, irregular lobular margins, and swollen/eosinophilic hepatocytes; three patients (nos. 2, 3, 4) also showed lobular architectural irregularity with fibrous septa and signs of developing cirrhosis; patient no. 1 showed chronic aggressive hepatitis in follow-up biopsies 3 and 6 months after withdrawal. Rapid normalization of serum transaminases after drug withdrawal; rechallenge with drug in patient no. 1 confirmed the association; matched control group had no elevated transaminase levels. Hypoalbuminemia and hypergammaglobulinemia developed during treatment; normal eosinophile counts peripherally but eosinophilic granulocytes in liver biopsies. All but patient no. 2 (who had pulmonary infiltrates) had hepatic reaction without other obvious toxic manifestations.

raw_record.support_text: The paper introduces the salient features of quinidine-induced liver injury from earlier reports: fever, a mixed type of hepatic injury, rapid return of enzyme tests to normal on withdrawal of quinidine, and a shortening of the latency period on reexposure with fever and disordered liver function appearing sooner and after progressively smaller doses; these features resemble those of a hypersensitivity type of liver injury caused by other hepatotoxic agents. The authors describe a patient whose clinical course after quinidine ingestion showed all of these features and additionally prolonged hepatocellular damage on sulfobromophthalein (Bromsulphalein) testing.

raw_record.support_text: In a prospective cohort of 224 tuberculosis patients treated with an isoniazid-based antituberculosis regimen, 33 (14.7%) were diagnosed with drug-induced hepatitis by the International Consensus Meeting definition. During isoniazid rechallenge, 14 of these patients (6.3%) developed serum ALT >3x ULN, which the authors classified as clinically significant isoniazid-induced hepatitis, prompting replacement of isoniazid with streptomycin or ofloxacin; the other 19 had transient hepatic dysfunction. Slow acetylator NAT2 status and older age were significant risk factors for isoniazid-induced hepatitis.

raw_record.extra_details: Isoniazid rechallenge confirmed causality: 14 patients (6.3%) had ALT >3x ULN during rechallenge and were classified as clinically significant hepatitis; 19 (8.5%) had ALT <=3x ULN (transient hepatic dysfunction) and continued isoniazid safely. Peak ALT 393.6 ± 353.9 U/L (range 98-1609) and peak total bilirubin 3.25 ± 3.57 mg/dL (range 0.5-20.2) in hepatitis cases. Hepatitis risk was higher in slow acetylators (26.4% vs 11.1%; OR 2.87, 95% CI 1.32-6.23), and slow acetylators had higher peak ALT/AST and were more likely to exceed 3x ULN on rechallenge (64.3% vs 26.3%; P=.040). Multivariate OR for slow acetylator 3.66 (1.58-8.49) and age OR 1.09 (1.04-1.14). Rapid acetylator was protective (OR 0.35, 95% CI 0.16-0.76).

raw_record.support_text: Applying the Karch-Lasagna algorithm and Paris Consensus criteria, the causal relationship between the liver injury in this 56-year-old woman and treatment with tamoxifen is classified as probable, based on a compatible chronological relationship between drug administration and altered liver enzymes, absence of other potential causes of liver disease (alcohol, prior chronic hepatopathy, hepatotropic viruses), and persistence of the liver changes when all other medications except tamoxifen were withdrawn. Lab values: total bilirubin 2.5 mg/dl, AST 199 U/l, ALT 184 U/l; later GGT 331 U/l and alkaline phosphatase 483 U/l. Discussion notes that published tamoxifen hepatotoxicity cases show two predominant injury patterns: cholestasis with or without cytolysis and steatohepatitis, including cholestatic jaundice without cytolysis, cholestasis with cytolysis, a case of hepatic peliosis, a case of fatty liver with liver failure and death, and several cases of non-alcoholic steatohepatitis; additional cases collected by pharmacovigilance systems with little detail.

APAP levels of 300 µg/mL (4 h) referenced in risk analysis nomogram; cases with SGOT ≥ 1000 IU were plotted. Toxicity follows a threshold effect related to plasma level; height above threshold did not further refine severity. Hepatic damage occurs at ~70% glutathione depletion; ~4% of an APAP dose converts to N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine (NAPQI), with calculated ~15.9 g APAP absorbed in a 70 kg human to reach threshold toxicity (~0.635 g NAPQI). NAC (N-acetylcysteine) administration discussed as the antidote, not as a cause.

raw_record.support_text: The paper concludes that metformin can induce hepatic injury (hepatocellular and/or cholestatic), and notes that metformin hepatotoxicity has rarely been reported, with possible mechanisms being direct, idiosyncratic, or a drug–drug interaction leading to acute hepatocellular and/or cholestatic jaundice.
raw_record.extra_details: Search of PubMed yielded six published metformin hepatotoxicity reports (Table 2): two cases of acute hepatitis, two cases of cholestasis, and two cases of mixed hepatocellular-cholestatic injury; the paper's own patient is the third reported case of mixed hepatocellular and cholestatic liver injury. raw_record.support_text: A case of metformin-induced liver injury is described in a patient with no other potential hepatotoxic drug use and no underlying liver disease. Discontinuation of metformin led to quick recovery of liver function within 2 weeks, with the clinical presentation, laboratory results, and temporal relationship between metformin initiation and the event supporting the diagnosis of metformin-induced liver injury, corroborated by a Council for International Organizations of Medical Sciences/Roussel Uclaf Causality Assessment Method (CIOMS/RUCAM) score of 8.
raw_record.extra_details: RUCAM/CIOMS causality score of 8; ALT, AST, and ALP values were reported on presentation, hospital days 2-4, and 2 weeks later. The paper notes metformin appeared beneficial in nonalcoholic fatty liver disease and ameliorated methotrexate-induced hepatotoxicity in animal models.

raw_record.support_text: Triazolam (Halcion), a benzodiazepine used widely in Japan for insomnia, is reported to rarely cause hepatotoxicity identified as cholestasis. raw_record.extra_details: 64-year-old woman with insomnia occasionally took 0.25 mg/day oral triazolam; presented with appetite loss, fatigue, jaundice (total bilirubin 6.1 mg/dl, AST 1066 IU/l, ALT 1272 IU/l), progressing to hepatic encephalopathy grade III and fulminant hepatic failure. Authors note cholestasis is a rare triad recorded hepatotoxicity pattern for triazolam.

Although the patient had also taken phenprocoumon and estrogens, these drugs had been used for several years with repeatedly normal previous liver tests, so they were excluded as causes. The WHO database of adverse drug reactions contains several reports of hepatitis under rofecoxib, hinting to a causal relationship between serious liver injury and rofecoxib.

Severe cholestasis with pruritus was treated with three sessions of extracorporal albumin dialysis (MARS, 8 h each, mean flow 80 ml/min) with marked improvement; symptoms and labs resolved ~10 weeks after ceasing MARS. Tamoxifen also implicated in porphyria cutanea tarda (PCT) in this patient (urinary uroporphyrins 25,200 nmol/L, falling from 1570 to 359 nmol/mmol creatinine after stopping tamoxifen); PCT itself is not treated as a liver-injury phenotype here.

Case 2: 49-year-old woman, mirtazapine 45 mg/d for 1 year, malaise, progressive jaundice, tea-colored urine; labs albumin 40 g/L; bilirubin 140 µmol/L; ALP 140 U/L; ALT 550 U/L; AST 434 U/L; GGT 57 U/L; PT 18 s; negative for HAV IgM, HBsAg, HCV Ab, HEV IgM, EBV, HSV, CMV, autoimmune markers (AMA, ASMA), normal IgA/IgG/IgM, copper/ceruloplasmin/iron/transferrin normal, normal liver ultrasound. raw_record.support_text: The paper states that an increase in liver enzymes is common in rheumatoid arthritis patients on methotrexate (MTX), though these elevations are often mild and do not require discontinuation of treatment. An analysis of 3808 RA patients treated an average of 55.8 months in 27 prospective studies found that 769 (20.2%) had at least one episode of raised liver enzyme and only 3.7% stopped MTX because of liver toxicity; another series (Khabbazi et al.) reported liver enzyme elevation in 108/809 (13.3%) patients, with only 0.5% requiring permanent MTX discontinuation.

Other studies cited: Khabbazi et al. 809 patients (13.3% liver enzyme elevation; 0.5% permanent discontinuation), Bologna et al. 56/452 (12.4%) with elevated liver enzymes leading to 63 (13.9%) discontinuing for toxicity. raw_record.support_text: The laxative (phenolisatin) hepatitis, which runs under the mask of various liver and biliary diseases, is only reliably unmasked by the rechallenge test with phenolisatin. Glutamate dehydrogenase (GLDH) proved a particularly sensitive parameter, and transaminases (GOT, GPT) generally supported the proof by clear activity increases; bilirubin elevation was not obligatory. The paper reports 14 female patients with phenolisatin-induced liver diseases, whose histologic findings ranged from periportal liver fibrosis to advanced postnecrotic liver cirrhosis and scarring liver, with chronic-active hepatitis among the diagnostic forms.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: All 14 reported cases were female; onset followed chronic long-term oral laxative use of 2 to 20 years; re-exposure (rechallenge) confirmed the diagnosis.
raw_record.extra_details: Rechallenge with 2 x 10 mg triacetyl-diphenolisatin on two consecutive days produced rises in GLDH (particularly sensitive), GOT and GPT; bilirubin elevation was not obligatory. Histologic spectrum included chronic-aggressive hepatitis (with transition to cirrhosis), acute recurrent and protracted hepatitis, chronic-persistent hepatitis, periportal liver fibrosis, postnecrotic scarring liver/cirrhosis, and one case of chronic-aggressive hepatitis with cholestasis (Fall 10, allegedly on oxyphenisatin-free laxatives). In six of ten examined cases low-titer antibodies against nuclei and smooth muscle were found by immunofluorescence; five of 14 were treated with immunosuppressives and/or glucocorticoids before the final diagnosis. Symptoms resembled acute/chronic liver or gallbladder disease. Before publication all 14 patients were fully investigated in hospital with entirely normal laboratory findings and histologically inactive stage. Reported hospitalizations and estimated total costs (e.g., 150,000 DM in Fall 1); some cases were reported as infectious disease or recognized as occupational disease, and some underwent cholecystectomy.

Two days later ALT had risen to 237 U/L, ALP to 440 U/L and bilirubin to 41 µmol/L. Acitretin was stopped and ALT returned to normal over 5 days; ALP peaked at 679 U/L and remained elevated at 191 U/L 6 months later, indicating acitretin-induced hepatotoxicity. The same episode also involved agranulocytosis/neutropenia and subsequently total scalp alopecia.
raw_record.extra_details: Acitretin 25 mg twice daily for erythrodermic/pustular psoriasis. ALT rose from 12 to 237 U/L, ALP from 93 to 440 U/L, bilirubin from 8 to 41 µmol/L within 2 days; after stopping, ALT normalized over 5 days, ALP peaked at 679 U/L and remained elevated at 191 U/L at 6 months. raw_record.support_text: The clinical course of acetaminophen toxicity is described, with Phase 3 (72-96 hours post ingestion) characterized by hepatic necrosis including jaundice, coagulation defects, renal failure and hepatic encephalopathy. raw_record.extra_details: Acetaminophen is metabolized mainly in the liver; ~5% oxidized by P450 (primarily CYP2E1) to the reactive electrophile NAPQI, which binds glutathione to a nontoxic mercapturic acid conjugate. Case demonstrated early hepatic failure within 24 hours post-overdose, with rising enzymes, elevated bilirubin (peak total 21.9 mg/dL at 72h), prolonged prothrombin time, hepatic encephalopathy and renal failure. raw_record.support_text: Jaundice from chlorpromazine usually runs a self-limited course briefer than that of viral hepatitis, and during the acute course liver biopsies usually show only minimal hepatocellular damage. raw_record.extra_details: Chlorpromazine jaundice is attributed to drug allergy; the paper concludes the probability that jaundice is due to drug allergy is high. Nine of eleven challenged patients demonstrated objective evidence of sensitivity for up to seventeen months after an attack. Other reports also reproduced jaundice upon challenge. Jaundice can be mild (serum bilirubin 2 mg/100 ml or less) and short (3-7 days) and may occur without clinical jaundice (liver enlargement/tenderness, fever, abnormal liver function tests, histologic 'allergic cholangiolitis'). Acute liver biopsies show minimal hepatocellular damage. After an estimated four million treated patients, 26 deaths in jaundiced patients were reported, with the drug thought responsible in 13; most fatal cases were complicated by agranulocytosis, heart failure, possible viral hepatitis, cirrhosis, or recent surgery, and one death with acute hepatic necrosis occurred in an 81-year-old. Jaundice runs a self-limited course briefer than viral hepatitis. Animal toxicity studies failed to reveal hepatic damage, but continued use in sensitized patients appears to lead to permanent toxic liver changes.

Ethionamide was stopped and treatment changed to isoniazid and PAS; symptoms disappeared and liver function tests returned to normal. In Case III (also on isoniazid) jaundice was noted with abnormal LFTs (bilirubin 5.8 mg/100 ml, thymol turbidity 6 units/ml, alkaline phosphatase 22.8 K.A. units) and urine showing bile and excess urobilin/urobilinogen; jaundice resolved within a month and LFTs normalized within six weeks after stopping drugs. raw_record.support_text: A letter to the editor reports two patients who had received phenelzine (a monoamine oxidase inhibitor for depression) for 4 months at 22.5 mg and 60 mg twice daily, respectively, and who required emergency orthotopic liver transplantation because of fulminant hepatic failure. Phenelzine-induced fulminant hepatic failure was diagnosed after biochemical, serologic, immunologic, hematologic, and histologic studies ruled out other known causes of liver damage. The cases fit the pattern of hydrazine-derivative-induced hepatotoxic injury: delayed toxic effect, no evidence of hypersensitivity-mediated injury, and predominantly hepatocellular rather than cholestatic damage. The paper states the mechanism by which a hydrazine derivative such as phenelzine causes hepatic injury appears to be idiosyncratic, and notes that advanced age, simultaneous enzymatic induction by alcohol or other drugs, and coincident viral infection may play roles, while the relation with the rapid acetylator phenotype remains controversial.

Presented as severe phenelzine-induced hepatitis; pattern matches hydrazine-derivative-induced injury: delayed toxic effect, no hypersensitivity, predominantly hepatocellular (rather than cholestatic) histology. Potential contributing roles of advanced age, enzymatic induction by alcohol/other drugs, and coincident viral infection proposed; possible relation with rapid acetylator phenotype noted as controversial.

Histologically this fatty liver was characterized as a more severe (schwerere) liver injury, yet it was not reliably detectable by any of the usual liver function tests and did not clearly manifest clinically; it appeared reversible within 10–12 weeks after discontinuing the drug. The fatty liver could not be reproduced in animal experiments, which the authors interpreted as the agent promoting/supporting an inherent tendency to fatty liver in human tuberculosis; no liver necroses were observed, and no fatty liver was found in their streptomycin-treated patients.

raw_record.extra_details: Fatty liver appeared regularly around the 10th–12th treatment week and was reversible within 10–12 weeks after drug withdrawal; in one case, relaparotomy 12 weeks after discontinuation showed a macroscopically normal red-brown liver, whereas laparotomy in the 11th treatment week had shown clear fatty liver. The injury was not reliably detected by usual liver function tests and was not clearly clinically manifest; associated anorexia and possible protein hypersensitivity were of unclear relation. The finding could not be reproduced in animal experiments; no liver necroses were observed in this series.

raw_record.support_text: The paper describes a case of granulomatous hepatitis probably due to the administration of aprindine. Although drug rechallenge was not done, the hepatic damage appeared within 6 weeks of initiating aprindine therapy and resolved rapidly after drug withdrawal, which the authors state is suggestive of aprindine-induced liver toxicity. The patient had received no other medication during the past year, had no history of liver disease or sarcoidosis/tuberculosis, and was negative for HBV/HCV/HAV markers.
raw_record.extra_details: Granulomatous hepatitis is the named phenotype. Drug rechallenge was not performed. Hepatic damage appeared within 6 weeks of initiating aprindine therapy and resolved after withdrawal. A liver biopsy 5 days after withdrawal showed moderate inflammatory infiltration consisting predominantly of eosinophils and granulomata in most portal tracts and lobules, without caseous necrosis or fibrosis; 6 months later granulomata had disappeared and fibrosis was present in expanded portal tracts. No competing medications, liver disease history, sarcoidosis, tuberculosis, hypotension, blood transfusion, or HBV/HCV/HAV markers were present. The paper also cites at least eight previously published cases of aprindine-induced hepatitis with mild to moderate clinical illness occurring within 12 days to 6 weeks of starting therapy and resolving after drug withdrawal, with rechallenge reproducing hepatitis in all four rechallenged patients; no granulomatous hepatitis was identified in the four prior biopsied cases.

raw_record.support_text: The paper describes disulfiram-induced hepatitis reported in humans: Keeffe and Smith first reported a case in 1974, Ranek and Andreason reported six additional cases in 1977 of whom five died, and Kristensen reported toxic liver damage in a nonalcoholic female treated with disulfiram for nickel dermatitis who developed liver-enzyme elevation upon rechallenge. Incidence of disulfiram-induced fatal hepatitis is reportedly 1 in 30,000 treated patients per year, and an analysis of reports to the Danish committee on adverse drug reactions implicated disulfiram in 5 of 52 (10%) drug-related fatalities.

raw_record.extra_details: Onset of hepatotoxicity occurs within 4-6 weeks (range 2-24 weeks) of starting treatment. Symptoms include fatigue, headache, fever, pruritus, rash, myalgia, malaise, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, jaundice, light stools, dark urine, and hepatomegaly; symptoms usually resolve within 2 weeks of stopping, and liver function may need up to 12 weeks to normalize. Biopsy may show predominantly hepatocellular degeneration with focal or extensive hepatocellular necrosis and portal/periportal eosinophilic infiltration. Disulfiram-induced liver failure requiring liver transplantation first reported in 1989 (Vanjak et al), with 3 total transplant cases reported; the paper's case is the first reported pediatric OLT for disulfiram-induced fulminant hepatic failure. Most reports suggest an idiosyncratic hypersensitivity reaction as the primary mechanism; an alternative proposed mechanism is carbon disulfide-induced hepatic injury from covalent binding of electrophilic reactive metabolites.

Vanishing bile duct syndrome was suspected but not confirmed. A prior published case of rofecoxib cholestatic hepatitis resolved after MARS therapy. A similar case of acute renal failure also occurred in this patient.

raw_record.support_text: The authors state that drug-induced hepatitis and drug-induced acute interstitial nephritis are recognized complications of NSAIDs, and that COX-2 inhibitors have been implicated in prior case reports of AIN and hepatitis, but simultaneous presentation of both with a single therapeutic agent had previously been reported once with clometacin and never with a COX-2 inhibitor. Given the temporal sequence, clinical findings, and liver and renal biopsy histology, they believe there is good evidence to implicate rofecoxib as the causative agent of this combined drug-induced hepatitis and acute interstitial nephritis in the patient. The liver biopsy demonstrated zone 3 cholestasis, a mixed periportal infiltrate of neutrophils and eosinophils, and mild bile duct proliferation; hepatic dysfunction and cholestasis resolved over weeks and liver function tests fully recovered within months.

Authors note this combined presentation had previously been reported once with clometacin and never with a COX-2 inhibitor.

Jaundice and malaise/anorexia began on postoperative day 6; markedly abnormal liver biochemistry (ALT 2188 U/L, AST 425 U/L, GGT 130 U/L, ALP 149 U/L, total bilirubin 118 umol/L); INR 2.29 on POD 8 and bilirubin 214 umol/L on POD 12; stage I/IV hepatic encephalopathy on POD 10; treated with methylprednisone 60 mg IV daily for 5 days; recovered and discharged on POD 21. Patient had advanced age and extra-hepatic malignancy and was not a transplant candidate.

raw_record.support_text: Repaglinide is a fast, short-acting meglitinide analog antidiabetic drug approved for type 2 diabetes. In rare cases elevated liver enzymes have been noted. The authors report a patient who developed cholestatic hepatitis while taking repaglinide.
raw_record.extra_details: First published report of cholestatic hepatitis related to repaglinide. A 72-year-old man with type 2 diabetes took repaglinide 1 mg/day, increased to 2 mg/day one month before presentation; presented with 2-week history of itching and jaundice and was admitted. Labs: AST 83 U/L (normal <37), ALT 183 U/L (normal <40), ALP 307 U/L (normal <136), GGT 303 U/L (normal <85), total bilirubin 12.2 mg/dl with direct bilirubin 9.4 mg/dl, serum creatinine 1.3 mg/dl. No toxic habits and denied other drugs/herbal remedies. Viral serology and autoantibody screening negative; MR cholangiography showed no pathology. Liver biopsy showed expanded portal areas with mild bile duct proliferation and moderate inflammatory infiltrate (mainly lymphocytes with some eosinophils) and hepatocyte ballooning. After repaglinide discontinuation laboratory findings normalized within a month. Causality strongly supported by temporal eligibility, exclusion of alternative causes, histologic features, and rapid improvement after drug withdrawal. Presence of some eosinophils in the inflammatory infiltrate suggests a possible immune mechanism.

raw_record.extra_details: Paper concludes the reproducibility, exposure dependency, high incidence and short latency of human trabectedin hepatotoxicity indicate an intrinsic (predictable) hepatotoxic drug. Increases in transaminases (grade 3 or 4 in 68% of subjects at the recommended 1500 µg m⁻² 24 h-schedule dose) are dose/exposure dependent, start 2–5 days after administration, peak at day 5–9 and resolve within 4 weeks; ASAT, ALAT, AP and bilirubin elevations observed. raw_record.support_text: In the case of fialuridine (FIAU), a thymidine analog, the potential for hepatotoxicity was not appreciated during preclinical evaluation. Subjects treated with FIAU for 9–13 weeks developed severe and sometimes fatal hepatotoxicity associated with lactic acidosis, occurring in the intended population with Hepatitis B. The hepatotoxic syndrome (hepatic steatosis, increased bilirubinemia, increased prothrombin time, and lactic acidosis) was attributed to mitochondrial DNA damage in hepatocytes involving thymidine kinase 2.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Fialuridine was administered to subjects with chronic Hepatitis B (the intended treatment population) for 9-13 weeks.
raw_record.extra_details: Preclinical evaluation in healthy rodent, dog, and nonhuman primates did not reveal hepatotoxicity; the syndrome of delayed toxicity (hepatic steatosis, increased bilirubinemia, increased prothrombin time, lactic acidosis) was reproduced in woodchucks infected with hepatitis. Mechanism attributed to mitochondrial DNA in hepatocytes with high affinity for thymidine kinase 2, leading to mitochondrial enzyme mutations, defective oxidative phosphorylation, electron leakage, superoxide anion production, and increased oxidative stress. Injury was severe and sometimes fatal.

raw_record.support_text: Liver needle biopsy showed bile canalicular dilation and proliferation, moderately expanded portal tracts infiltrated by lymphocytes and plasma cells, and bile canalicular obstruction, intracytoplasmic bile retention and confluent necrotic foci; these findings were considered to be due to drug-induced liver injury. Combined hepatocellular and cholestatic features: histology showed bile canalicular dilation/proliferation, portal lymphocytic and plasma cell infiltration, bile canalicular obstruction, intracytoplasmic bile retention and confluent necrotic foci; marker eosinophilia was present. Dechallenge (stop of paroxetine only, other medications continued) led to normalization of hepatic and cholestatic enzymes and bilirubin within 14 weeks. Abdominal ultrasound, CT, endoscopy and ERCP ruled out biliary/pancreatic abnormalities; no viral damage seen. Discussion notes six prior paroxetine hepatotoxicity case reports, four of which were hepatocellular and mixed-type (hepatocellular and cholestatic) damage.

Clinically this was painless cholestatic jaundice with ascites and progressive hepatic insufficiency; two patients slowly improved. A transient asymptomatic liver enzyme elevation pattern was seen in 19 patients. Fatal in 8/10 (8.6%); 2 recovered. The median dose for single paracetamol ingestion was 345 mg/kg (range 91-645). Two patients who took supratherapeutic doses (97 and 127 mg/kg) showed significant hepatotoxicity without encephalopathy and survived. 27% with significant hepatotoxicity received N-acetylcysteine treatment despite paracetamol level being less than the nomogram treatment line.

Mortality was 27%, with 8% undergoing liver transplant.

raw_record.support_text: The authors describe a case of chloroform (halogenated hydrocarbon) intoxication diagnosed by an abdominal radiograph showing radiopaque material in the bowel, with associated hepatotoxicity. This is reported as the first documented case of chloroform ingestion with both diagnostic radiopacity and hepatotoxicity. Hepatotoxicity occurred on post-ingestion day 3, and liver enzyme elevation reached peak levels on post-ingestion day 5; the patient was treated with haemoperfusion, activated charcoal, laxatives, and N-acetylcysteine, improved from hepatic dysfunction, and was discharged on post-ingestion day 11.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Acute oral ingestion (overdose) of an unknown substance in a single patient presenting comatose with suppressed respirations; treated with haemoperfusion, activated charcoal, and laxatives.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of a single emergency-department patient; hepatotoxicity first appeared on post-ingestion day 3 with peak liver enzyme elevation on post-ingestion day 5; patient received N-acetylcysteine and supportive care, recovered from hepatic dysfunction, and was discharged without complication on post-ingestion day 11. Chloroform is a radiopaque halogenated hydrocarbon visible on abdominal radiograph; oral chloroform poisoning is rare.

raw_record.support_text: In a US ALFSG prospective study of 275 consecutive patients with acetaminophen (ACM)-related acute liver failure (ALF), the annual incidence of ALF due to ACM rose from 28% in 1998 to 51% in 2004. Nearly 50% of cases were nonintentional 'therapeutic misadventures', with 48% of ALF-ACM cases nonintentional; most were taking excessive doses, about 50% of the nonintentional group consuming 4-10 g/day and 7% of the entire cohort ingesting less than 4 g/day. The majority (81%) of nonintentional overdose patients had an acute or chronic painful medical condition and 63% were taking a narcotic-ACM analgesic chronically.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Exposure limited to overdose context, including both intentional and nonintentional 'therapeutic misadventure' supratherapeutic doses; some patients taking narcotic-ACM combination analgesics.
raw_record.extra_details: US Acute Liver Failure Study Group (ALFSG) prospective data, 275 consecutive ACM-related ALF patients. Annual ALF incidence due to ACM rose from 28% in 1998 to 51% in 2004. 48% were nonintentional overdose cases; ~50% of these consumed 4-10 g/day and 7% of the entire cohort ingested <4 g/day. 81% of nonintentional patients had acute or chronic painful conditions, 63% used narcotic-ACM analgesics chronically. Nonintentional patients had lower serum ACM (median 106 vs 554 µmol/L, P<0.001), lower ALT (3319 vs 5326 U/L, P<0.001), and more advanced encephalopathy (53% vs 39% grade 3-4). Outcomes: 9% vs 7% required liver transplantation, 28% vs 29% fatal. 87% of intentional and 95% of nonintentional patients received N-acetylcysteine. Reference to 60,000 intentional ACM overdose cases/year in the US with 500 fatalities.

raw_record.support_text: A diagnosis of rofecoxib-induced cholestatic hepatitis was made. Rofecoxib was discontinued and ursodeoxycholic acid 1500 mg/day was introduced; within two months the patient's liver biochemistry normalized and symptoms resolved, and at six months the patient was asymptomatic with normal liver biochemistry. The patient had jaundice with ALT 1826 U/L, ALP 741 U/L, gamma-glutamyltransferase 897 U/L, total bilirubin 242 µmol/L and elevated serum bile acids (279 µmol/L); a liver biopsy showed mild hepatocellular necrosis, moderate interface hepatitis and isolated eosinophils without evident cholestasis or fibrosis.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patient had underlying lymphoma and was subsequently treated with adjuvant radiotherapy; rofecoxib was used at therapeutic dose in a general adult setting.
raw_record.extra_details: Diagnosis framed as 'rofecoxib-induced cholestatic hepatitis'. Dechallenge was positive with resolution of symptoms and normalization of liver biochemistry within two months. Liver biopsy showed mononuclear infiltration of portal triads and perivenular areas, mild hepatocellular necrosis, moderate interface hepatitis and isolated eosinophils; histologic cholestasis was not evident despite the cholestatic biochemical label. Ursodeoxycholic acid 1500 mg/day was given as treatment. Viral hepatitis serologies (A, B, C, EBV, CMV) and autoantibodies (ANA, smooth muscle) were negative.

raw_record.support_text: The paper discusses flutamide-induced hepatotoxicity in prostate cancer patients, proposing that clinical flutamide hepatotoxicity occurs when CYP1A2 inhibition, reactive-metabolite production by extensive metabolizers, and lowered GSH content coincide. Preliminary clinical results from 11 prostate cancer patients showed that those who developed severe hepatitis with flutamide had lower CYP1A2 enzyme activity than the normal population, and higher flutamide and lower OH-flutamide plasma concentrations have been reported in patients with flutamide-induced hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Prostate cancer patients taking flutamide as an antiandrogen; susceptibility proposed to involve lower CYP1A2 activity (assessed by caffeine test), concurrent CYP1A2-inhibiting medication, and lowered glutathione content due to poor nutritional status and aging.
raw_record.extra_details: Referenced clinical findings: lower CYP1A2 enzyme activity in the 11 patients who developed severe hepatitis; higher flutamide and lower OH-flutamide (4-hydroxyflutamide) plasma concentrations in patients with flutamide-induced hepatotoxicity; higher FLU-1 plasma concentration in patients with flutamide-induced hepatic disorders. Proposed mechanism involves CYP1A2-mediated reactive-metabolite (originating from FLU-1) formation and glutathione (GSH) depletion; caffeine test (urinary caffeine metabolites) proposed as noninvasive CYP1A2 assessment.

raw_record.support_text: The study confirms that a significant proportion of children with ALL treated with 6-TG (6-thioguanine) as maintenance chemotherapy may develop chronic hepatotoxicity with portal hypertension, which can lead to variceal haemorrhage; the complication may present without antecedent veno-occlusive disease, and no children randomized to 6-MP maintenance were referred.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric population (children with acute lymphoblastic leukemia) receiving 6-TG as maintenance chemotherapy.
raw_record.extra_details: Chronic hepatotoxicity complicated by portal hypertension and oesophageal variceal haemorrhage; 10 children followed since hepatology assessment (5-46 months, median 30 months); one child had variceal bleeding 2 years after chronic hepatotoxicity was recognized and entered an endoscopic variceal banding programme; persistent splenomegaly and thrombocytopenia; 3 children had abnormal liver function tests at referral; variceal bleeding developed in 3 of the reported cases. On biopsy, 8 of 9 showed some sinusoidal dilatation, 1 had established nodular regenerative hyperplasia (NRH) and 4 had features compatible with early NRH; the injury is proposed to represent a spectrum of non-cirrhotic portal hypertension including NRH and hepatoportal sclerosis.

raw_record.support_text: A patient with bone mycetoma being treated with oral voriconazole developed cholestasis after the first month (alkaline phosphatase 616 IU/l; γ-glutamyl transpeptidase 1126 IU/l) with mild cytolysis (AST up to ~3N, ALT 2–3N). After 18 months of treatment she presented right hypochondrium tenderness and significant cytolysis (ALT 17N, AST 8N) with normal prothrombin time; infectious and autoimmune causes were excluded, and a liver biopsy showed lesions compatible with toxic hepatitis. Voriconazole was stopped on 25 September; hepatic enzymes returned to normal within one week and cholestasis markedly diminished within four weeks.
raw_record.extra_details: Oral dosing was 400 mg twice daily for 2 days then 200 mg twice daily (Pfizer, Paris, France). Cholestasis appeared after the first month and remained stable (alkaline phosphatase 616 IU/l [100–280]; γ-glutamyl transpeptidase 1126 IU/l [7–38]); significant cytolysis appeared at month 18 (ALT 17N, AST 8N) with right hypochondrium tenderness and normal prothrombin time. Infectious and autoimmune causes were negative; liver biopsy showed lesions compatible with toxic hepatitis. After stopping voriconazole (25 September), enzymes normalized within one week and cholestasis declined (alkaline phosphatase 50 IU/l, γ-glutamyl transpeptidase 480 IU/l) at four weeks. The drug had been well tolerated for 18 months without visual disturbances.

raw_record.support_text: Acute APAP (acetaminophen) toxicity is described as the most common identifiable cause of acute liver failure in children aged ≥3 years (21%), with an even higher frequency (40%) in adults. The mechanism involves formation of APAP-protein adducts: when usual APAP metabolism and excretion pathways are exhausted, the reactive APAP metabolite binds to intracellular proteins resulting in cell death; these serum adducts may serve as a biomarker of APAP toxicity. Instances of prolonged or inappropriate dosing (therapeutic misadventures) are noted as not easily captured by the study.

raw_record.support_text: Causality of the atomoxetine-induced hepatitis was assessed using the CIOMS diagnostic scale (final score 7, defined as 'probable') and the Naranjo scale (final score 6, indicating the association of atomoxetine and hepatitis as 'probable'). The calculated ALT/AP R-value of 9.8 was consistent with hepatocellular injury. Rechallenge would have made the association 'definitive' but could not be justified clinically.
raw_record.extra_details: Single case of atomoxetine-induced hepatitis. R-value (ALT/AP) = 9.8 indicating hepatocellular injury. CIOMS score 7 ('probable') and Naranjo score 6 ('probable'); rechallenge not performed as not clinically justified. Patient received 1.03 mg/kg/day (recommended dose up to 1.2 mg/kg/day). Liver biopsy showed inflammatory process of lymphocytes, eosinophils and neutrophils extending through the lobule with moderate piecemeal necrosis, considered inconsistent with acetaminophen, salicylate, mebendazole, or Reye's injury. Atomoxetine is a selective norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor metabolized by CYP2D6; ~90% extensive metabolizers, ~5-10% of Caucasians poor metabolizers with altered pharmacokinetics; patient not genotyped. Authors note severe atomoxetine-induced hepatitis appears to occur rarely but this serious toxicity should be considered; discontinue drug and do not restart if liver injury symptoms occur.

raw_record.support_text: Following post-marketing exposure, two cases of reversible hepatocellular liver injury were reported by different healthcare professionals, suggesting drug-related liver injury had occurred. In both patients, hepatic biochemical test abnormalities resolved when atomoxetine was stopped, and one case of hepatitis recurred following rechallenge with atomoxetine, supporting a causal relationship. These cases were deemed sufficient evidence of an increased risk of liver toxicity to warrant a 2004 label change for atomoxetine. Considering the now extensive exposure (>4 million patients after 4 years), these reactions are very rare and fit the pattern of an idiosyncratic drug reaction.
raw_record.extra_details: Three cases of liver injury probably related to atomoxetine are known to Eli Lilly and Company; case 4 was reclassified as only possibly related because of a second hepatitis episode after atomoxetine was discontinued, while cases 2 and 3 were deemed probably related. Estimated global exposure was about 2.2 million patients when the initial cases arose, and >4 million patients after 4 years. Spontaneous adverse event reporting rate of liver injury, regardless of aetiology, was <0.01% (351 cases among 4,328,000 exposed patients); reporting rate was 23.7 per 100,000 person-years, within the range of background liver injury rates (0.7–164.9 per 100,000 person-years). A 2004 US package insert label change included a warning with a Dear healthcare professional letter. Preclinical testing in rats, mice and dogs showed no liver toxicity.

raw_record.support_text: A patient, approximately 5 weeks after starting thalidomide, developed jaundice with tea-colored urine, mild nausea, abdominal discomfort, fatigue, and decreased appetite. Laboratory tests showed AST 2376 U/L, ALT 2205 U/L, total bilirubin 5.59 mg/dl, stable chronically low albumin 2.0 g/dl, and INR above 15. All home drug therapy including thalidomide was stopped and the patient was transferred for evaluation; after thalidomide discontinuation, liver function test results began to improve toward near-baseline levels, with no hepatic encephalopathy or overt bleeding during the hospital stay.
raw_record.extra_details: Single patient case report. Jaundice and markedly elevated aminotransferases (~5 wks after starting thalidomide); INR >15 corrected overnight after warfarin held and treatment with fresh-frozen plasma and subcutaneous vitamin K. Liver function tests had been normal before starting the drug and improved after thalidomide discontinuation (positive dechallenge). CT showed diffuse fatty infiltration of the liver parenchyma and scattered hepatic cysts. Serologic work-up (hepatitis A/B/C, EBV, HSV, CMV DNA, autoimmune markers ANA, anti-smooth muscle, anti-mitochondrial) was negative. Patient had chronically low albumin and was on warfarin therapy.

raw_record.support_text: The current study monitored 74 alcoholic patients who received 25 mg of naltrexone (NTX) daily in the first week and then 50 mg daily for the remaining 12 weeks. After 12 weeks, hepatic enzyme alanine aminotransferase (ALT) and aspartate aminotransferase (AST) levels showed no elevation except in one subject, and the results strongly supported that NTX did not induce abnormalities in liver function tests or elevate liver enzymes; a statistically significant decrease in ALT and AST was observed. The paper concludes NTX is not hepatotoxic at the recommended daily dose.

raw_record.support_text: Amiodarone hepatotoxicity most commonly manifests as mild asymptomatic elevations of serum aminotransferases, but more severe injury can occur simulating alcoholic liver disease with steatohepatitis, Mallory bodies, and cirrhosis, and four fatal cases of hepatotoxicity had been reported. Phospholipid-laden lysosomal lamellar bodies on electron microscopy are a characteristic feature of amiodarone hepatotoxicity, and latency from treatment start to recognition ranges from several weeks to several years.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of the reported fifth fatal amiodarone hepatotoxicity: mild asymptomatic serum aspartate aminotransferase elevation appeared 5 months after starting amiodarone; liver tests not repeated until 3 years later when hospitalized with massive ascites and apparent pancreatitis. Liver biopsy (micro-nodular cirrhosis, bile ductular proliferation, hepatocyte destruction, polymorphonuclear infiltrate, Mallory bodies; electron microscopy showed multilamellated lysosomal inclusion bodies) was consistent with severe amiodarone-induced liver disease. Ascites attributed primarily to severe cirrhosis. Phospholipidosis and oxygen free radical damage proposed as pathogenic mechanisms. Postmortem studies show high amiodarone and metabolite concentrations in adipose tissue, liver, lung, and pancreas. Competing cause considered but no evidence of a common duct stone.

raw_record.support_text: The study developed a novel scoring system to differentiate amiodarone induced liver injury (AILI) from alcoholic steatohepatitis (ASH). Patients with AILI had mean amiodarone use of 20.4 months at a mean dose of 300 mg. Histologically, compared with ASH, AILI was less frequently associated with ductular reaction, macrovesicular steatosis, abundant ballooning degeneration, neutrophilic lobular inflammation, satellitosis, megamitochondria, and hepatocellular/canalicular cholestasis, with a trend for Mallory hyalines restricted to periportal hepatocytes and periportal-predominant pericellular fibrosis. The scoring system correctly classified 100% of cases, all AILI cases scoring <8 and all ASH cases >11.
raw_record.extra_details: Amiodarone induced liver injury (AILI) at a mean dose of 300 mg over a mean duration of 20.4 months. Histology resembled alcoholic steatohepatitis: macrovesicular steatosis, hepatocyte ballooning without degeneration, Mallory hyalines, satellitosis, periportal pericellular fibrosis, and lamellar lysosomal inclusions on transmission electron microscopy; less ductular reaction, cholestasis, and megamitochondria than ASH. A novel biochemical+histologic scoring system (score <10 suggests AILI, >10 ASH) correctly classified 100% of cases, with all AILI cases scoring <8.

raw_record.support_text: Human safety data on alpha-lipoic acid (ALA) are reported from more than 35 clinical studies (>1300 individuals, 600-2400 mg/day, up to 24 months). In the double-blind placebo-controlled ALADIN II study (24 months, 600 and 1200 mg/day), treatment-related adverse events were monitored across body systems and clinical chemistry parameters including SGOT, SGPT, gamma-GT, alkaline phosphatase and total bilirubin; the authors report no differences in safety parameters between treatment groups and placebo over the entire study, and general tolerability was very good (94% for 1200 mg/day group versus 100% placebo). raw_record.support_text: The authors state that a causal relation between the use of bentazepam and hepatic injury can confidently be established because alternative explanations were ruled out and withdrawal was followed by rapid clinical improvement and return of laboratory findings to normal. Bentazepam is a benzodiazepine marketed in Spain since 1981 for anxiety disorders; rechallenge was not attempted for ethical reasons.
raw_record.extra_details: 65-year-old man with prior peptic ulcer, chronic constipation, and transient ischaemic attacks; previously stopped triflusal due to gastrointestinal bleeding and took only oral lactulose during bentazepam therapy. Bentazepam given at the manufacturer's recommended dose of 25 mg three times daily for severe anxiety; symptoms (abdominal discomfort, progressive asthenia, anorexia, weight loss) appeared ~4 months after start, with no improvement after dose reduction to 25 mg/day, and the drug was stopped at 13 months. At presentation AST 152 U/L, ALT 142 U/L, total bilirubin 18.6 µmol/L (direct 6.8), γ-GT 109 U/L, with normal alkaline phosphatase, plus leukopenia (3.5 × 10⁹/L) and thrombocytopenia (130 × 10⁹/L). Liver biopsy showed expanded portal areas with dense lymphocytic/monocytic infiltrate disrupting the limiting plate, lymphoid aggregates, marked portal-to-portal fibrosis with transition to cirrhosis in some areas, and marked parenchymal collapse. Viral (Hep A/B/C, CMV, EBV) and autoimmune serologies were negative. After stopping the drug, symptoms improved dramatically; by the eleventh week AST fell to 66 U/L, ALT to 53 U/L, and γ-GT to 85 U/L, and counts normalized by 4 months. Authors attributed the injury to an idiosyncratic metabolic mechanism (no rash, fever, eosinophilia, or granulomatous infiltrate; long latency), and noted benzodiazepines generally have very low hepatotoxic potential.

Liver biopsy before transplant showed portal tract enlargement with inflammation and cholangiolar proliferation, periportal activity with edema, and predominantly centrolobular hepatocyte necrosis with congestion and polymorphic inflammation; native liver showed complete loss of hepatocytes replaced by macrophages and inflammatory cells. The patient with peliosis developed ascites and died from hepatic failure despite drug withdrawal. Laboratory hallmark was elevated gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase and alkaline phosphatase. One patient died from hepatic failure with ascites; one developed jaundice, ascites and severe infection following right hepatectomy. raw_record.support_text: The clinical course of acetaminophen toxicity is described in four phases after ingestion. Phase 2 (24–72 hours) is marked by right upper quadrant pain indicating beginning hepatic injury, with hepatic enzymes, bilirubin, and prothrombin time rising. Phase 3 (72–96 hours) is characterized by evidence of hepatic necrosis with jaundice, coagulation defects, renal failure, and hepatic encephalopathy, and fulminant hepatic failure is usually fatal. Phase 4 involves resolution if the patient survives.

raw_record.extra_details: Phase-based course described: Phase 1 (30 min–24 h) nausea, vomiting, anorexia, pallor, diaphoresis, malaise, often asymptomatic; Phase 2 (24–72 h) right upper quadrant pain, rising hepatic enzymes, bilirubin and PT, possible renal deterioration (decreased consciousness, oliguria); Phase 3 (72–96 h) hepatic necrosis with jaundice, coagulation defects, renal failure, hepatic encephalopathy, with fulminant hepatic failure usually fatal; Phase 4 (4 days–2 weeks) resolution with liver returning to normal in ~3 months. In the patient, acetaminophen level was 240 mcg/mL and potassium 3.0 mEq/L; toxicity plotted on the standard nomogram.

Liver biopsy showed active parenchymal inflammation and bile duct injury without fibrosis; Fibroscan 12.9 kPa (fibrosis and/or severe inflammation). In the acute stage he was at high risk for liver failure. Treated with prednisone 40 mg daily (tapered, stopped after 7 months) and azathioprine 100 mg daily (maintained); liver function tests returned to normal. Later restarted alirocumab. Authors note prior ezetimibe-induced liver injury cases were mostly reported with statin combination therapy and the drug label only warns of liver enzyme elevation with statins, not monotherapy. raw_record.support_text: A newborn infant who received repeated oral doses of acetaminophen every 4 hours (an infant formulation after circumcision) developed clinical manifestations consistent with acetaminophen toxicity, including encephalopathy with recurrent seizures, coagulopathy requiring fresh frozen plasma and cryoprecipitate transfusions, and hepatic and renal dysfunction. The paper attributes the hepatotoxicity to an acetaminophen overdose mediated by the reactive metabolite N-acetyl-p-benzoquinoneimine (NAPQI), noting that glutathione reserves may be depleted after supra-therapeutic or repeated therapeutic doses, especially given the prolonged elimination half-life in newborns. The infant recovered fully after a 20 h intravenous N-acetylcysteine infusion regimen.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Neonatal (newborn) patient with prolonged acetaminophen elimination half-life (reported ~3.5 h vs 1.9-2.2 h in adults) leading to drug accumulation; repeated oral dosing every 4 h after circumcision; unusual exposure setting of repeated therapeutic doses behaving as supratherapeutic in the neonate.
raw_record.extra_details: Serum acetaminophen concentrations declined from 94.8 to <10 µg/ml over 56 h on NAC; treatment used a 20 h IV N-acetylcysteine protocol (150 mg/kg bolus, then 50 mg/kg over 4 h, then 100 mg/kg over 16 h at 40 mg/ml in 5% dextrose). Hepatotoxicity mechanism via NAPQI normally detoxified by reduced glutathione; neonate resilience to hepatic necrosis/failure attributed to reduced CYP450 metabolism and increased glutathione synthesis. Recovery included normalization of PT 12.4 s, PTT 44.7 s, INR 1.2, factor V 93%, AST 107 IU/l, ALT 326 IU/l, serum bilirubin 2.4 mg/dl (conjugated 0.6 mg/dl), creatinine 0.4 mg/dl by the third hospital day; discharged on day 7 and developing normally at 9 months. Supportive measures included furosemide, lactulose, ranitidine, and phenobarbital for seizures.

The graded histologic spectrum (fibrosis, bridging fibrosis, cirrhosis) reflects liver injury attributed to chronic MTX exposure in these patients.

Graded features include fibrous spurs in the portal area, fibrosis in the space of Disse, thickened liver cords, septal fibrosis, portal-to-portal or portal-to-central vein bridging, spotty hepatocellular necrosis, and steatohepatitis. In the study cohort (29 patients), MTX cumulative doses ranged from 1.5 to 12.6 g, therapy exposure from 2 to 17 years, and weekly doses from 7.5 to 25 mg/week; observed grades ranged from 1 to 3b.

raw_record.support_text: This is described as the largest published series of cases of hepatocellular damage associated with use of diclofenac. Onset was often delayed several weeks after the start of diclofenac treatment, and the biochemical abnormalities were predominantly those of an acute hepatitic reaction with pronounced rises in transaminase levels; rash and eosinophilia were not usually reported. Recovery was generally rapid after diclofenac was stopped. An apparent relation between the cumulative dose of diclofenac reported to have been taken and certain biochemical measures of the severity of the hepatic injury was noted, which the authors state increases the likelihood of causal relations in a series of cases that generally were not extensively investigated.

Significant dose-severity correlations: log dose vs log peak AST deviate ratio r²=0.68, slope 0.91, p=0.0001; vs log peak ALT r²=0.71, slope 1.04, p=0.001; mean AST vs log cumulative dose r²=0.49, p=0.003, mean ALT r²=0.59, p=0.006; log cumulative dose vs log GGT r²=0.350, p=0.01 and vs log bilirubin r²=0.29, p=0.01. Duration of treatment and daily dose did not correlate well with severity. Liver histology available for only one patient and showed acute hepatitis. Peak deviates (mean): AST 13.0, ALT 16.0, ALP 2.3, GGT 7.2, bilirubin 3.6. Most reports came from family practitioners/general physicians and included incomplete case data.

raw_record.support_text: In a series of 20 pediatric patients hospitalized with isoniazid (INH)-related fulminant liver failure, 4 (20%) spontaneously recovered, 10 (50%) underwent orthotopic liver transplantation (OLT), and 6 (30%) died without transplant; 12 of 20 (60%) overall survived. Four of five patients who did not discontinue INH at the first symptoms of hepatitis developed irreversible liver disease (two OLTs, two deaths), all four being on INH monotherapy. Liver histology in 17 of 18 specimens showed massive necrosis with parenchymal collapse and swollen residual hepatocytes, consistent with INH-induced toxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric population; INH-related fulminant liver failure; four of five non-discontinuers (INH monotherapy) developed irreversible disease (2 OLT, 2 death).
raw_record.extra_details: 20 pediatric patients with INH-related acute liver failure. Symptoms at hospitalization in 18/20: jaundice (16, 89%), coagulopathy (16, 89%), nausea/vomiting (13, 72%), abdominal pain (9, 50%), encephalopathy (9, 50%), fatigue (8, 45%). Mean admission AST 1399 mg/dL (range 324-5952), ALT 1030 mg/dL (306-4822), total bilirubin 13.7 mg/dL (1.8-30). Histology (18 pts): 17 showed massive necrosis with parenchymal collapse and swollen residual hepatocytes; one biopsy after enzyme normalization showed mild chronic portal inflammation with focal peliosis. Outcomes: 4 recovered (mean recovery ~42 days), 10 OLT (8 survived, 2 died posttransplant of sepsis/exsanguination from gastric ulcer), 6 died without OLT (5 from hepatic failure complications, 1 from sepsis after chemotherapy). Mean time from hospitalization to death/OLT 21 days (range 1-60). One patient on INH plus rifampin and pyrazinamide recovered spontaneously. Four of four BCG-vaccinated patients did not recover. No parameter (duration on INH, concurrent drugs, encephalopathy) differed significantly between recovery (4) and non-recovery (16) groups. From Oct 1 1987 to Jan 31 1997, 8 OLTs for INH-related liver failure in this study = 14% (8/56) of pediatric OLTs for drug toxicity and 0.2% of all pediatric liver transplants (UNOS, 4,679 total pediatric OLTs, 56 for drug toxicity).
