raw_record.support_text: A patient treated with imatinib mesylate developed hepatotoxicity including an increase in total bilirubin to a maximum of 513.4 µmol/l on hospital day 7, with normalization after 6 weeks following discontinuation of imatinib and short steroid therapy. After resuming imatinib mesylate at a reduced dose of 400 mg daily, the patient experienced no further hepatotoxicity. The authors attribute the liver abnormalities to imatinib mesylate.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of imatinib mesylate-induced hepatotoxicity in a patient with Philadelphia chromosome-positive chronic myeloid leukemia. Transaminase activity and bilirubin increased after 10 days of imatinib use; levels normalized after interruption for 6 weeks with minimal corticosteroid use. Bilirubin level and ALP activity reached grade 4 toxicity, aminotransferase and γ-glutamyltransferase activities grade 3. Liver biopsy (day 4) showed portal tract inflammation with cholestasis, acute hepatocyte injury, scattered acidophilic bodies, occasional ballooning degeneration, canalicular cholestasis, moderate inflammatory infiltration of lymphocytes, plasma cells, neutrophils and many eosinophils, and eosinophil infiltration of interlobular bile ducts with ductal epithelial damage. Associated skin rash and hypereosinophilia (max 2.47 x 10^9/l, ~40% WBC) resolved after stopping imatinib. Rechallenge at reduced dose 400 mg daily produced no further hepatotoxicity and patient continued imatinib for 18 months. Authors concluded the single dose of a Korean ginseng herbal remedy did not cause the hepatic function abnormalities.

raw_record.support_text: The patient developed acute mixed liver injury during dasatinib treatment. The causal relationship between dasatinib treatment and the occurrence of this acute mixed liver injury was assessed as probable according to the criteria for drug-induced liver disorders proposed by an International Consensus Meeting. Time to onset after dasatinib initiation was compatible, the course after dasatinib discontinuation was suggestive of drug-induced hepatitis, extensive investigations found no other cause, and zopiclone was excluded as a cause because it was continued uneventfully. raw_record.support_text: The paper reports that hepatotoxicity is a well-known complication of non-steroidal anti-androgens and that fatal hepatotoxicity due to nilutamide has been described previously only twice. The reported fatal case in this paper is attributed to nilutamide therapy in a patient with metastatic prostate cancer; the only other medication taken was leuprolide, an LHRH analogue for which severe hepatotoxicity has not been noted. Nilutamide's manufacturer profile describes serum aminotransferase elevations in about 8% of patients, and the incidence of abnormal liver function tests was reported as 2-33% across various studies.
raw_record.extra_details: Fatal DILI case report in a patient with metastatic prostate cancer treated with nilutamide for combined androgen blockade; the only co-medication was leuprolide (LHRH analogue), for which severe hepatotoxicity was not noted. Liver biopsy showed a mixed inflammatory infiltrate (lymphocytes, plasma cells, eosinophils, neutrophils) with cholestasis, ductular proliferation, interface injury, and spotty necrosis; lab values showed total bilirubin 30.2 mg/dl, direct bilirubin 17.7, AST 1540 U/l, ALT 977 U/l, alkaline phosphatase 138 U/l. Patient developed encephalopathy and acute-on-chronic liver failure, received plasmapheresis for 72 h without sustained improvement, developed pancytopenia, fungemia and bacteremia, was not a transplant candidate due to metastatic prostate cancer, and died 11 days after transfer. Manufacturer label reports aminotransferase elevation in ~8% of patients (vs 4% placebo); abnormal LFT incidence 2-33% in various studies; nilutamide is a nitroaromatic drug with potential nitroreductive bioactivation (oxidant stress) and mitochondrial complex I inhibition proposed as mechanisms.

Histology of a laparoscopic liver biopsy showed severe drug-induced necrotic hepatitis, leading to prednisolone treatment, after which AST returned to baseline and bilirubin decreased. The authors describe this as the first patient reported with sorafenib-induced liver failure.

condition_text: Pediatric/adolescent population (157 patients at eight pediatric hospitals); overdose exposure setting.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that acetaminophen (APAP) overdose is a common cause of pediatric ingestions and, in severe cases, may result in acute liver failure (ALF). It further reports that APAP overdose is a major cause of ALF in adults (~50% of cases) and accounts for ~13% of ALF cases in children, establishing a human DILI relationship for acetaminophen at overdose. Supporting these claims, the study found that of 157 adolescents and children presenting with APAP overdose at eight pediatric hospitals, two required liver transplantation while the others recovered spontaneously, and peak APAP protein adducts correlated with peak hepatic transaminase values.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric/adolescent population (157 patients at eight pediatric hospitals); overdose exposure setting.
raw_record.extra_details: APAP overdose causes acute liver failure in adults (~50% of ALF cases) and in children (~13% of cases); morbidity in children is generally lower than in adults. In the study cohort, 2/157 patients required liver transplantation and the remainder recovered spontaneously. Peak APAP protein adduct concentrations correlated with peak hepatic transaminases, time-to-treatment with N-acetylcysteine (NAC), and Rumack-Matthews nomogram risk determination; model-derived adduct value at 48 h correlated with adduct Cmax, adduct Tmax, Rumack-Matthews risk, peak AST and peak ALT. Mechanism involves cytochrome P450 (CYP2E1, CYP1A2, CYP3A4) oxidation to the reactive metabolite NAPQI; covalent binding of NAPQI to cysteinyl sulfhydryl groups on cellular proteins (3-(cystein-S-yl)APAP protein adduct) under glutathione depletion underlies toxicity. APAP accounts for ~50% of adult ALF and ~13% of pediatric ALF.

raw_record.support_text: National estimates for acetaminophen toxicity in the United States include 26,000 hospitalizations and more than 450 deaths annually. raw_record.extra_details: Mechanism attributed to toxic acetaminophen metabolites: covalent binding to mitochondrial proteins, depressed mitochondrial respiration and ATP synthesis, mitochondrial oxidant stress with peroxynitrite production, collapse of mitochondrial membrane potential, release of mitochondrial proteins, and oncotic necrosis of hepatocytes; innate immunity (Kupffer cells, NK cells, neutrophils) exacerbates hepatic injury. Epidemiology: 26,000 hospitalizations and >450 deaths annually in the US; acetaminophen identified as cause of ALF in 20% (late 1990s) then 39% to 42% of cases, with suicidal intent in 27% to 44% and unintentional overdose in 48% to 61%; incidence rose from 28% in 1998 to 52% in 2003; pediatric multicenter study attributed 14% of ALF to acetaminophen overdose. UK study: <10% of overdoses cause severe liver damage, 1% to 2% develop ALF.

A separate retrospective analysis of liver function tests measured before, during and after i.v. paracetamol use in 149 term and preterm infants (30-55 weeks) concluded there was a lack of hepatotoxicity with regular i.v. paracetamol dosing using lower dosing regimes (20 mg·kg⁻¹·day⁻¹ age <31 weeks, 30 mg·kg⁻¹·day⁻¹ age 31-36 weeks, 40 mg·kg⁻¹·day⁻¹ age >36 weeks).

raw_record.extra_details: Palmer et al. dosed i.v. paracetamol at 60 mg·kg⁻¹·day⁻¹ (>36 weeks PMA), 50 mg·kg⁻¹·day⁻¹ (32-36 weeks), and 40 mg·kg⁻¹·day⁻¹ (28-32 weeks) for 1-9 days in infants aged 32-45 weeks PMA; retrospective analysis covered 149 term and preterm infants (30-55 weeks) with liver function tests before/during/after use. raw_record.extra_details: Case report of coumarin-induced hepatitis; no history of other drug usage, excluding competing causes; ALT was 52 and liver enzymes normalized with complete resolution of symptoms two months after cessation. Reports of adverse effects in humans are rare and idiosyncratic, whereas coumarin is a well-recognized dose-dependent rat hepatotoxicant.

Suggested mechanism is a mitochondrial defect aggravated by co-factors (HCV, alcohol, drugs). Patients tolerated buprenorphine well at recommended sublingual doses; risk of acute hepatitis applies to IV intravenous misuse. Drug intended for treatment of opioid addiction.

raw_record.support_text: According to the International Consensus Meeting, the type of liver damage in this case was hepatocellular. Applying the CIOMS (Council for International Organizations of Medical Sciences) score, the causality assessment of clopidogrel-induced liver injury was probable, based on no history of liver or biliary disease, negative diagnostic work-up excluding other causes of acute hepatitis, clopidogrel being the recently added drug, worsening of liver injury during drug administration, and resolution-linked evidence; the presence of thrombocytopenia (a known clopidogrel side effect) provided additional evidence of drug involvement.
raw_record.extra_details: A 63-year-old man with diabetes and ischaemic disease, on chronic human insulin, captopril, molsidomine, simvastatin and aspirin (>3 years without adverse reaction), started clopidogrel 75 mg daily for percutaneous coronary stenting. Nineteen days after starting clopidogrel he developed tea-coloured urine and jaundice; he was hospitalized on day 54 (clopidogrel and all other drugs stopped) and died on day 56 after grade IV encephalopathy, significant haemoptysis, and 2 days after hospitalization. Autopsy not performed. Liver biochemistries on day 54/day 56: total bilirubin 78/80 µmol/L, ALT 336/297 U/L, AST 303/208 U/L, GGT 160/156 U/L, ALP 186/185 U/L, prothrombin time 27%/28%. Thrombocytopenia 90×10³/mm³; negative viral/autoimmune serologies; normal liver and biliary tract on ultrasound; CIOMS causality score = probable.

raw_record.support_text: The patient was diagnosed with clopidogrel-induced severe hepatitis. After discontinuing clopidogrel, AST increased to 2,107 U/L, ALT to 1,567 U/L, and bilirubin to 37 mg/dL (predominately direct), and INR rose to 2.1 despite empiric vitamin K. A brief course of prednisone and ursodiol led to normalization of liver biochemistries.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report: liver biopsy showed severe acute hepatitis with mixed inflammatory portal tract infiltrates (plasma cells, neutrophils, eosinophils), bile ductular reaction, patchy hepatocyte ballooning degeneration, and extensive periportal hepatocyte dropout without fibrosis. Peak ALT 1,567 U/L, AST 2,107 U/L, bilirubin 37 mg/dL (predominantly direct), INR 2.1 with coagulopathy and jaundice. Naranjo and RUCAM scores both 8, indicating probable drug-induced hepatitis. Patient treated with prednisone and ursodiol and recovered with normalization of liver biochemistries. Prior reported clopidogrel-induced hepatitis cases range from reversible injury and recovery to acute hepatic failure and death, with onset between 3 and 180 days and rechallenge-confirmed injury in some cases; clopidogrel liver injury has been reported as cholestatic, hepatocellular, or mixed.

Other passages attribute acetaminophen-induced fulminant hepatic failure to ingestion, with acetylcysteine therapy continued until recovery from encephalopathy or death, implying that acetaminophen overdose causes dose-dependent human hepatotoxicity that can progress to acute liver failure.

raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity follows acute acetaminophen overdose; leads to fulminant hepatic failure, encephalopathy, coagulopathy, and possible death. Treatment studied with intravenous (20-hour, 300 mg/kg total, 6.25 mg/kg per hour maintenance) versus oral (72-hour, 1,330 mg/kg total, 17.5 mg/kg per hour) acetylcysteine protocols; oral route proposed to give higher hepatic concentrations via first-pass splanchnic circulation. Oral protocol dose based on assumptions of 70 kg body weight, 1.5 L liver containing 6 mmol glutathione, 70% glutathione depletion to cause hepatic damage, 4-hour acetaminophen elimination half-life, and 15.9 g absorbed dose; increased to 17.5 mg/kg per hour with 72-hour duration after FDA discussions.

raw_record.support_text: In paracetamol overdose patients at severe risk, the relation between plasma alanine aminotransferase and 3-(cystein-S-yl)paracetamol protein adducts at admission supports a dominant mechanistic role of this protein binding, described as the first direct evidence of a similar mechanism of paracetamol-induced hepatic necrosis in man and in laboratory animals.

raw_record.extra_details: Based on 30 patients presenting with paracetamol poisoning at Rigshospitalet, Copenhagen; 11 were at high risk, 3 at moderate risk, and 16 at low risk of hepatotoxicity on the Prescott classification. raw_record.support_text: Four patients aged 3–18 years of multiple ethnicities developed VPA-induced hepatotoxicity, all having received VPA for intractable partial seizures (three with epilepsia partialis continua). The time from VPA exposure to liver failure was 2–3 months, and liver failure was reversible in one patient. Molecular studies revealed homozygous p.R597W or p.A467T POLG mutations in two patients and compound heterozygous mutations (p.A467T/p.Q68X and p.L83P/p.G888S) in the other two; clinical findings and POLG mutations were diagnostic of Alpers–Huttenlocher syndrome. The authors conclude VPA dosing at any stage of Alpers–Huttenlocher syndrome can precipitate liver failure.

raw_record.extra_details: Four patients across multiple ethnicities. Latency from VPA exposure to liver failure 2–3 months. Liver failure reversible in one patient. Molecular findings: homozygous p.R597W or p.A467T POLG mutations in two patients; compound heterozygous p.A467T/p.Q68X and p.L83P/p.G888S in the other two. Authors propose POLG gene testing consideration before VPA dosing in children/adolescents presenting with intractable seizures, particularly with psychomotor regression, given VPA dosing can precipitate liver failure in Alpers–Huttenlocher syndrome.

raw_record.support_text: The patient was diagnosed with ciprofloxacin-induced cholestatic liver injury after excluding other causes of cholestasis (hepatitis A/B/C/E serology and autoimmune antibodies were negative). The onset of symptoms and liver enzyme derangements following ciprofloxacin use, improvement in clinical and biochemical parameters after cessation, and liver biopsy findings (centrivenular cholestasis with focal mixed steatosis) all suggested ciprofloxacin-induced cholestatic liver injury. The RUCAM causality assessment scored the case as "highly probable." The discussion further states ciprofloxacin can cause dose-independent idiosyncratic DILI and that most ciprofloxacin-induced liver injury cases manifest within two to three weeks of therapy, usually with a hepatocellular or cholestatic LFT pattern, rarely mixed.

Liver biopsy showed centrivenular canalicular and hepatocellular cholestasis with focal macrovesicular steatosis, fibrosis score 0/6, favoring drug-induced cholestasis. RUCAM "highly probable." Other possible culprits fosfomycin and cefixime were used three months prior and deemed unlikely to contribute. Ciprofloxacin-associated injury is dose-independent and idiosyncratic; symptoms typically begin within 2-3 weeks of initiation. Phenotype: drug-induced cholestasis/cholestatic liver injury.

Outcomes were spontaneous survival (survival without liver transplantation) or death (a group that also included transplanted patients). Acetaminophen dose did not significantly predict spontaneous survival by multivariate analysis (P = 0.146; OR, 1.000), and no survival difference was found between patients ingesting more versus less than 10–50 g. raw_record.support_text: The authors report a case of acetaminophen intoxication in which the patient received first medical care almost 72 hours after a first ingestion of 24,375 mg of the agent and presented with worsening general condition and signs of severe liver failure. They note that a negative serum acetaminophen concentration does not preclude a significant overdose, and that up to 0.35% of fatalities in a tertiary poison treatment center were due to acetaminophen overdosage.

Mechanism: ~10% of the drug is oxidized by P450 to the reactive metabolite NAPQI, which is detoxified by hepatic glutathione conjugation; when glutathione is depleted (overdose) NAPQI binds hepatic cell macromolecules and initiates tissue necrosis. Patient discharged after one month; LFTs and PT returned to normal.

raw_record.support_text: The major finding is the high prevalence of moderate to severe sinusoidal lesions (54%) in patients receiving OX-based chemotherapy. Among OX recipients (n=204), sinusoidal obstruction syndrome (SOS) lesions occurred in 77.4% (grade 1: 15.2%, grade 2-3: 62.2%), peliosis was present in 14.6%, nodular transformation in 63.7% (grade 3 NRH 28.9%), and centrilobular/venular fibrosis in 52%, versus essentially none in the no-chemotherapy group (n=111). Prevalence in OX group: SOS 77.4% (grade 1: 15.2%, grade 2-3: 62.2%), peliosis 14.6%, nodular transformation 63.7% (NRH 28.9%), centrilobular/venular fibrosis 52%. raw_record.support_text: The paper concludes that Gd-EOB-DTPA-enhanced MRI findings revealed the clinical features of oxaliplatin-induced sinusoidal obstruction syndrome (SOS), proposing the imaging as a biomarker for diagnosing oxaliplatin-induced SOS at an early stage. In the retrospective study of oxaliplatin-treated patients, non-tumorous hepatic parenchymal heterogeneity was graded in 57 patients: 21 grade 0, 24 grade 1, seven grade 2, five grade 3; hepatic distribution was diffuse in four (7.0%), peripheral in ten (17.5%), and multifocal in 22 (38.6%). Hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, gallbladder wall thickening, and narrowing of the hepatic vein correlated with heterogeneity grade. Elevated AST, elevated ALT, high AST-to-platelet ratio index, and low platelet count were significantly associated with a high grade (≥2). raw_record.support_text: This is reported as the first case of drug-induced severe acute hepatitis in a patient treated with sorafenib after liver transplantation. The authors conclude that sorafenib carries a risk of acute hepatitis not only in patients with underlying liver cirrhosis but also in patients with normal liver function, attributing the severe hepatitis to an idiosyncratic drug reaction based on the patient's fever, typical liver histology, and positive lymphocyte stimulation test. Most likely the incidence of severe hepatitis is less than 1%.

raw_record.extra_details: Index case of sorafenib-induced severe acute hepatitis after liver transplantation; clinical presentation with fever, typical liver histology, and positive lymphocyte stimulation test supported idiosyncratic mechanism. Two prior cases occurred in Child-Pugh A cirrhosis (NASH or hepatitis C with multinodular HCC) and one in a patient without known liver disease. Sorafenib-induced hepatitis was diagnosed within 4 days to 8 weeks in the three prior cases; one had concomitant fever. After cessation, one prior patient progressed to liver failure and died within 3 months, while others improved with or without steroid medication. Authors recommend liver enzyme monitoring and immediate cessation upon enzyme increase.

raw_record.support_text: In a patient presenting with jaundice, competing etiologies of intrahepatic cholestasis were excluded by serology and imaging, and all the patient's drugs were examined. It was concluded that the jaundice can be a very rare adverse reaction of rivaroxaban, so rivaroxaban was stopped and enoxaparin was substituted; the patient showed rapid biochemical and clinical recovery within one day, with liver function tests nearly normal after two weeks.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of rivaroxaban-induced intrahepatic cholestasis causing severe, long-lasting jaundice. Authors state the most probable diagnosis is rivaroxaban-induced intrahepatic cholestasis based on exclusion of other causes and dramatic resolution after drug cessation (dechallenge). Lab values after 2 weeks off drug: ALT 24, AST 28, GGT 36, ALP 168 U/l, total bilirubin 4.5 mg/dl, conjugated bilirubin 4.3 mg/dl; skin and scleral icterus not fully resolved 6 weeks after discontinuation. Labeled adverse reactions of rivaroxaban include jaundice and increased transaminases, ALP, and total and conjugated bilirubin. Mechanism stated as unknown, possibly immune-mediated; rechallenge not described; no cross-reactivity among anticoagulants suspected.

raw_record.support_text: Leflunomide (LEF) is reported to cause drug-induced hepatotoxicity in humans. In the original RCTs, transaminase rises to ≥2x the upper limit of normal occurred in 2.2-19% of patients, and serious drug-induced hepatotoxicity leading to hospitalization was rare (0.02%), yet isolated fatalities from liver failure were documented, prompting an early drug-information amendment requiring liver function monitoring. In the CORRONA cohort, LEF+MTX combination therapy increased the odds of elevated liver enzymes (OR 2.15 with MTX ≤7.5 mg up to 3.98 with MTX ≥20 mg), while LEF monotherapy showed no increased OR (0.83) relative to LEF/MTX-naïve patients.

raw_record.support_text: Across multiple phase I trials of the single agent trabectedin in soft-tissue and bone sarcoma and other solid-tumor patients, the most commonly encountered toxicities included reversible hepatic toxicity and increased liver transaminases. In a Children's Oncology Group phase I study of trabectedin in children with refractory tumors, reversible hepatic toxicity was the most common toxicity, occurring in 58% of patients. A phase I study in solid tumors reported increased liver transaminases among the most frequent non-hematologic toxicities, and the EORTC phase II trial reported a rise in liver transaminases as a common side effect.
raw_record.extra_details: Reversible hepatic toxicity was the most common toxicity in a Children's Oncology Group phase I pediatric study (58% of patients, recommended phase II dose 1.1 mg/m2 as 3-hour IV infusion). Phase I solid-tumor single-agent studies reported increased liver transaminases as frequent non-hematologic toxicity; phase I combination studies with doxorubicin or pegylated liposomal doxorubicin reported severe but reversible hepatic toxicity and similar transaminase elevations, and a weekly trabectedin plus gemcitabine phase I trial was terminated early due to an unacceptable frequency of dose adjustments from hepatic toxicity. The EORTC phase II study of 1.5 mg/m2 24-hour continuous infusion every 3 weeks reported a rise in liver transaminases among common toxicities.

raw_record.support_text: The study characterizes the time course of serum aminotransferase (AT) rise in patients after acute acetaminophen (APAP) overdose, describing hepatotoxicity as AT exceeding 1,000 IU/L, severe coagulation disturbances (INR), and an early leak from severely injured zone 3 hepatocytes. Nearly all patients developed elevated AT within 12–24 h after acute APAP ingestion, and two-thirds of cases destined to reach 1,000 IU/L did so within 48 h.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Acute drug overdose; patients treated with antidotal acetylcysteine; population recruited from regional tertiary care and referral hospitals.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity defined as serum AT > 1,000 IU/L; initially abnormal AT doubled roughly every 8 h in patients who met the threshold within 48 h and developed severe coagulation disturbances; AT peak height not predictive of encephalopathy or death; early rise attributed to leak from severely injured zone 3 hepatocytes plus a later healing/turnover spike; all study patients were above the Rumack–Matthew nomogram treatment line and received antidote (20-h Prescott protocol); severe coagulopathy unlikely when serum AT is relatively low after 12 h of acetylcysteine therapy; INR, international normalized ratio; AT/aminotransferase is AST/ALT.

raw_record.support_text: At exploratory laparotomy on September 23, 1944, the patient's liver was smooth with no visible tumor; a biopsy showed fibrosis of the portal areas, dilated bile capillaries surrounding the central veins, considerable bile pigment retention, and cloudy swelling in areas. The diagnosis was toxic hepatitis, attributed to the course of diethylstilbestrol the patient had received.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of a patient with metastatic prostate carcinoma treated with diethylstilbestrol, total 2,700 mg over a 328 day period (average 8.2 mg/day). Developed progressive erythematous macular rash, marked ankle and leg edema, jaundice (icteric index up to 200), tender liver enlarged 3 fingers below costal margin, gallbladder-region mass, distended superficial abdominal veins, clay-colored stools with negative bile, alkaline phosphatase 18 Bodansky units. Liver biopsy showed portal-area fibrosis, dilated bile capillaries around central veins, bile pigment retention and cloudy swelling; diagnosis of toxic hepatitis. Non-functioning gallbladder on cholecystogram.

By contrast, myelosuppression was the dose-limiting toxicity in the adult dose-finding study, with a maximum-tolerated dose of 1,000–1,250 mg/m² per day for 3 days as a short infusion. The single-agent maximum-tolerated dose of dexrazoxane in children is significantly higher than the dosage range used in the protocols studying its use as a cardioprotective agent.

raw_record.support_text: In paracetamol poisoning, the UK standard treatment regimen of N-acetylcysteine (NAC) prevents hepatic injury primarily by restoring hepatic glutathione. NAC has been used for over 30 years and almost eliminates the risk of hepatic damage when given within 8 h in paracetamol overdose; in patients who have taken very large overdoses the half-life of paracetamol may be prolonged so an extended NAC course may be required. The paper also frames paracetamol toxicity as causing hepatocyte necrosis that NAC may help prevent.

raw_record.support_text: In this phase I study, PHA-793887 was poorly tolerated, with two patients experiencing severe acute hepatic failure, one of them dying because of drug-related toxicity, leading to halting of further clinical development. The severe hepatotoxicity of PHA-793887 was considered not target-related because hepatotoxicity had not been documented for other CDK inhibitors in clinical use. In animals, liver effects were observed only at lethal doses with AUC ≥20 µM·h and Cmax ≥14 µM, whereas the mean AUC₀⁻∞ in patients at 44 and 66 mg/m² was 10.14 and 13.07 µMh with mean Cmax of 3.60 and 5.80 µM, indicating hepatotoxic exposure in humans was a fraction of that causing toxicity in animals.
raw_record.extra_details: Phase I dose-escalation study in patients with advanced solid tumors (dose levels 11, 22, 44, and 66 mg/m²). Two of 18 evaluable patients experienced severe acute hepatic failure; one died of drug-related toxicity. Further clinical development was halted. Toxicity judged not target-related (no other CDK inhibitor in clinical use showed hepatotoxicity); PHA-793887 is a pyrrolo[3,4-c]pyrazole structurally different from other CDK inhibitors. Preclinical liver effects only at lethal doses (AUC ≥20 µM·h, Cmax ≥14 µM); human mean AUC₀⁻∞ at 44 and 66 mg/m² was 10.14 and 13.07 µMh, mean Cmax 3.60 and 5.80 µM. DILI liver_injury_identifier corresponds to acute liver failure (UMLS:C0162557).

raw_record.support_text: In this phase I trial of PHA-793887, one patient treated at 66 mg/m² experienced a drug-related grade 4 hepatic failure with pancytopenia, and one patient treated at 44 mg/m² had a fatal hepatorenal failure. There was no dose relationship in the rate of clinical adverse events, but there was a clear dose relation with regard to their severity. Biochemical abnormalities related mainly to liver biochemistry tests, with evidence of a dose relation in the frequency and severity of AST, ALT and bilirubin elevations; all grade ≥3 liver biochemistry toxicity developed during cycle 1 within 2–4 days after initial drug administration and generally improved over 3–4 weeks.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Phase I dose-escalation study in patients with advanced solid tumors; an investigational agent.
raw_record.extra_details: One drug-related grade 4 hepatic failure with pancytopenia at 66 mg/m²/day and one fatal hepatorenal failure at 44 mg/m²/day; two patients died during study (one from fatal hepatorenal failure, one from disease progression). Grade ≥3 AST and ALT elevations occurred in 2 of 9 patients at 44 mg/m² and 1 of 3 at 66 mg/m²; bilirubin grade ≥3 in 1 of 9 at 44 mg/m² and 2 of 3 at 66 mg/m². All grade ≥3 liver biochemistry toxicity developed during cycle 1 within 2–4 days of first dose and improved over 3–4 weeks; affected patients were not re-treated. Kinetic parameters: terminal half-life 6–13 h, Vss 1.9–2.2 L/kg, clearance 0.14–0.48 L/h/kg.

raw_record.support_text: Thirteen days after starting azathioprine 100 mg daily a rheumatoid arthritis patient developed fever, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhoea with raised alkaline phosphatase (240 U/l) and gamma-glutamyltransferase (76 U/l); transaminases and amylase were normal. Azathioprine was discontinued, and an accidental single-tablet rechallenge reproduced diarrhoea and fever within two hours; liver enzymes returned to normal within two weeks, supporting azathioprine as a probable cause of the liver injury.

raw_record.support_text: Azathioprine, a cytotoxic agent that blocks DNA synthesis, is well established in rheumatoid arthritis management. Cholestatic hepatitis is an important but uncommon complication of azathioprine treatment, while its association with hepatocellular necrosis is considered less clear. The authors describe a case in which azathioprine was clearly implicated as the cause of an idiosyncratic hepatitis on biochemical grounds, with liver biopsy showing no abnormality beyond marked lipofuscin deposition.
raw_record.extra_details: Azathioprine given orally 50 mg twice daily, started two weeks before admission, in a 58-year-old man with seropositive rheumatoid arthritis (previous failed trials of indomethacin, phenylbutazone, gold sodium thiomalate, and D-penicillamine due to rash/ulceration). Presented with anorexia, nausea, vomiting, myalgia, night sweats, icterus and 3 cm tender hepatomegaly; bilirubin 39 mmol/l (NR 0-17), alkaline phosphatase 898 IU/l (NR 100-300), aspartate transaminase >300 IU/l (NR 32-50); eosinophils 0.83 x 10^9/l. Hepatitis B surface antigen, Monospot, and serology for hepatitis A, cytomegalovirus, toxoplasma and mycoplasma were negative. Also on ketoprofen 200 mg daily at the time. Liver biopsy showed no abnormality beyond marked lipofuscin deposition.

In one study, the majority of patients with chronic hepatitis B treated with fialuridine for more than 2 months developed weight loss, jaundice, pancreatitis and lactic acidosis, with hepatic mitochondrial DNA depletion and accumulation of fialuridine in mitochondrial and nuclear DNA documented.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Chronic hepatitis B patients in the described study population.
raw_record.extra_details: Microvesicular fatty liver form of DILI. In one study most chronic hepatitis B patients treated for more than 2 months developed weight loss, jaundice, pancreatitis and lactic acidosis; tissue analysis showed depletion of hepatic mitochondrial DNA and accumulation of fialuridine in both mitochondrial and nuclear DNA. Primary mechanism proposed as indirect inhibition of mitochondrial function via a 3' hydroxyl group that enables incorporation into nascent DNA chains.

raw_record.support_text: A case of fulminant hepatitis in a patient taking lisinopril (20 mg daily) for 5 weeks for arterial hypertension is reported. Jaundice, fever, myalgia, and marked increases in serum aminotransferase activities occurred after 2 weeks of treatment. Continuing lisinopril for 3 weeks after onset of jaundice was associated with grade III encephalopathy and decreased prothrombin and proaccelerin levels. The authors state this case strongly suggests that lisinopril may induce acute hepatitis and that continued administration after jaundice onset can lead to life-threatening hepatic failure.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of a 55-year-old man treated with lisinopril 20 mg daily for arterial hypertension. Jaundice/fever/myalgia appeared ~2 weeks into treatment (September 15-19, 1988); lisinopril continued until October 10 (5 weeks total), when grade III encephalopathy and marked decreases in prothrombin (20%) and proaccelerin (30%) developed. Fulminant hepatitis with acute liver failure (peak bilirubin 1200 µmol/L, ALT 2561 U/L). Liver biopsy showed extensive hepatocyte necrosis predominating in centrilobular area with cholestasis and inflammatory infiltration; no fibrosis or iron overload. Liver function progressively improved after lisinopril withdrawal (dechallenge), but the patient died on December 7, 1988, after surgery for a perforated duodenal ulcer followed by bacterial infections and gastrointestinal bleeding. Viral hepatitis A/B/C, CMV, EBV, HSV, HIV, rickettsial, and spirochetal infections excluded; no prior liver/biliary disease or alcohol abuse. Enalapril had been discontinued 2 weeks before jaundice; furosemide and bisoprolol (not known hepatotoxic) had been used 11 and 6 months without adverse reaction, so lisinopril was the only recently started drug.

raw_record.support_text: This case series of 18 patients strongly suggests that etifoxine can cause acute hepatitis with a predominant hepatocellular pattern of biological abnormalities, occurring within one month of treatment in 89% of cases. Severe liver injury was observed in 39% of patients, of whom one developed fulminant hepatic failure, and the only patient not recovering fully required liver transplantation. The causal relationship is supported by exclusion of other common causes of hepatitis and improvement or complete recovery after etifoxine discontinuation; the authors characterize the reaction as idiosyncratic rather than immune-allergic, noting no clinical or biological signs of hypersensitivity.
raw_record.extra_details: 18 cases; acute hepatitis with predominantly hepatocellular pattern in 89% within one month of treatment; severe liver injury in 39%; one case of fulminant hepatic failure (case 4) that required liver transplantation; RUCAM causality scores from 5 to 11 (possible to highly probable) across 17 scored cases; all but one patient recovered or improved after etifoxine discontinuation; two of three patients who continued etifoxine after symptom onset developed severe hepatitis; a previously published single case report described severe acute icteric cytolytic hepatitis after 11 days of etifoxine in a 76-year-old woman with full recovery after withdrawal; the potentially severe adverse effect is not mentioned in the summary of product characteristics; no clinical or biological signs of hypersensitivity.

raw_record.support_text: The survey reports that etifoxine can be associated with acute hepatitis showing a cytolytic or mixed biological pattern of liver injury, based on 18 previously reported cases plus 11 additional cases. Evidence supporting a causative role includes uniform liver damage (64% cytolytic hepatitis among acute liver injury cases), time to onset after starting etifoxine of ≤2 months in 92% of cases, lack of association with known hepatotoxicants in 68%, exclusion of non-drug causes of hepatitis in most patients, and favorable outcome after etifoxine discontinuation in all patients with available follow-up. The causal relationship was considered plausible in 64% of patients who developed acute liver injury; the mechanism is unknown, and the lack of clear clinical or biological signs of hypersensitivity supports an idiosyncratic rather than immune-allergic mechanism.
raw_record.extra_details: Total of 29 acute hepatitis cases (18 previously reported in detail plus 11 additional). Time to onset ≤2 months in 92% of cases; 64% cytolytic pattern on acute liver injury; no known hepatotoxic co-medication in 68% of cases; other common causes (viral hepatitis, biliary tract abnormalities) excluded in most patients; favorable outcome after etifoxine discontinuation in all patients with available follow-up. Causal relationship judged plausible in 64% of acute liver injury patients. Mechanism unknown; classified as idiosyncratic (non-immune-allergic). Setting is ordinary therapeutic use of etifoxine as anxiolytic.

raw_record.support_text: The patient developed biochemical evidence of hepatocellular injury without any related clinical symptoms. Differential diagnosis included metformin-induced drug hepatitis, NASH, and autoimmune hepatitis; autoimmune hepatitis was deemed unlikely given absence of musculoskeletal symptoms, lower ESR compared to her rheumatism flare ups, and normalization of ALT despite subsequent flare ups. After metformin was stopped, the ALT fell from a peak of 738 U/l to 273 at 5 days and normalized to 16 U/l at 1 month, remaining normal over 2 years follow-up; a rechallenge test was declined.

raw_record.extra_details: Current case: ALT rose from 31 U/l at 2 weeks to 738 U/l at ~20 weeks poststarting metformin; GGT peaked at 42 IU/l (5 months); ALP normal throughout; negative viral hepatitis serology (A, B, C) and negative ANA, AMA, ASMA; abdominal ultrasound showed diffuse fatty infiltration, no biliary obstruction. Dechallenge: ALT fell to 273 U/l at 5 days and normalized to 16 U/l at 1 month postcessation, remaining normal for 2 years; rechallenge declined. Paper also tabulates 11 previous case reports of metformin-induced hepatic damage (Swislocki, Kutoh, Nammour, Deutsch, Desilets, Shailaja, Cone, Scott, Parikh, Aksay, Babich), with hepatocellular and cholestatic biochemical classifications, jaundice and symptoms in many cases, liver biopsy findings (pericentral necrosis, bile stasis, necroinflammatory injury, lymphocytic vasculitis) in some, and normalization of liver tests after metformin cessation.

raw_record.support_text: The authors present a fatal case of nafcillin-induced hepatotoxicity confirmed by liver biopsy, with total bilirubin peaking to 21.8 mg/dl and an extensive negative evaluation for other causes of hepatic injury.

No fulminant hepatic failure, coagulopathy, or encephalopathy at that time; GGTP and ALP remained >1500 IU/L on follow-up. Prior ertapenem had been discontinued before nafcillin. Patient had pre-existing renal insufficiency (creatinine 2 mg/dL, GFR 26 mL/min).

Registrations for paracetamol-induced liver transplantation fell from 18 to 7 per quarter (an estimated −11, 95% CI −20 to −1; about 482 fewer registrations); the conservative estimate (−4, 95% CI −14 to 5) was not significant. Liver transplantations for paracetamol-induced hepatotoxicity fell from 8 to 5 per quarter (−3, 95% CI −12 to 6, non-significant), while all liver transplantations in the UK rose from 132 to 149 per quarter. Deaths involving paracetamol compounds constituted a small proportion of paracetamol-related deaths and showed no major change after the 1998 legislation. No step change was seen when the intervention point was moved back to the start of 1998.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports that in this case the delayed elimination of methotrexate caused mucosal, digestive, hepatic, and hematologic toxicity that could be lethal. It describes methotrexate (MTX) hepatic toxicity as presenting as hepatic cytolysis (cytolyse hépatique), which is frequently observed, transient, and reversible within one to two weeks, and which does not prevent subsequent continuation of MTX. The hepatotoxicity occurred after accidental rapid intravenous infusion of high-dose MTX in a patient treated for acute B-cell lymphoblastic leukemia, alongside acute renal failure, pancytopenia, digestive signs, and odynophagia/grade 2 mucositis.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Accidental overdose of high-dose MTX administered intravenously in less than 2 h instead of 24 h, in the course of treatment for B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia
raw_record.extra_details: Case: female patient with B-cell ALL. Hepatotoxicity consisted of hepatic cytolysis, transient and reversible within 1-2 weeks, not precluding later MTX continuation; patient was jaundiced (ictère) with total bilirubinemia 100 µmol/L at J17. Associated toxicities: acute renal failure (creatinine up to 398 µmol/L), digestive disturbances, pancytopenia (thrombocytopenia then leuconeutropenia), odynophagia/grade 2 mucositis, mucosal ulcerations. Methotrexatemia peaked at 99 µmol/L (J2) and declined to 0.27 µmol/L (J17); hemofiltration (CVVH) used (marked *). Delayed elimination defined as methotrexatemia >1 µmol/L at H48 or persistence >0.2 µmol/L beyond H72; renal toxicity attributed to tubular precipitation of MTX and its metabolites, possible direct toxic effect on tubule, and afferent arteriole vasoconstriction. Outcome favorable; patient discharged.

raw_record.support_text: Lapatinib (Tykerb/Tyverb, GlaxoSmithKline), a HER2 and EGFR inhibitor approved for advanced or metastatic HER2-positive breast cancer, has been associated with liver injury and a low incidence of National Cancer Institute CTCAE grade 3 isolated alanine aminotransferase (ALT) elevation (3%) and potentially life-threatening concurrent ALT elevation with hyperbilirubinemia (Hy's Law, 0.6%). Previous investigations found the Class II allele HLA-DRB1*07:01 (and DQA1*02:01 in linkage disequilibrium) is associated with lapatinib-induced liver injury and Hy's Law cases, and this association was prospectively validated in a large, well-controlled, randomized clinical trial.
raw_record.extra_details: Low incidence (~3%) NCI CTCAE grade 3 isolated ALT elevation and ~0.6% potentially life-threatening concurrent ALT elevation with hyperbilirubinemia (Hy's Law) in treated breast cancer patients. HLA-DRB1*07:01 (with DQA1*02:01) associated with lapatinib-induced liver injury and Hy's Law; high negative predictive value but moderate positive predictive value limits it as a prospective predictive biomarker. Association prospectively validated in the EGF105485 (TEACH, NCT00374322) randomized Phase III trial of lapatinib vs placebo for 12 months in HER2-positive early breast cancer; GWAS and whole-genome sequencing identified no additional associations beyond HLA-DRB1*07:01. Approved for use in combination with other targeted chemotherapy agents.

raw_record.support_text: Both patients in this report developed hepatic failure following flutamide treatment, and neither had been exposed to known hepatotoxins; the authors conclude that an unpredictable reaction caused by flutamide seems plausible. For patient 1, previous case descriptions also noted severe liver damage with jaundice, ascites, impaired coagulation and hepatic coma following flutamide, while in the present second patient jaundice resolved and liver function improved after flutamide cessation, with a liver biopsy read as drug-induced.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Two patients with prostatic cancer; patient 1 additionally received Zoladex and dextropropoxyphene, though Zoladex was argued unlikely to contribute, and had renal impairment possibly raising metabolite levels.
raw_record.extra_details: Two case reports. Case 1: severe liver damage with jaundice, ascites, impaired coagulation and hepatic coma; developed after therapeutic flutamide during period of therapeutic Zoladex. Case 2: serum alkaline phosphatase 1202 U/l, ALAT 56 U/l, bilirubin 255 µmol/l; liver biopsy showed slight portal lymphocytic/histiocytic infiltrate without obstruction, scattered focal necroses, and centrilobular cholestasis with bile thrombi and bile pigment in Kupffer cells, interpreted as drug-induced; liver tests improved and jaundice disappeared ~2 months after flutamide cessation; the patient died 1 year later from prostatic cancer. Flutamide is metabolized to hydroxyflutamide plus minor metabolites; renal impairment hypothesized to raise metabolite levels, though animal toxicology showed no serious hepatotoxicity. Prior reports described only slight transaminase elevations that normalized despite continued therapy.

raw_record.extra_details: Four cases (1M, 3F) with severe delayed cholestatic hepatitis; jaundice, pruritus, dark urine, pale faeces appeared 17-28 days after commencing flucloxacillin and 7-14 days after cessation before presentation. Marked elevations of serum bilirubin, ALP, GGT and AST in all patients; extrahepatic biliary obstruction excluded by ERCP in three and ultrasound/CT in one; negative serology for hepatitis A/B, CMV, ANA, AMA. Biopsy showed centrilobular canalicular cholestasis, hepatocyte swelling, mild lobular inflammation, sinusoidal eosinophil infiltration, portal infiltrate of lymphocytes, macrophages, neutrophils and eosinophils; no portal oedema or bile duct proliferation. Symptoms resolved with bilirubin normalisation in 19-60 days in all patients; two patients had persistent ALP/GGT elevations 111 and 380 days after cessation. One patient had mild peripheral eosinophilia; none had rash or fever.

raw_record.support_text: To assess the correlation between albendazole and liver injury, the RUCAM scale was applied. The R ratio (ALT/ULN divided by ALP/ULN) was 48, meeting the hepatocellular pattern criterion (R ≥5). Scoring: drug taken 2 weeks before symptom onset (2 pts), improvement within 30 days of stopping the drug (2 pts), no risk factors (0), no co-administered drugs (0), no viral hepatitis, biliary obstruction, alcoholic or ischemic hepatitis (2 pts), and known hepatotoxic drug (2 pts). Including the response to re-exposure item (3 pts, attributing a liver injury 8 years earlier to albendazole), the total score was 11, indicating a definitive (definite) drug-induced liver injury.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of albendazole-induced drug-induced liver injury (DILI). RUCAM score 11 (definitive), with R ratio 48 (hepatocellular). RUCAM items: drug taken 2 weeks before symptom onset, improvement within 30 days of stopping drug, no risk factors, no co-administered drugs, alternative causes (viral hepatitis, biliary obstruction, alcoholic/ischemic hepatitis) excluded. Re-exposure item (3 pts) reflects a prior liver injury 8 years earlier also attributed to albendazole. Other causes (viral hepatitis, biliary obstruction, alcoholic hepatitis) excluded; abdominal ultrasound showed normal liver, gallbladder, bile ducts, and pancreas. Patient treated with supportive therapy including fluids, discharged on hospital day 9 with improvement, and liver enzymes normalized on outpatient follow-up. Paper also notes amoxicillin/clavulanate and acetaminophen are the most common DILI causes, and herbal medicine (한약) accounts for 40.2% of DILI cases in Korea.

raw_record.support_text: Hepatotoxicity remains a significant concern in those receiving isoniazid therapy. In 1970-1971, the US Public Health Service monitored 14,000 people receiving isoniazid for development of hepatotoxicity; the rate of hepatitis was found to be between 1% and 2.3%, and a number of fatal cases during that surveillance period prompted awareness of this potentially serious adverse effect. More recent data suggest a greater (3.8%) risk of serious hepatotoxicity during a 9-month course of isoniazid. This risk of hepatitis is increased in those with chronic liver disease and with alcohol consumption.

raw_record.extra_details: Case report of sertraline-induced hepatotoxicity (acute liver injury). In a separate cited case (Persky and Reinus), inadvertent rechallenge with sertraline in a 23-year-old woman produced a prompt rise in ALT, suggestive of an anamnestic response; intentional rechallenge was not performed in the authors' patient due to medical risk. Theories of mechanism include immunologically mediated hepatitis supported by eosinophils on liver biopsy and the idiosyncratic reaction, and mitochondrial dysfunction with ATP depletion and inhibition of mitochondrial respiration. raw_record.support_text: The paper's case demonstrates that buprenorphine (BPN) misuse by the intranasal route can also lead to severe hepatitis, in a patient without chronic HCV but with a history of alcohol consumption. The hepatitis is described as BPN-induced (BPN-induced hepatitis), attributed primarily to mitochondrial dysfunction exacerbated by cofactors such as HCV, alcohol, and concomitant medications.

raw_record.extra_details: Primary mechanism is mitochondrial dysfunction: BPN is a lipophilic tertiary amine taken up by mitochondria that impairs fatty acid beta-oxidation and/or mitochondrial energy production, causing ATP depletion and liver cell necrosis. A second possible mechanism is formation of reactive metabolites (BPN or norbuprenorphine) that covalently bind to microsomal proteins and deplete glutathione, though the mitochondrial mechanism is considered predominant. Concentration-dependent mechanism supported by case reports and animal models. After sublingual dosing of 8-16 mg/day, peak plasma concentrations reach 5.8-14 µg/L (therapeutic range usually 1-10 µg/L); IV administration gives higher, more rapid levels (0.3 mg IV gives mean Cmax ~15 µg/L); sublingual bioavailability 15-30% vs intranasal 38-44%, with intranasal concentrations 2-3-fold higher than sublingual.

raw_record.support_text: The paper studies patients with acetaminophen (APAP)-induced liver injury, including 69 acute liver failure (AALF) patients. It reports that circulating mitochondrial damage biomarkers (nDNA fragments, GDH, mtDNA) were increased, supporting that mitochondrial damage is central in APAP hepatotoxicity in humans after APAP overdose.

raw_record.extra_details: Cohort of 69 AALF patients (34 survivors, 35 non-survivors; 76% female, median age 34, range 18-80); peak ALT 5870±535 U/L, peak bilirubin 7.6±0.6 mg/dL, peak PT 41±3 s, peak creatinine 3.3±0.3 mg/dL. Mitochondrial damage biomarkers (nDNA fragments, GDH, mtDNA) were increased 1.5-2.1-fold in serum of AALF patients who died vs survivors, while ALT was similar; primary mode of cell death in human APAP hepatotoxicity is described as oncotic necrosis; mechanism attributed to mitochondrial dysfunction and sterile inflammation.

raw_record.support_text: In patients with advanced renal cell carcinoma receiving first-line pazopanib (n = 44), 34 % developed liver toxicity (elevated bilirubin or liver transaminase levels), reaching maximum toxicity at a median of 60 days after starting therapy; resolution occurred within a median of 3-21 days after stopping in all but one patient, and liver dysfunction recurred in 27 % after restarting. In an analysis of pazopanib monotherapy clinical trial patients, 18 % of renal cell carcinoma patients (n = 586) had ALT elevations >=3x ULN and 5 % >=8x ULN, with 87 % occurring within 18 weeks; among 1,830 pazopanib study patients there were two adjudicated cases of pazopanib-related liver failure.
raw_record.extra_details: Pazopanib is a VEGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor used at 800 mg orally once daily for advanced renal cell carcinoma. Liver toxicity with elevated bilirubin or transaminases in 34 % of 44 first-line patients; ALT >=3x ULN in 18 % and >=8x ULN in 5 % of 586 RCC patients, mostly within 18 weeks; recovery in 91 % (30 % while continuing therapy); 65 % of 31 rechallenged patients had no ALT recurrence; two adjudicated pazopanib-related liver failure cases among 1,830 patients. In the COMPARZ trial pazopanib showed higher incidences of ALT and bilirubin elevations than sunitinib (95 % CI for relative risk excluding unity).

raw_record.support_text: Hepatotoxicity is described as an expected event for pazopanib, manifested by increases in serum transaminases (ALT and AST) and bilirubin. In clinical trials in renal cell carcinoma and soft tissue sarcoma, approximately 18% of patients experienced ALT >3×ULN, 5% ALT >8×ULN, and 2% had concurrent ALT >3×ULN and bilirubin >2×ULN in the absence of alkaline phosphatase >3×ULN. Hepatotoxicity was also reported as a dose-limiting toxicity in this pazopanib plus paclitaxel study.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity is an expected/known event of pazopanib. Majority (92.5%) of transaminase elevations occurred within the first 18 weeks of treatment. In RCC and STS clinical trials ~18% had ALT>3×ULN, 5% had ALT>8×ULN, 2% had concurrent ALT>3×ULN and bilirubin>2×ULN without ALP>3×ULN (Hy's Law-like pattern). In the present pazopanib+paclitaxel study 4 patients had grade 3 or 4 transaminase elevations, and hepatotoxicity was a DLT. Pharmacogenetic exploration of HFE, UGT1A1, CYP3A4, CYP2C8, ABCB1, ABCG2, OATP1B1 markers. Pazopanib is a weak inhibitor of CYP3A4/CYP2C8.

raw_record.support_text: The case report concludes that reversible severe liver toxicity with pazopanib treatment is a known rare side effect of pazopanib, and that low-dose personalized rechallenge in responding patients is a therapeutic option in experienced hands, though this conflicts with the current Summary of Product Characteristics and requires close monitoring of liver function, e.g., weekly liver function testing.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states explicitly that pazopanib is known to cause liver toxicity and that a relationship between pazopanib exposure and alanine transaminase (ALT) elevations has been described in clinical trials. The study investigated this exposure-liver toxicity relationship in real-world patients and evaluated management of pazopanib-induced liver toxicity in routine care.
raw_record.extra_details: Retrospective observational cohort study (Pazopanib Exposure and Liver Toxicity). Liver toxicity observed in 25 of 133 patients (19%); pazopanib exposure was comparable in patients with vs without liver toxicity (27.7 mg/L vs 28.1 mg/L). The study did not demonstrate a clear relationship between pazopanib exposure and occurrence of pazopanib-induced liver toxicity. Seven patients permanently discontinued pazopanib after liver toxicity; of the remaining 18, continuation/restart was successful in 16, with half continuing at the same dose as prior to liver toxicity. Liver toxicity definition centered on ALT elevations.

raw_record.support_text: Methotrexate sodium is used as monotherapy in the long-term management of severe psoriasis, and liver fibrosis is described as its main disadvantage. The text notes that studies vary on the prevalence of methotrexate-induced liver injury in patients with psoriasis, and recommends evaluation of liver enzyme levels, procollagen III peptide (PIIINP) levels, and periodic liver biopsies during therapy. The conclusions further frame transient elastography and FibroTest as effective noninvasive tools for monitoring hepatotoxicity in patients receiving methotrexate for psoriasis.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Findings in patients with psoriasis receiving long-term methotrexate; comorbidities such as obesity, alcohol intake, and diabetes mellitus may increase the risk of liver disease.
raw_record.extra_details: Liver fibrosis is cited as the main disadvantage of methotrexate; recommended monitoring includes serial liver enzymes, PIIINP, periodic liver biopsy, and (per 2009 AAD guidelines) biopsy consideration in low-risk patients with persistent abnormal LFTs or after cumulative methotrexate dose of 3.5-4.0 g. In the study cohort (77 patients), transient elastography was abnormal in 9/50 (18%; range 7.1-11.3 kPa) and FibroTest (METAVIR >F1) abnormal in 11/70 (16%); cumulative methotrexate dose (r=0.31) and duration of therapy (r=0.36) correlated with abnormal FibroTest results. All 5 biopsied patients showed steatosis, and 2 had hepatic fibrosis, 1 with a sinusoidal pattern attributed to steatohepatitis.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report a case of symptomatic acute hepatotoxicity secondary to the use of bicalutamide, a nonsteroidal anti-androgen used during initiation of androgen deprivation therapy for metastatic prostate cancer, noting that while uncommon, acute drug-induced liver injury is possible with bicalutamide therapy, typically presenting as transient liver function derangement.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Elderly patient (81 years old) with metastatic prostate cancer receiving bicalutamide for anti-androgen flare suppression during androgen deprivation therapy; single-agent use.
raw_record.extra_details: An 81-year-old African American male with metastatic prostate cancer started bicalutamide 3 weeks before presenting with nonspecific symptoms and 1-day jaundice; physical exam showed scleral icterus; workup showed acutely elevated transaminases (>5x ULN), elevated alkaline phosphatase, conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, and coagulopathy. Competing etiologies (viral, common toxins, drugs, autoimmune, copper-induced hepatitis) were considered. Bicalutamide was discontinued and the patient managed with supportive care, with improvement of clinical and laboratory abnormalities within days. The authors note that while rare, clinically significant and potentially life-threatening liver injury can result from bicalutamide and that prompt recognition and discontinuation are necessary.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a patient with metastatic prostate cancer who developed cyproterone acetate (CPA)-induced hepatic failure, which manifested as bilirubinuria initially misinterpreted as gross hematuria. The patient died despite receiving critical care.

raw_record.extra_details: CPA-induced fulminant/acute hepatic failure. The introduction documents the spectrum of reported CPA hepatotoxic reactions including immunoallergic cytotoxic reactions, cholestasis, autoimmune hepatitis, acute hepatitis, and fulminant hepatic failure, and notes that only 1 of 14 reported patients with CPA-induced hepatic failure has survived. In this case, hepatic failure developed months after starting daily 200 mg CPA; laboratory findings included AST/ALT 529/223 IU/L, total/direct bilirubin 10.6/5.2 mg/dL, ammonia 294, INR 2.4; the patient died 20 days after admission of multi-organ failure. Two-year survival was 89.5% in the APAP SS, 75.5% in non-APAP SS, and 92.4% in LT recipients. Acetaminophen overdose is described as a cause of ALF, with spontaneous survivors of APAP overdose experiencing ongoing psychiatric and substance abuse morbidity.

APAP spontaneous survivor group comprised 306 patients with 2-year survival 89.5%. Independent predictors of 2-year mortality in the APAP group were high serum phosphate level and patient age (c-statistic = 0.65 (0.54, 0.76)). ALF defined by jaundice or illness of <26 weeks, mental status changes, and INR > 1.5 without known underlying chronic liver disease.

raw_record.support_text: The paper is a retrospective case study of 25 children (aged 11-16 years) with severe acetaminophen poisoning, exploring the dose-response relationship between ingested acetaminophen and hepatotoxicity, early biochemical/clinical predictors, the impact of early N-acetylcysteine treatment on hepatotoxicity, and the incidence of nephrotoxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patients aged 11-16 years with severe acetaminophen poisoning (overdose setting).
raw_record.extra_details: Retrospective case study (n=25 children). Hepatotoxicity was assessed by maximum INR and maximum ALT. Early predictors of hepatotoxicity included initial bilirubin (p=0.0003 vs max INR), initial phosphate (p=0.003 vs max INR), initial INR (p=0.0003 vs max ALT), initial creatinine (p=0.002 vs max ALT), prehospital vomiting episodes, and time of N-acetylcysteine initiation. Nephrotoxicity incidence was 12%. No significant relationship between the amount of ingested acetaminophen and degree of hepatotoxicity. The paper states that acetaminophen overdoses may cause hepatotoxicity and fulminant liver failure.

Four patients homozygous for POLG1 p.W748S and p.E1143G had hepatic mtDNA depletion; one of these died prior to anticipated transplantation and the other three survived 4-19 years after liver transplantation. One patient with a heterozygous POLG1 p.Q1236H mutation but no mtDNA depletion died suddenly two years after transplantation. Three patients had been suspected to have Wilson's disease. POLG1 analysis recommended before introducing valproate therapy.

raw_record.support_text: A 12-yr-old girl was prescribed dapsone for PPD. Twenty days later she developed high fever, followed by a skin rash, and required hospitalization; dapsone was discontinued on HD 1. Laboratory findings showed elevated total bilirubin (1.8 mg/dL), ALT (141 IU/L) and AST (158 IU/L). Her liver function subsequently deteriorated with rising bilirubin, AST and ALT and coagulopathy, and she developed fulminant hepatic failure, hepatic encephalopathy (grade 3) and hepatorenal syndrome.

raw_record.extra_details: Case report titled 'Dapsone hypersensitivity induces fulminant liver failure'. Latency ~20 days from dapsone start; high fever up to 40 �C, body skin rash; laboratory evolution (HD 12: total bilirubin 11.6 mg/dL, AST 737 IU/L, ALT 372 IU/L, prothrombin time 15.0 s/1.4 INR; HD 14: bilirubin 19.6 mg/dL, AST 1146 IU/L, ALT 199 IU/L, PT 26.8 s/2.58 INR; HD 15: grade 3 hepatic encephalopathy, hepatorenal syndrome, ammonia 124 µg/dL). Positive direct Coombs test, low C3/C4, elevated IgG/IgM, negative FANA/anti-dsDNA/anti-cardiolipin. Treated with steroids, rituximab and plasmapheresis; registered UNOS status 1; emergent LDLT on HD 17 (Child-Pugh 11, MELD 38, donor cousin).

raw_record.extra_details: PTU-attributed liver failure during pregnancy is a rare entity; serious hepatotoxicity during pregnancy has been reported. PTU is advocated as treatment of choice in the first trimester, with monitoring of hepatic function every 4 weeks.

raw_record.support_text: This commentary letter describes the progressive hepatotoxic consequences of long-term lomitapide use in a patient treated for 13 years, with deterioration to steatohepatitis and fibrosis and elevated alkaline phosphatase levels over time. It notes that FDA labeling for lomitapide recommends discontinuing the drug in patients with this presentation, that hepatic steatosis greater than 5% develops in 78% of lomitapide users, and that severe hepatotoxic effects were observed with lomitapide use despite significant triglyceride-level reductions, warranting careful assessment before and during off-label therapy.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Used off label for hypertriglyceridemia-associated pancreatitis; long-term (13 years) therapy.
raw_record.extra_details: Progression to steatohepatitis and fibrosis with elevated alkaline phosphatase over time; hepatic steatosis >5% occurs in 78% of lomitapide users; mean serum fasting LDL-C 63 mg/dL before therapy; FDA labeling recommends discontinuing lomitapide in this presentation; significant reductions in triglyceride levels; off-label indication despite available LDL-C reductions of approximately 65% with lomitapide; annual cost >$250,000.

It notes only one death recorded over 20 years among patients in the 100–149 nomogram range of acute paracetamol concentrations, with high-risk patients treated with acetylcysteine. raw_record.support_text: Hepatic toxicity is described as a frequent side effect of intrahepatic FUDR (5-fluoro-2-deoxyuridine) infusion via an implantable pump. In a Memorial Sloan-Kettering Cancer Center study, bilirubin elevations above 3 mg/dL occurred in 20% of patients and transaminase elevations in 71%, with roughly 25% of patients across the various pump studies showing bilirubin elevation. There is disagreement about the nature of the toxicity: some view it as hepatitis based on documented hepatocyte necrosis and cholestasis on liver biopsy, while others attribute it to pericholangitis and fibrosis of biliary radicals. In early stages hepatic enzyme elevations return to normal on drug withdrawal and rest, but in some patients jaundice does not improve and biliary strictures may develop at the hepatic duct bifurcation, common bile duct, or intrahepatic radicals.

raw_record.support_text: The authors conclude that cephalosporins appear to be a relatively common cause of antibiotic-associated liver injury, with a latency of typically 1-3 weeks, and that a single infusion of cefazolin can lead to DILI. The course of cefazolin-induced DILI is usually a mild-to-moderate, self-limited cholestatic injury, although severe and even fatal DILI may occur in a small number of patients, and some cases may be followed by evidence of chronic injury.
raw_record.extra_details: DILIN adjudicated case series of 19 patients with cefazolin-induced DILI following single prophylactic infusion. Latency from administration to symptom onset: <1 week in 16%, 2-4 weeks in 68%, >4 weeks in 16%; jaundice 95%, itching 100%, nausea 79%, rash 32%, fever 47%, eosinophilia 26%, hospitalization 69%. Severity distribution: mild 5%, moderate 32%, moderate and hospitalized 53%, severe 11%, fatal 0. DILIN causality: probable 5%, highly likely 84%, definite 11%. Persistent abnormal liver tests >6 months in 16%. Histology shows cholestatic hepatitis with mild portal/lobular inflammation and prominent canalicular cholestasis (zone 3). ALT/AST/ALP/bilirubin at onset and peak values reported per patient; disease site as ulceration (DILIN score: definite >95%, very likely 75-95%, probable 50-75%). Immuno-allergic features often present but usually transient and mild; DRESS syndrome uncommon; rapid recurrence upon re-exposure common.

Across clinical trials serious hepatotoxicity occurred in 109/760 (14%) with 1 fatality (1/1192) attributed to acute liver failure in a patient receiving idelalisib plus ofatumumab (grade 4 sepsis present at death). raw_record.support_text: Elevation in ALT and AST levels can occur during treatment with idelalisib, and hepatotoxicity was one of the most common reasons for discontinuation of the drug in clinical trials. It typically manifests 4–12 weeks after treatment initiation in asymptomatic patients, is reversible in most cases after dose interruption, and grade 3–4 ALT/AST elevation (>5x ULN) was reported in 14% of patients, leading to death in one case. In the phase I trial 28% of patients experienced liver enzyme elevation of any grade, and in the phase III study transaminase elevations were more common in the idelalisib plus rituximab arm, with grade ≥3 elevations in 5–8% and any-grade increases in 25–35%.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity was a common reason for idelalisib discontinuation in clinical trials. Phase III (idelalisib plus rituximab): grade ≥3 elevations in 5–8% and any-grade increase in 25–35%; drug withheld and successfully reinitiated in two thirds of patients. Prescribing information recommends against concomitant hepatotoxic drugs and close ALT/AST monitoring (3–5x ULN maintain with monitoring; 5–20x ULN interrupt until resolution; >20x ULN permanently discontinue). In frontline trials grade ≥3 elevations occurred in 67% (O'Brien) and 57% (Lampson); liver biopsies in the Lampson study showed increased activated cytotoxic T cells within the liver parenchyma.

raw_record.support_text: Hepatotoxicity is described as a common adverse event during idelalisib combination therapy or monotherapy, characterized by ALT and AST elevations rarely accompanied by alkaline phosphatase or bilirubin elevation, suggestive of hepatocellular damage. The transaminase elevations are mostly noticeable in the first 8–12 weeks (median 5.3 weeks) with a plateau within week 20, often normalize after dose cessation or dose reduction, but in some cases an acute liver insufficiency based on an autoinflammatory reaction may be observed. The autoimmune nature was confirmed by lymphocytic infiltrate in liver biopsies, increased CCL-3 and CCL-4, and decreased peripheral blood regulatory T cells.
raw_record.extra_details: Transaminitis onset in first 8–12 weeks (median 5.3 weeks), plateau within week 20 in the relapse/refractory setting; activity normalizes following dose cessation or dose reduction; occasional acute liver insufficiency due to an autoinflammatory reaction. In treatment-naïve patients ALT/AST elevation seen more often; ALT/AST elevation noted in 79% of younger patients with CLL treated with idelalisib and ofatumumab (54% grade ≥3). Younger age and mutated IGHV identified as significant risk factors. Autoimmune nature confirmed by lymphocytic infiltrate on liver biopsy, increased proinflammatory cytokines CCL-3 and CCL-4, decreased peripheral regulatory T cells; transaminitis resolved after drug hold or steroids. HBV/HCV/CMV/HIV status assessment recommended before treatment initiation or in case of unexpected hepatotoxicity. In a separate co-exposure setting, the combination of idelalisib, lenalidomide and rituximab was poorly tolerated and led to premature termination of two clinical trials; Cheah et al. noted grade ≥3 transaminitis in six of seven patients with two deaths, one from acute liver failure.

Across the combined datasets, ALT >3 × ULN and >5 × ULN events occurred in 20% and 11% of pazopanib-treated patients, respectively, and HLA-B*57:01 carriage was associated with higher risk of ALT elevation ({OR, 2.0 for >3 × ULN and OR, 2.1 for >5 × ULN}).

raw_record.support_text: Paracetamol (acetaminophen) overdose is described as the leading cause of acute liver failure in the Western world, with roughly 150 direct deaths per year in the UK through liver injury. The mechanism is stated to be well defined: in overdose the reactive metabolite NAPQI is generated in excess, depleting glutathione and binding covalently to cellular proteins, producing oxidative stress and hepatocyte death predominately by necrosis, which can be translated from rodent models to humans using mechanistic biomarkers.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Single acute overdose of paracetamol in the context of hospital admission for treatment with intravenous acetylcysteine (NAC) started within 24 h of ingestion.
raw_record.extra_details: Acute liver injury (ALI) defined as peak serum ALT >150 U/L and double the admission value; hepatotoxicity defined as peak ALT >1000 U/L. The reactive metabolite N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine (NAPQI) is generated in excess in overdose, depleting cellular glutathione (GSH) then binding covalently to cellular proteins, causing oxidative stress and hepatocyte death predominantly by necrosis. Cohort of 727 hospital presentations; higher admission plasma paracetamol concentrations were associated with increased ALI/hepatotoxicity despite prompt intravenous NAC (ALI by nomogram 0-100: 6%, 101-150: 3%, 151-200: 3%, 201-300: 9%, 301-500: 13%, over 501 mg/L: 27%; p<0.0001), a dose-response persisting in patients treated with NAC within 8 h and in those with normal presenting ALT. UK context: ~100,000 emergency department presentations and ~50,000 acute hospital admissions annually, ~150 direct deaths, ~65,000 NAC bed days per year. Study concluded standard intravenous NAC dose may be too low for higher paracetamol exposure.

raw_record.extra_details: Paracetamol poisoning is described as a cause of acute liver failure (ALF) requiring transplantation, in the same category as Amanita phalloides poisoning. In this cohort, serum bilirubin elevation was a statistically significant negative prognostic factor for 5-year survival (bilirubin >17.5 mg/dl is one of the King's College criteria for urgent transplantation in non-paracetamol indications), along with transfused red blood cell and fresh frozen plasma units. raw_record.support_text: The paper states that there have been several case reports of clinically apparent liver injury associated with deferasirox (DFX) therapy, which was often severe and occasionally fatal. Onset of acute liver injury ranged from a few days to 8 weeks after starting DFX, the pattern of injury was typically hepatocellular with marked elevations in serum aminotransferase levels, recovery was usually rapid once DFX was stopped, but some cases were associated with progressive liver injury and hepatic failure.
raw_record.extra_details: Iron chelator given to iron-overloaded, regularly transfused patients (thalassemia, sickle cell disease, myelodysplastic anemia, aplastic anemia, hereditary hemochromatosis, congenital dyserythropoetic anemia). Onset of acute liver injury a few days to 8 weeks after starting DFX; typically hepatocellular pattern with marked aminotransferase elevations; rapid recovery on discontinuation, but some cases had progressive liver injury and hepatic failure. Summary table lists 3 previously reported acute liver failure cases (ages 12-63 y): one full recovery with conservative management, one death with management of sepsis/multiorgan failure, one full recovery after N-acetylcysteine. DFX-treatment stopped liver-test elevation occurred in 6% of patients and led to drug discontinuation in 1-2%. Underlying diagnoses in the case table were hereditary hemochromatosis, sickle cell disease, and congenital dyserythropoetic anemia type I.

raw_record.extra_details: Overall prevalence of AZA-associated hepatotoxicity was 15.2%. GGT-predominant elevation was the most common pattern, seen in 67.8% of patients with hepatotoxicity; isolated GGT elevation was seen in 6.9%. raw_record.support_text: The authors report a rare case of propofol-induced hepatitis, noting only six other cases of propofol hepatic toxicity have been reported worldwide. In this case of acute hepatitis no preconditions such as underlying liver disease or general allergic sensitivity were present, and the authors state that the effectiveness of steroid therapy demonstrates that propofol toxicity is primarily immunological in nature, with correct diagnosis and therapy avoiding progression to advanced liver disease.
raw_record.extra_details: Propofol was used to induce anesthesia in an interventional endoscopic procedure. Therapy with intravenous N-acetyl cysteine (Fluimucil 20%, 10 g in 500 ml NaCl 0.9% in 24 h) and prednisolone (250 mg IV, then 50 mg with tapering) was effective; patient discharged on the seventh day in good condition. Only six other cases of propofol hepatic toxicity reported worldwide. Authors attribute toxicity primarily to an immunological (immune) mechanism.

The mechanism of DILI is unknown and likely idiosyncratic, with a clinical picture of cholestatic injury remarkably similar to that found with anabolic steroids. Histology showed bland cholestasis with minimal inflammation and absent hepatocellular or bile duct injury.
raw_record.extra_details: Single patient treated with mifepristone for hypercortisolism (Cushing syndrome). Clinical picture of bland cholestasis with minimal inflammation and absent hepatocellular injury or bile duct injury, similar to anabolic-steroid-induced DILI; mechanism unknown and likely idiosyncratic. During follow-up, ALT peaked at 169 IU/L, AST at 157 IU/L, Alk P at 170 IU/L, and bilirubin peaked at 33 mg/dL (baseline ~0.9 mg/dL); patient developed fatigue, clay-colored stools, and jaundice requiring two hospitalizations, with liver tests returning to normal by 40 weeks. Histology showed extensive bile plugging, scattered lobular lymphocytes, portal eosinophils, and minimal portal fibrosis.

raw_record.support_text: TGR-1202 is a PI3Kδ inhibitor studied in a Phase I trial in patients with relapsed/refractory hematologic malignancies. Notably, in comparison with other PI3Kδ inhibitors, no cases of hepatotoxicity or colitis were observed among the patients; in the combination trial with ublituximab, no hepatotoxicity or grade 3/4 toxicities were reported. These statements explicitly rule out hepatotoxicity for this agent.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients with relapsed/refractory hematologic malignancies (CLL; phase I settings).
raw_record.extra_details: PI3Kδ inhibitor (also named Filanesol). In a Phase I dose-escalation monotherapy study, no cases of hepatotoxicity or colitis were observed, notably in comparison with other PI3Kδ inhibitors; PRL was seen in 4 of 6 CLL patients at doses above 800 mg/day, with 5/9 evaluable CLL patients achieving PR. In a separate phase I trial combining TGR-1202 with ublituximab (anti-CD20 mAb) in B-cell malignancies, no hepatotoxicity or grade 3/4 toxicities were reported.

raw_record.support_text: Belinostat, a new HDACI, was studied as a single agent in refractory/relapsed lymphoma as daily infusions on days 1–5 every 21 days. Adverse effects were nausea, fatigue, and fever; severe reactions included acute kidney injury, thrombocytopenia, and toxic liver failure, with 7.8 % of patients dying of drug reaction. Fatalities were attributed to drug-related tumor lysis syndrome, hepatic failure, and ventricular fibrillation from QTc prolongation.

raw_record.support_text: The study demonstrates that the cytochrome P450 enzyme-mediated mechanism of APAP (acetaminophen) toxicity translates to humans, with a higher percentage of circulating CYP metabolites present in patients with APAP overdose and liver injury. APAP overdose is described as a common medical emergency, and the CYP metabolites were superior to both ALT and APAP for early acute liver injury (ALI) risk stratification.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose setting; patients received N-acetylcysteine treatment; the CYP-metabolite-based stratification shows APAP and ALT lacked predictive value for ALI in discovery and validation cohorts.
raw_record.extra_details: CYP metabolites (e.g., APAP-Cys/APAP-Sul) predicted ALI with ROC-AUC 0.83 (0.71-0.94) in validation cohort, superior to APAP (ROC-AUC 0.57, 0.41-0.73) and ALT (ROC-AUC 0.51, 0.35-0.67). In the SNAP trial, post-hoc adjustment for APAP-Cys/APAP-Sul showed ondansetron's reported increase in ALI was no different from placebo (OR 0.465, 0.097-2.226, P=0.338). Modified NAC regimen did not alter APAP half-life or AUC(0-20.25h) CYP/total compared to conventional NAC. Cytochrome P450-mediated mechanism described in rodent models is reported to translate to humans.

raw_record.support_text: The study systematically assessed outcomes of massive paracetamol overdose. Key findings were that, despite receiving standard therapy with acetylcysteine, patients with massive overdoses were more likely to develop significant liver injury (hepatotoxicity), kidney injury, and coagulopathy, with the APAP p1:APAP t ratio predicting organ toxicity. This relationship persisted even when acetylcysteine was administered within 8 hours of reported ingestion.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Massive paracetamol overdose setting; patients received standard acetylcysteine therapy.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity occurred despite acetylcysteine started within 8 hours of reported ingestion; risk was higher in the highest plasma paracetamol concentration subgroups; delayed absorption (double plasma peaks), extended half-life with progressive hepatotoxicity, and NAPQI generation after acetylcysteine infusion may explain injury in early presenting poisoning.
