raw_record.support_text: The study of patients taking paracetamol overdoses reports risks of organ injury, including hepatotoxicity and acute liver injury, rising with increasing extrapolated 4-hour plasma paracetamol concentrations and a higher APAPpl:APAPt ratio. In the cohort, hepatotoxicity frequencies increased from 0.0% at 4-hour concentrations <100-150 mg/L to 30.8% at >500 mg/L, and acute liver injury from 4.4% to 53.8%. The authors conclude that under current protocols patients taking massive paracetamol overdoses may be undertreated and that increased dose intensity and/or duration of acetylcysteine therapy could be beneficial.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose (including massive paracetamol overdose) with ingestion-to-treatment timing; treated with standard or early acetylcysteine in many cases.
raw_record.extra_details: Clinical database cohort (single hospital; blinded data entry). Hepatotoxicity frequency 0.0% at 4-hour extrapolated paracetamol <100-150 mg/L rising to 30.8% at >500 mg/L; acute liver injury rising from 4.4% to 53.8%. Peak serum aminotransferase, INR (coagulopathy) and serum creatinine correlated with reported dose, extrapolated 4-hour plasma concentration and APAPpl:APAPt ratio. APAPpl:APAPt ≥3 associated with increased risk (OR 7.15, 95% CI 4.20-12.06) and ≥6 strongly predictive (OR 13.93, 95% CI 6.24-31.79) of serum aminotransferase elevations >2-fold ULN. Concerns that massive overdose patients may be undertreated with standard acetylcysteine; possible role for extended/dose-intensity acetylcysteine or multiple-dose activated charcoal. Kidney injury also reported.

raw_record.support_text: The patient, with no specific past medical history and negative serologic/radiologic findings, developed jaundice-related liver injury after taking LCZ (levocetirizine) for 2 months, with normalization of all liver enzymes within 3 weeks of discontinuation and biopsy showing portal inflammation, hepatitis, and apoptotic hepatocytes. Based on timing of LCZ administration and clinical course, the authors suspected, and then confirmed after biopsy and recovery on drug withdrawal, an LCZ-induced liver injury, which was considered an idiosyncratic drug reaction.
raw_record.extra_details: LCZ is the R-enantiomer of cetirizine dihydrochloride, used for allergic diseases and not listed in prescribing information for hepatotoxicity. The patient presented with jaundice after ~2 months of LCZ. Laboratory findings: AST 1,208 IU/L, ALT 2,043 IU/L, total bilirubin 8.68 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 7.23 mg/dL, ALP 184 U/L, GGT 253 IU/L. No extrahepatic obstruction or biliary ductal disease on imaging; viral, autoimmune, ceruloplasmin and copper markers negative. Liver biopsy showed portal inflammation and hepatitis with apoptotic hepatocytes and increased portal connective tissue. All liver enzymes normalized within 3 weeks after LCZ discontinuation, and liver function remained normal at follow-up. The paper also cites a prior report of LCZ-induced hepatitis with milder elevation (AST 113 IU/mL, ALT 115 IU/mL) detected by routine LFT after 2 weeks of use.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report a case of acute liver injury (DILI) attributed to levocetirizine, describing a highly probable association with the use of levocetirizine according to the Roussel Uclaf Causality Assessment Method based on a score of 9.4. They classified the injury as idiosyncratic (rare, typically dose-independent with variable onset) and noted that the patient had previously taken levocetirizine for very short periods without injury but developed clinically relevant liver injury when taking it for 11 consecutive days. After ruling out other etiologies, they concluded the most likely diagnosis was idiosyncratic levocetirizine-induced liver injury, supported by timing of drug administration, improvement of clinical and laboratory parameters after drug discontinuation, and histological findings similar to another reported case.
raw_record.extra_details: RUCAM score 9.4 (highly probable). Patient developed injury only after 11 consecutive days of use despite multiple prior short-term exposures without injury, consistent with dose-independent idiosyncratic mechanism. Acute DILI confirmed by liver biopsy showing portal inflammation (lymphocytes, plasma cells, eosinophils, neutrophils), intrahepatic cholestasis and prominent cholestatic injury, intralobular and periportal collapse, and mild periportal fibrosis on trichrome stain; abdominal ultrasound showed no cholelithiasis/ductal obstruction, MRI showed periportal edema. Laboratory trends showed elevated total bilirubin, AST, and ALT. Treated with prednisone 60 mg daily, with dramatic improvement in symptoms and transaminases within 2 days. Authors note limited evidence for corticosteroid therapy in DILI/ALF generally.

raw_record.support_text: This population-based Swedish study of paracetamol (acetaminophen) poisoning, defined by laboratory-measured high serum paracetamol levels linked to hospital discharge and causes-of-death data, reports that paracetamol poisoning is the most common cause of acute liver failure in Sweden and elsewhere. Among poisoning cases (830 unintentional, 8841 intentional self-harm, 784 undetermined, 1613 missing intent), hepatic diagnoses occurred in 2-5% within 30 days, liver transplantation in up to 7 intentional self-harm cases within 30 days, and deaths within 30-90 days ranged from 2-6%. The majority of poisonings were intentional overdoses associated with impulsivity, ease of access, and frequent alcohol misuse.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose setting; most cases were intentional self-harm overdoses (8841 of ~12068); a history of alcohol misuse was frequent; cases include unintentional, undetermined, and missing-intent poisonings.
raw_record.extra_details: Incidence of poisonings rose ~40% after paracetamol became available from non-pharmacy outlets; mortality rate and incidence of high-serum-paracetamol cases remained stable over time. Outcomes: hepatic diagnosis within 30 days 2-5% by intent group; liver transplant within 30 days (0 unintentional, 7 intentional self-harm, 1 undetermined, 2 missing intent); death within 30 days 2-11%, within 90 days 3-12%, within 1 year 4-14%. Paracetamol was prescribed to a comparable proportion of patients prior to events as in prior reports; study based on ICD-based hospital/cause-of-death linkage with case definition confirmed by high serum paracetamol concentration.

raw_record.support_text: Paracetamol is a commonly overdosed drug, and toxicity from accumulation of the harmful intermediate metabolite N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine (NAPQI) is stated to be the most common cause of acute liver failure and indication for liver transplantation in the developed world. The text notes that in large ingestions (paracetamol dose >500 mg/kg total body weight) patients develop mitochondrial dysfunction presenting with altered consciousness and lactic acidosis, often before the onset of acute liver injury.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose context (large ingestion); mitochondrial-dysfunction phenotype seen in extremely large overdoses; patient had very low body mass index and was malnourished.
raw_record.extra_details: Toxicity attributed to accumulation of the reactive metabolite NAPQI, which overwhelms glutathione and is conjugated by NAC (N-acetylcysteine) antidote; mitochondrial dysfunction with lactic acidosis and altered consciousness can precede acute liver injury; NAC may be inadequate for very large overdoses; EXTRIP recommends adjunct haemodialysis for evidence of mitochondrial dysfunction or paracetamol level >900 mg/L; modified Kings College Criteria used for transplant listing; our patient ingested 864 mg/kg and had paracetamol levels >500 mg/L, consistent with higher ALI and hepatotoxicity risk (Cairney et al: 27% vs <=13% ALI; 18% vs <=6% hepatotoxicity). Death and transplantation are reported possible sequelae.

raw_record.support_text: This cohort of 41 psoriasis patients receiving long-term methotrexate therapy was evaluated for methotrexate-induced liver injury using liver biopsy (Roenigk grade ≥3a) as the gold standard and transient elastography. Methotrexate is treated as the cause of the liver fibrosis/injury being monitored; TE values >7.0 kPa provided acceptable accuracy (AUROC=0.78, 95% CI 0.63-0.93) and a high NPV of 84% for excluding methotrexate-induced liver injury.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Psoriasis indication requiring long-term methotrexate therapy; non-obese Asian population; histopathologic assessment (Roenigk grading).
raw_record.extra_details: 41 patients evaluated by transient elastography and liver biopsy; histopathologic evidence of methotrexate-induced liver injury defined as Roenigk grades ≥3a. Total cumulative methotrexate dose and host factors (age, gender, metabolic syndrome and its components) were not significantly associated with TE values ≥7.1 kPa or Roenigk grades ≥3a. TE cut-off 7.1 kPa gave sensitivity 50%, specificity 83.9%, PPV 50%, NPV 83.9%, accuracy 75.6% in this study.

raw_record.support_text: Trabectedin is described as a drug with predictable hepatotoxic effects in animals and humans. Even with dexamethasone prophylaxis and careful dosing, monotherapy shows significant hepatic injury potential; in soft tissue sarcoma patients the incidence of grade 3/4 ALT elevations was 47%, and 1.2% of patients met Hy's Law criteria. An irreversible liver failure case was attributed to a multihit process involving ABCC2 genetic variants and concomitant medication, showing chronic hepatobiliary toxicity with portal fibrosis and cholangiolitis.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Reported in selected soft tissue sarcoma patients with dexamethasone prophylaxis (20 mg IV) and detailed dose adjustment criteria; an irreversible liver failure case involved ABCC2 genetic variants and concomitant medication.

Mechanism: covalent DNA minor-groove guanine adducts; hepatotoxic metabolites formed by CYP3A cleared by transporters ABCB1, ABCC2, ABCC3. Liver failure case showed portal fibrosis, cholangiolitis damage, chronic hepatopathy.

raw_record.support_text: Paracetamol is described as one of the most common pharmaceuticals taken in overdose in the developed world and the leading cause of acute liver failure. In Australia, the modified-release paracetamol formulation (Panadol Osteo) contains 69% modified-release and 31% immediate-release paracetamol, and in overdose there may be a delay in peak serum concentration with persistently supratherapeutic concentrations for extended periods. The study conclusions add that in modified-release paracetamol overdose treated with acetylcysteine, an APAP×ALT multiplication product above 10,000 mg/L × IU/L (especially >8 h post-ingestion) was very strongly associated with development of acute liver injury and hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Modified-release paracetamol (Panadol Osteo) formulation overdose treated with acetylcysteine.
raw_record.extra_details: Paracetamol overdose is the leading cause of acute liver failure. Study evaluates the paracetamol-aminotransferase (APAP×ALT) multiplication product as a hepatotoxicity risk predictor; product >10,000 mg/L × IU/L was very strongly associated with acute liver injury/hepatotoxicity, especially >8 h post-ingestion; product <1500 mg/L × IU/L was associated with very low hepatotoxicity risk; specificity suffers when computed <8 h after acute overdose. Australian modified-release formulation contains 69% modified-release and 31% immediate-release paracetamol.

raw_record.support_text: This cohort study reports on modified-release paracetamol overdose treated with acetylcysteine and evaluates the paracetamol × aminotransferase multiplication product as a predictor of hepatotoxicity. Regardless of ingestion type (acute vs. staggered), a product ≥10,000 mg/L × IU/L was associated with a high likelihood of developing hepatotoxicity despite acetylcysteine treatment, while a product <1500 mg/L × IU/L was highly sensitive in excluding the development of hepatotoxicity. The paper frames paracetamol overdose as the cause of the hepatotoxicity and ALI observed in the exposed patients, discussing risk of progression to fulminant hepatic failure.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Modified-release paracetamol formulation; poisoning context treated with acetylcysteine; includes both single and staggered (staggered) overdose presentations.
raw_record.extra_details: Cohort of patients with modified-release paracetamol overdose treated with acetylcysteine; 5 patients developed hepatotoxicity (4/5 with calculable serial multiplication products) and 68 did not. Outcome definitions: hepatotoxicity by traditional biochemical criteria; ALI defined as at least a doubling of ALT and >50 IU/L. Paracetamol × ALT multiplication product cut-offs: ≥10,000 mg/L × IU/L (LR 27, 95% CI 4-207 for ALI; LR 28, 95% CI 7-107 for hepatotoxicity with single ingestion), 1500-10,000 (LR 0.9), <1500 (LR 0.3 for ALI; highly sensitive to exclude hepatotoxicity). Product within 8 h of ingestion mildly elevated and fell quickly in patients without ALI/hepatotoxicity; delayed repeat testing improves specificity. Acetylcysteine started within 8 h of overdose prevented hepatotoxicity despite high product. Severity outcome discussed: 'patients are unlikely to develop fulminant hepatic failure unless meeting the traditional biochemical criteria of hepatotoxicity first', with product proposed as an inclusion criterion for trials of intensified acetylcysteine to prevent fulminant hepatic failure.

raw_record.support_text: The text describes human hepatotoxicity from acute paracetamol (acetaminophen) overdose, establishing that the risk of hepatotoxicity increases with both larger ingested dose and higher serum paracetamol concentration, with risk lines starting at 300 mg/L and 200 mg/L at 4 h post-ingestion carrying hepatotoxicity risks of 93% and 24%, respectively. Delayed initiation of antidotal treatment (acetylcysteine) leads to higher risk of developing hepatotoxicity. A single fatal case of liver failure is also attributed to paracetamol overdose in a patient who did not initially meet treatment-line indications.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Acute overdose setting; nomogram use restricted to patients with a known time of ingestion; cases described include those where acetylcysteine was not administered; reported ingested dose may be inaccurate (retrospective data).
raw_record.extra_details: Nomogram used to determine acetylcysteine need after acute overdose (Rumack-Matthew, lines at 150/200/300/100 mg/L at 4 h post-ingestion). Hepatotoxicity risk 93% (300 mg/L) and 24% (200 mg/L); ~1% risk below the 150 mg/L threshold. Up to 10% of patients develop hepatotoxicity despite early acetylcysteine. Case series report hepatic injury with reported ingested dose of 3.5–10 g without acetylcysteine administration. Single fatal liver-failure case prompted UK lowering of treatment line to 100 mg/L at 4 h. Not validated in staggered ingestions, delayed presentations, unknown ingestion time, repeated supra-therapeutic ingestion, or modified-release paracetamol.

raw_record.support_text: The authors reported the case of a patient undergoing hemodialysis (HD) who experienced acute liver dysfunction caused by febuxostat therapy. They noted that previous reports on acute severe liver dysfunction induced by febuxostat are scarce and recommended monitoring liver function test parameters to avoid progression of febuxostat-induced liver damage, especially in patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD) and those undergoing HD.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patient had chronic kidney disease and was undergoing hemodialysis (HD), a non-default restricted population.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of acute severe liver dysfunction (acute liver injury) attributed to febuxostat in an HD patient. Febuxostat was administered as an alternative to allopurinol for hyperuricemia; the patient had previously been on oral allopurinol. The drug-induced lymphocyte stimulation test (DLST) was negative for both febuxostat (92% SI) and allopurinol (101% SI). The case also involved severe hyperkalemia with severe liver dysfunction, and no HLA-B*58:01 (patient profile HLA-A*24:02, HLA-B*52:01, HLA-DRB1*15:02); no study has reported an association between these HLA alleles and DILI, so the HLA association with the febuxostat reaction remains unclear. Authors recommend frequent liver function monitoring and possibly lower than usual febuxostat doses in CKD/HD patients.

raw_record.support_text: In a pharmacogenetic cohort of children with juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) treated with methotrexate (MTX), gastrointestinal- and liver-associated adverse events (AE) were the two main reasons for MTX discontinuation. Liver-associated AE ('hepatotoxicity') was attributed to MTX and was analyzed against genetic markers: 11 SNPs were significantly associated with hepatotoxicity. Carriers of MTRR rs1801394 had about a 2.5-fold higher hazard rate to develop hepatotoxicity and to discontinue MTX because of AE, and wild-type MTHFD1 rs2236225 had a 1.64-fold higher hazard rate for hepatotoxicity compared with mutated patients.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric population with juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA); folic acid supplementation reduced hepatic AEs.
raw_record.extra_details: MTX was withdrawn due to adverse events in 10/119 patients (8.4%) in the cohort. Gastrointestinal- and liver-associated AEs were the 2 main reasons for MTX discontinuation. 11 SNPs were significantly associated with MTX hepatotoxicity; MTRR rs1801394 carried ~2.5x higher hazard for hepatotoxicity and for AE-related MTX discontinuation; wild-type MTHFD1 rs2236225 gave 1.64x higher hazard for hepatotoxicity. Results were consistent with prior JIA and rheumatoid arthritis studies.

raw_record.support_text: The case is presented as the first report of ibrutinib-induced acute liver failure (ALF), defined by the AASLD as acute hepatic injury of less than 26 weeks duration with coagulopathy (INR ≥1.5) and encephalopathy in a patient without preexisting cirrhosis. RUCAM was used to attribute causality.
raw_record.extra_details: First report of ibrutinib-induced acute liver failure. RUCAM causality score 7, stated as consistent with 'probable'. R-ratio of 7.3 indicated hepatocellular injury. ALF evidenced by coagulopathy (INR ≥1.5) and encephalopathy without preexisting cirrhosis in a patient with Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia. Coagulopathy resolved within 30 days of discharge and liver chemistries normalized by 60 days; patient was not re-challenged with ibrutinib; WM disease markers (M-spike 2.8 g/dL, IgM 4330) increased and alternative treatment was pursued.

raw_record.support_text: Nafcillin-induced fatal hepatotoxicity with very elevated bilirubin levels has been described. Alam and co-workers reported a 53-year-old woman with a prior history of diabetes and heart disease who developed severe transaminitis and cholestasis starting day 15 after starting nafcillin for staphylococcal bacteremia and osteomyelitis of the toe. Nafcillin was discontinued on day 15 after recognition of hepatic injury, but the patient died of cardiorespiratory arrest 84 days after nafcillin was initiated.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Prolonged high-dose nafcillin therapy; the reported patient had pre-existing diabetes and heart disease.
raw_record.extra_details: Latency of hepatic injury ~15 days; death from cardiorespiratory arrest on day 84. Severe transaminitis and cholestasis (cholestatic hepatitis). In a broader nafcillin case series (ages 52-80, predominance of female patients), dominant pathology was cholestasis with cholestatic hepatitis lasting 15 days to 3 months or more; eosinophilia in two patients, renal failure in five, two patients died, and one treated with prednisone recovered. Mechanism discussed as immunoallergic cholestasis and hepatocellular dysfunction with probable genetic predisposition and possible HLA involvement.

raw_record.support_text: The paper presents a case of drug-induced autoimmune hepatitis (AIH) attributed to anastrozole, supported by the temporal relationship of elevated liver function tests after initiation of anastrozole, elevated aminotransferases with normal or marginally elevated alkaline phosphatase and bilirubin, elevated ANA autoantibody titers, extrahepatic autoimmune manifestations, and a favorable response to immunosuppressive therapy. The authors state the presentation is characteristic of drug-induced AIH and that timing of onset, ANA positivity, the LFT pattern, improvement after anastrozole discontinuation, and response to immunosuppressive therapy point toward drug-induced AIH (paragraph 26). A liver biopsy was used to exclude other causes of liver disease, including anastrozole-related steatosis.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of drug-induced autoimmune hepatitis (AIH) attributed to anastrozole. Presentation included elevated LFTs following drug initiation, elevated aminotransferases with normal or marginally elevated alkaline phosphatase and bilirubin, elevated ANA titers, extrahepatic autoimmune manifestations, and favorable response to immunosuppressive therapy. Liver biopsy showed chronic hepatitis with increased plasma cells at the portal-lobular interface and rosetting; fibrosis may be associated depending on duration/severity. Biopsy was used to exclude anastrozole-related steatosis (which was suggested on CT but not present on biopsy). Differential highlighted the challenge of distinguishing idiopathic spontaneous AIH, drug-induced AIH, and other types of DILI.

raw_record.support_text: The authors describe three multiple sclerosis patients who developed severe acute hepatotoxicity after methylprednisolone (IVMP) infusion, after discarding other etiological agents. All three cases were classified in the 'probable adverse drug reaction' category of the Naranjo scale and the WHO causality assessment criteria, leading to the hypothesis that IVMP was the possible cause of the hepatotoxicity. The paper notes that pharmacological hepatotoxicity is usually idiosyncratic and based on individual and genetic susceptibility.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Relapsing-remitting or progressive MS patients treated with high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone for relapses; patients had no prior hepatopathy history and excluded viral/autoimmune hepatitis, alcohol, alternatives, and supplements.
raw_record.extra_details: Three cases: (1) 28-year-old woman developed jaundice, choluria, acholia, nausea, vomiting ~7 weeks after last IVMP bolus; hepatic biopsy showed mild architectural damage; subsequent relapse treated again with IVMP led to another severe acute hepatitis episode (~1 month later) with biopsy showing lymphocyte-edematous background and fibrotic mild chronic hepatitis. (2) 37-year-old man with IVMP for transverse myelitis; ~6 weeks later liver enzymes increased 18x with prolonged INR and no clinical manifestations; biopsy after resolution showed no inflammatory findings. (3) 35-year-old woman; 3 days after IVMP, 42-fold increase in liver enzymes, clinically asymptomatic. Falls in 'probable' category of Naranjo scale and WHO causality criteria. Methylprednisolone given at 1000 mg for 3-5 days (± 500 mg courses); glatiramer acetate subsequently initiated given its low hepatotoxicity rate.

raw_record.support_text: The study's objective was to evaluate oxaliplatin-based chemotherapy (OBC)-induced hepatic parenchymal heterogeneity detected on contrast-enhanced CT and its influence on liver metastasis response, based on the assumption that such heterogeneity may indicate the presence of chemotherapy-induced sinusoidal obstruction syndrome (SOS).
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Colorectal cancer patients with hepatic metastases receiving oxaliplatin-based combination chemotherapy as treatment; SOS presence was inferred from CT hepatic parenchymal heterogeneity rather than confirmed histologically.
raw_record.extra_details: Retrospective study of 104 patients with hepatic metastases from colorectal cancer (male:female 66:38, age 20-80) treated with OBC and serial CT. Hepatic parenchymal heterogeneity scored on a 5-point scale (interobserver kappa=0.825). Conclusion: post-OBC hepatic parenchymal heterogeneity may indicate the presence of SOS, and more severe SOS predicts worse hepatic metastasis tumor response to oxaliplatin. Suggestion that oxaliplatin-based therapy induces sinusoidal obstruction syndrome (vascular liver injury).

raw_record.support_text: In the described patient, pure cholestasis and acute liver failure developed after stanozolol use; the case is presented as stanozolol-induced cholestatic hepatitis, with hepatocanalicular bile noted in the centrilobular area on liver biopsy. After the patient discontinued stanozolol, all hepatic enzymes and bilirubin returned to normal over five months, supporting recovery following dechallenge.
raw_record.extra_details: Case of a patient using stanozolol (anabolic-androgenic steroid) who developed cholestatic hepatitis with acute liver failure. Bilirubin rose to 56.64 mg/dl, INR increased to 1.7, LDL and HDL became undetectable; patient was hospitalized about two months. Biopsy showed hepatocanalicular bile in the centrilobular area. Five months after stopping stanozolol, liver enzymes and bilirubin normalized. Treatment was conservative with L-ornithine L-aspartate, timonacic, ursodeoxycholic acid, vitamin K1, and low-to-high dose intravenous hydrocortisone (100-200 mg/day), which correlated with bilirubin reduction. Authors note most previously reported similar cases also had renal failure or high ALT/AST, unlike this patient who had normal renal function, ALP, and GGTP. The molecular mechanism proposed involves inhibition of canalicular bile excretion via Na+/K+ ATPase or bile-acid receptor competition, and a stanozolol binding protein (STBP) modulating glucocorticoid activity.

raw_record.support_text: In a clinical trial of LY3031207, all six cases of DILI were judged to be related to LY3031207 dosing based on negative viral hepatitis serologies, negative serology for autoimmune hepatitis, limited alcohol consumption during the trial, and denial of use of medications with known hepatotoxicity (including acetaminophen). A retrospective analysis showed that females and older subjects were more susceptible to DILI than males and younger subjects.
raw_record.extra_details: Six cases of DILI in the trial; five showed a hepatocellular pattern (R ratio 10-38) and one a mixed hepatocellular-cholestatic pattern (R ratio 4); eosinophilia 6-21% (normal 0-6%) in all; 2 patients had generalised urticaria; 4 patients female and all but one aged >50 years. Three patients developed DILI symptoms after 225 mg daily dosing was stopped early (Patients 3-5: urticaria, abdominal pain, nausea, loss of appetite); Patient 6 completed 28 days of 75 mg daily with modest ALT increases and remained asymptomatic. Total dose ranged from 2100 mg over 28 days (Patient 6) to 4950 mg over 22 days (Patient 3). Dose-dependent increase in likelihood of DILI; plasma concentrations in DILI patients were comparable with subjects in the same dose group without DILI and lower than the NOAEL exposure in both dog and rat. Patients were monitored as outpatients until liver tests returned to predose ranges. Females and older subjects were more susceptible (P ≤ 0.05).

raw_record.support_text: The paper concludes that APAP (acetaminophen) overdoses remain the leading cause of acute liver failure (ALF), and that both intentional and unintentional APAP overdoses cause APAP-related acute liver failure (ALF) and acute liver injury (ALI) in humans. Conditions such as depression, alcohol use disorder, substance use disorder, and chronic pain were strongly associated with risk of APAP-related ALF and ALI.
raw_record.extra_details: Registry-based evidence from the Acute Liver Failure Study Group (ALFSG) registry. Acetaminophen overdose is described as the leading cause of acute liver failure in the US, with both intentional and unintentional overdoses associated with ALF and acute liver injury (ALI). Study included 95 APAP overdose cases (median reported dose 10,000 mg/day overall; 6,000 mg/day in unintentional and 20,000 mg/day in intentional overdoses). Depression, alcohol use disorder, substance use disorder, chronic pain, and impulsivity were strongly associated with and may influence APAP-related ALF/ALI risk.

raw_record.support_text: An overdose of paracetamol may present with nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, diaphoresis, and malaise; these effects are mediated by the toxic by-product NAPQI, formed by paracetamol metabolism via P450 cytochromes. In large doses glutathione becomes saturated, raising NAPQI levels and inducing hepatic necrosis. The paper further cites a study of 663 paracetamol-induced severe acute hepatotoxicity patients, in which 82% reported an intentional overdose with intent of suicide.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose setting; both intentional (suicide attempt, ~86% of overdoses) and unintentional (pain relief overuse) abuse forms are described.
raw_record.extra_details: Mediated by the toxic metabolite NAPQI (N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine), whose detoxification by glutathione becomes saturated at high doses. raw_record.support_text: The paper describes nifedipine-induced hepatitis as a rare type of drug-induced liver injury that presents in an idiosyncratic manner, acutely within days or subacutely within 4-8 weeks after medication start, with chronic/latent cases diagnosed up to 3 years later. Symptoms include jaundice, nausea, chills, rigors, diaphoresis, fatigue, and abdominal pain; laboratory investigations show profound elevations in AST, ALT, GGT, and conjugated bilirubin, with possible eosinophilia, and liver biopsy typically shows immune cell infiltration, cholestasis, and a steatohepatitis picture. Treatment is drug discontinuation with supportive care; all published instances were self-limiting without mortality due to fulminant liver failure but can take months to resolve.
raw_record.extra_details: Known but very rare clinically-apparent hepatitis that can take months to resolve; a case is presented in a 78-year-old Caucasian female with no prior liver or autoimmune disease. Latency: acute (within days) or subacute (4-8 weeks); chronic/latent cases up to 3 years after drug start. Symptoms: jaundice, nausea, chills, rigors, diaphoresis, fatigue, abdominal pain. Labs: profound elevations in AST, ALT, GGT, conjugated (and total) bilirubin; peripheral eosinophilia possible. Histology: immune-cell infiltration, cholestasis, steatohepatitis. Treatment: immediate drug discontinuation and supportive care; no randomized evidence for corticosteroids. All published cases self-limiting, no mortality from fulminant liver failure. Listed among idiosyncratic antihypertensive causes of DILI.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports niacin-induced liver injury in humans, describing histopathologic features including necrosis, cholestasis, fibrosis, and hepatocyte vacuolization (Table 2), and presents a case of fatal anicteric acute liver failure with diffuse microvesicular hepatic steatosis due to ER or SR niacin, concluding this scenario may be underrecognized. Time-release (SR) niacin is linked to dose-dependent serum aminotransferase elevations in up to 52% of patients, typically with symptoms above 2 g/day and onset from as early as 2 days to months of exposure.
raw_record.extra_details: Forms include immediate-release (IR), sustained-release (SR), extended-release (ER), and intramuscular (IM) niacin; time-release formulations have higher liver-injury potential, with dose-dependent aminotransferase elevations in up to 52% of SR users, symptoms usually above 2 g/day, latency from 2 days to months, and hepatotoxicity observed within days of switching from IR to SR. Reported histology includes necrosis, cholestasis (canalicular bile plugging), fibrosis, hepatocyte vacuolization, and microvesicular steatosis. Impaired hepatic synthesis may present with coagulopathy (clotting factor deficiency) and low serum albumin with minimal transaminase elevations. The described index case was fatal anicteric acute liver failure with microvesicular hepatic steatosis as the only pathologic finding (case received ~1.5 g/day ER niacin, lower than most reported ER/SR cases >2 g/day; underlying bullous pemphigoid, steroid use, and diabetes may have increased susceptibility). Schaffellner et al. case was a 22-year-old female on 20 g/day dead with panlobular parenchymal necrosis. Proposed mechanism involves mitochondrial redox (NAD/NADPH) imbalance and dose-dependent metabolism to an unknown toxic intermediate.

raw_record.support_text: Halothane hepatitis occurred in seven children aged between 11 months and 15 years, all of whom had received multiple halothane anaesthetics (range 2-6, median 3); one 3.5-year-old boy died with fulminant hepatic failure. In all cases other causes of liver diseases were excluded, and in all but one the diagnosis was confirmed serologically by antibodies to halothane-altered liver cell membrane antigens. The findings suggest halothane hepatitis occurs in children and should be considered when choosing anaesthetic agents for children requiring multiple anaesthetics.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric population (children aged 11 months to 15 years); required repeated/repeated halothane exposure across multiple anaesthetics.
raw_record.extra_details: Seven affected children; multiple halothane anaesthetics (range 2-6, median 3); one 3.5-year-old boy died with fulminant hepatic failure; diagnosis confirmed serologically in six cases by antibodies to halothane-altered liver cell membrane antigens; other causes of liver disease excluded. Paper notes that in adults severe liver damage is an established but rare event after repeated halothane exposure, and this report extends it to children.

raw_record.support_text: Thioguanine is associated with liver toxicity, especially nodular regenerative hyperplasia (NRH). The paper assessed whether liver histology alters during long-term maintenance thioguanine treatment in inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) patients.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: IBD patients on long-term thioguanine maintenance after prior thiopurine (azathioprine/mercaptopurine) therapy; vascular abnormalities were non-progressive with limited clinical relevance over a median 25-month follow-up; portal hypertension occurred in 2 patients with phlebosclerosis.
raw_record.extra_details: Sequential liver biopsies in 25 IBD patients (median 25 months, range 14-54 between first and second biopsy). Rates: perisinusoidal fibrosis 91%, sinusoidal dilatation 68%, nodularity 18% (unchanged between biopsies); phlebosclerosis trended from 36% first to 68% second biopsy (p=0.092). Histological abnormalities were not associated with clinical outcomes. Nodularity resolved upon thioguanine withdrawal in 2 patients, and portal hypertension was observed in 2 patients with phlebosclerosis.

raw_record.support_text: In a cohort of 22 thioguanine (TG)-treated inflammatory bowel disease patients with sequential liver biopsies, thioguanine was associated with histopathological liver changes including mild inflammation, steatosis, fibrosis and vascular irregularities that were mostly asymptomatic and non-progressive. Perisinusoidal fibrosis (91%), sinusoidal dilatation (68%) and nodularity (18%) were present in both first and sequential biopsies, with a trend for phlebosclerosis (36% first vs 68% second, p=.092); nodularity of any degree was present in six patients (27%). Three patients ceased thioguanine due to hepatotoxicity, and in two patients nodularity of the liver resolved upon thioguanine withdrawal, while two patients had portal hypertension in the presence of phlebosclerosis.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Inflammatory bowel disease patients (including Crohn's disease) treated with thioguanine; three of these patients had previously received thiopurines (mercaptopurine, azathioprine).
raw_record.extra_details: 22 IBD patients (predominantly Crohn's disease) with sequential liver biopsies. Histological findings included nodular regenerative hyperplasia (NRH; nodularity in 27% of patients at any grade, grade 1-2 with none reaching grade 3), phlebosclerosis, perisinusoidal fibrosis, sinusoidal dilatation, and perivenular fibrosis. Three female Crohn's disease patients ceased thioguanine due to hepatotoxicity (TG duration 18-25 months); dechallenge biopsies showed reduced phlebosclerosis, perisinusoidal fibrosis, and nodularity with improved liver tests in two patients. Four patients had preexisting splenomegaly/liver test abnormalities, and thrombocytopenia occurred in three patients. Liver test abnormalities at first and second biopsy in nine (26%) and five (20%) patients; mild steatosis and elevated gamma-glutamyl-transferase (43-92 U/L) noted. Two patients had portal hypertension in the presence of phlebosclerosis.

raw_record.support_text: In this series of acute liver failure (ALF) patients at the Victorian Liver Transplant Unit, transplant-free survival (TFS) was significantly higher in patients with paracetamol-induced ALF (74%) than in non-paracetamol aetiologies (31%, P<0.0001). Only three patients with paracetamol-induced ALF underwent liver transplantation (4%).
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose/poisoning exposure (paracetamol poisoning); patients referred to and managed at a single specialist liver transplant unit for ALF.
raw_record.extra_details: Paracetamol was the most common aetiology of ALF in this cohort (50% overall, 49.7% in 2002-2017 vs 36.3% historical 1988-2001, P=0.046). TFS for paracetamol-induced ALF was 74% vs 31% for non-paracetamol aetiologies; overall survival to hospital discharge 77% vs 67% (P=0.13). Only 4% of paracetamol-induced ALF patients were transplanted. Paracetamol was the cause of ALF in 89% of patients deemed transplant-contraindicated. Significant per-capita increase in paracetamol-induced ALF across 30 years (R2=0.275, P=0.003).

raw_record.support_text: In the long-term safety evaluation of lomitapide, a phase 3 extension study reported only a few events definitely related (diarrhoea and dehydration) or probably related (increased international normalized ratio for one patient and hepatotoxicity for another) to lomitapide. The paper notes that lomitapide, through MTP inhibition blocking hepatic VLDL release, may cause increases in hepatic fat and possible transient increases in liver function tests above three times the upper limit of normal, though no increment in liver enzymes or liver fat was detected by hepatic ultrasound in some patients up to 24 months of treatment.
raw_record.extra_details: Phase 3 extension study reported hepatotoxicity as probably related to lomitapide in one patient (and increased INR probably related in another patient). Long-term safety monitored over >5 years under the LOWER registry. Lomitapide acts via MTP inhibition, blocking hepatic VLDL release and possibly increasing hepatic fat; possible transient LFT elevations above 3x ULN were described, usually managed by brief dose reduction. Hepatic ultrasound in some patients up to 24 months showed no increment in liver enzymes or liver fat, but was limited by non-use of MRI/MRS. Drug administered for homozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia (HoFH).

raw_record.support_text: Voriconazole-induced hepatotoxicity is described as a relatively rare but serious clinicopathologic entity. The paper reports a patient with alcoholic cirrhosis who developed hepatic encephalopathy due to voriconazole administered for invasive pulmonary aspergillosis and who showed marked improvement in mental status with dose adjustment of the drug. Histopathologic examination of the explanted liver revealed numerous rhomboid-shaped crystals deemed secondary to liver injury after voriconazole-induced hepatotoxicity. Voriconazole was considered the likely cause of the hepatic encephalopathy; the drug was discontinued, mental status gradually improved, and therapy was restarted at a reduced dose that was tolerated without further supratherapeutic levels.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pre-existing alcoholic cirrhosis (advanced decompensated liver disease, MELD 37-41); supratherapeutic plasma voriconazole trough (13 μg/mL) despite standard therapeutic dosing.
raw_record.extra_details: 51-year-old man with alcoholic cirrhosis and prior Crohn's disease; voriconazole (Vfend) dosed 400 mg twice daily for 1 day then 150 mg twice daily, later reduced to 175 mg/day after rechallenge. Presented with progressive jaundice, ascites, splenomegaly; labs at second admission serum ammonia 194 μmol/L, ALT 35 U/L, ALP 94 U/L, total bilirubin 21.4 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 20.8 mg/dL, INR 2.1. Developed hepatic encephalopathy (confusion and stupor) about 10 days after discharge; improved after discontinuation and tolerated lower dose. Native liver biopsy at deceased donor liver transplant showed severe hepatocellular degeneration associated with cholestasis and marked hepatic cholangial/ductular proliferation with cirrhosis, suggestive of acute/subacute liver injury, plus intracellular and extracellular deep amber-yellow rhomboid crystals staining golden yellow under polarized light (voriconazole drug crystals). Alcoholic cirrhosis and decompensated liver failure required liver transplant; death not attributed directly to voriconazole.

raw_record.support_text: The authors attributed the patient's liver injury to levothyroxine because drug exposure preceded onset, underlying liver disease was excluded, cessation led to improvement in liver enzymes, and symptoms recurred rapidly upon rechallenge. A Naranjo Adverse Drug Reaction Probability Scale total score of 8 supported a causal effect, and a Roussel Uclaf Causality Assessment Method score of 11 indicated that an adverse drug reaction was highly probable. The improvement on drug cessation argued against transaminitis due to hypothyroidism itself.
raw_record.extra_details: Single-patient case report of levothyroxine-induced liver injury; Naranjo score 8 and RUCAM score 11 (highly probable). Disproportionate elevation of serum aminotransferases versus alkaline phosphatase, with elevated bilirubin and reduced albumin (albumin reduction attributed to negative acute-phase response). Liver enzymes normalized after drug cessation and recurred on rechallenge. No liver biopsy performed. DIAIH considered but argued against by negative autoimmune antibodies and no need for immunosuppression. One prior report (Kang et al.) observed DILI with levothyroxine tablet but not powder form, suggesting a possible causal role of additives, leaving the mechanism unclear. Treating hypothyroidism with triiodothyronine was effective without liver enzyme derangement.

raw_record.support_text: In Chinese NSCLC patients receiving gefitinib, several NF-κB pathway SNPs were associated with gefitinib-induced hepatic toxicity: RELA rs11227247 (Fisher's exact test P=0.038, recessive model), NFKBIB rs2053071 (P=0.004, Fisher's; P=0.021 dominant model), and NFKBIA rs2233407 which was associated with severe hepatic toxicity (grade ≥2) (P=0.04, recessive model). Stepwise logistic regression confirmed RELA rs11227247 as a factor for gefitinib-induced hepatic toxicity (GG vs non-GG: OR=0.212, 95% CI 0.062–0.726, P=0.013). Gefitinib is thereby identified as the agent producing hepatic toxicity in these patients, with the studied SNPs framed as biomarkers predicting these adverse drug reactions.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Findings restricted to Chinese patients with non-small cell lung carcinoma receiving gefitinib as their anti-cancer therapy.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatic toxicity graded 0, 1, and 2+ (severe defined as grade ≥2). Multiple other SNPs (ARFGEF3, DPT, IKBKB, IKBKE, NFKB1, NFKB2, NFKBIA, NR1H2, REL, SUMO4, TAB2, TAGAP, TNFAIP3) showed no significant association (NS). Gefitinib trough concentrations were available in 75 patients (median 231.15 ng/mL, range 47.8–773.6 ng/mL) with no significant genotype-dependent difference after FDR adjustment; the SNPs are presented as potential predictive biomarkers rather than the injuring entities.

raw_record.support_text: The patient ingested approximately 65 g of acetaminophen in an overdose. Follow-up acetaminophen level at approximately twelve hours post-ingestion was 322 mcg/mL and the patient remained on NAC until the level became undetectable on day 3. Peak AST/ALT were 1791/743 U/L with an INR of 1.44 on day 2; the patient was discharged after 4 days with no hepatic function abnormalities. The authors also note acetaminophen is the leading cause of liver transplantation in the United States and that toxic ingestions lead to depletion of hepatic glutathione, covalent binding to hepatocyte proteins, and centrilobular hepatocyte necrosis and hepatic failure if untreated.

Mechanism: therapeutic doses metabolized by CYP2E1 to NAPQI, which binds glutathione; in overdose NAPQI depletes glutathione and covalently binds hepatocyte proteins causing centrilobular necrosis and hepatic failure. Paper notes acetaminophen is the leading cause of liver transplantation in the US with ~450 acetaminophen-related deaths/year and ~50-70 thousand ED visits/year; toxic alcohol screen negative for ethylene glycol/methanol.

Most unintentional patients had taken paracetamol in supratherapeutic doses over many days with delayed presentation, and the poorer outcome was attributed to staggered intake, postponed presentation, and late initiation of antidote therapy.

Unintentional overdose patients were mostly pain patients self-medicating with supratherapeutic paracetamol due to insufficient pain relief; delayed presentation and late NAC initiation contributed to worse outcomes. Available paracetamol packs in Switzerland contain up to 10 g (12 g as suppositories), max 500 mg/pill (750 mg as suppository), with larger amounts available by prescription; only two cases involved a paracetamol–tramadol combination product and none involved multiple paracetamol-containing products. raw_record.support_text: The authors describe the histopathologic changes of methotrexate (MTX)-induced hepatotoxicity as well recognized, reporting on the hepatotoxic effects of long-term (10-year) MTX therapy. In most of the patients' biopsy material the pathologic findings ranged from normal to mild changes, including portal fibrosis, steatosis, inflammation, cholestasis, and sinusoidal dilatation/congestion, and the study failed to show progression to severe fibrosis and cirrhosis.

raw_record.extra_details: Case series of 21 patients (with 5 repeat biopsies) on long-term MTX therapy. Initial biopsies: mild portal fibrosis with infrequent short septa and minimal patchy sinusoidal centrilobular (zone 3) fibrosis in 5 samples; no loss of architecture, complete septa, or nodular regeneration. Other changes included cholestasis (1 sample), epithelioid cell granulomas with inflammation (2 samples), lipogranulomas (1 sample), and sinusoidal dilatation/congestion with mild focal sinusoidal fibrosis (3 samples). Repeat biopsies (grade IIIA initial samples): no increase in fibrosis and no cirrhosis in 4 patients; 1 downgraded to grade II. Repeat biopsies in patients 3 and 21 (12-44 months after first biopsies, while still on MTX) showed portal/periportal inflammation, focal limiting-plate disruption, mild piecemeal necrosis, and perilobular inflammation (grade IIIB); patient 21 had >50% fat accumulation and moderate lymphoplasmacytic portal inflammation with eosinophils and polymorphonuclear cells involving one duct. Study concludes no progression to severe fibrosis or cirrhosis over 10 years. Pathogeneses (mechanism of liver cell damage/fibrosis) stated as unknown.

Acetaminophen-induced liver injury was corroborated by ALT/AST and TBIL levels; the lethal poisoning case showed the highest ALT and AST at the early time point, and one non-lethal overdose case without elevated ALT was indistinguishable from healthy participants. The degree of PCA shift was proportional to the degree of liver injury.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of a single lethal acetaminophen (paracetamol) poisoning followed longitudinally from hospitalization to death, compared with previously studied non-lethal acetaminophen overdose cases and healthy participants. Acetaminophen is described as the most commonly used analgesic/antipyretic with frequent supra-therapeutic poisonings. Liver injury was assessed via ALT, AST, TBIL, INR and MELD scores; the lethal case developed acetaminophen-induced lethal acute liver failure (ALF), with severe coagulopathy (INR reaching ~5 within 40 h of admission) and loss of liver function accompanied by rising TBIL and decreasing ALT; one non-lethal case without elevated ALT was indistinguishable from healthy participants. GSE analysis of PC1 implicated pathways related to autophagy, cell-cycle and Notch signaling consistent with molecular mechanisms of acetaminophen hepatotoxicity; PC2-related pathways involved fibrosis, coagulation and thrombosis.

raw_record.support_text: Cocaine use can cause acute liver injury, which customarily arises within hours to a few days after an acute overdose. Cocaine-induced hepatotoxicity, documented in humans and well studied in rodents, ranges from mildly elevated transaminases to severe hepatic failure associated with rhabdomyolysis and can be a cause of drug fever. In the reported patient, serial liver tests showed elevated transaminases that normalized over twelve weeks after cessation. Histology typically shows centrilobular or zone three necrosis, portal triaditis, and microvesicular steatosis.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Recreational/acute overdose exposure; concomitant multi-drug abuse (MDMA); young male patient; recovery took longer possibly due to co-exposures.
raw_record.extra_details: Latency hours to a few days after acute overdose; in severe overdose aminotransferase and lactate dehydrogenase rise markedly with minimal alkaline increase followed by hyperbilirubinemia after day three; histology typically centrilobular/zone three necrosis, portal triaditis, microvesicular steatosis resembling ischemic or hyperthermia-induced injury; mechanism uncertain (toxic metabolite vs hyperthermia/anoxia/ischemia); cytochrome P450 modulation alters pattern/zonal extent; presented as fever of unknown origin with anicteric injury; serial values: ALT 946 to 43 IU/L, AST 338 to 32 IU/L over 12 weeks.

In this prospective cohort of 99 poisoned inpatients (67.68% consumed yellow phosphorus), hepatic injury manifested as jaundice (22.21%), elevated aspartate transaminase (48.47%), alanine transaminase (49.50%), and prolonged prothrombin time/INR (15.15%), with acute and fulminant hepatic failure; mortality was 9.1% (n=9), of which 77.78% (n=7) died of fulminant hepatic failure, mean time to death 4.22 days.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Rodenticide poisoning (intentional/supratherapeutic ingestion); paste formulation, often in combination with zinc phosphide (23.23% of patients); ingested amount not ascertainable.

raw_record.support_text: Hepatotoxicity is described as the second major, occasionally lethal side effect of antithyroid drugs. In an analysis of 18,558 Japanese patients with Graves disease treated with antithyroid drugs, severe liver injury (alanine aminotransferase >8-fold or total bilirubin >3-fold the upper limit) was significantly higher in the propylthiouracil (PTU)-treated group (6.3%) than in the methimazole (MMI)-treated group (1.4%); median time to development of antithyroid-drug-induced hepatic injury was 30 (range 7-314) days and no deaths were reported. raw_record.support_text: Hepatotoxicity with aromatase inhibitors is rare, and specific instances of exemestane-induced hepatotoxicity have been documented in only two prior case reports, both showing signs and symptoms of cholestatic liver injury after three to eight weeks of medication exposure. Described cases include a jaundiced patient with pruritis whose bilirubin peaked at 13.8 mg/dL and a hospitalized patient with grade 4 hyperbilirubinemia and grade 3 transaminitis whose bilirubin peaked at 21.2 mg/dL; both resolved approximately four months after exemestane was discontinued. The present report documents exemestane-induced cholestasis in a patient with underlying primary biliary cholangitis. The conclusion states that although rare, liver injury due to exemestane has been reported.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Index patient had pre-existing primary biliary cholangitis (PBC), an underlying hepatic dysfunction proposed as a risk factor for developing cholestasis with exemestane.
raw_record.extra_details: Steroidal aromatase inhibitor used for breast cancer. Mechanism of hepatotoxicity unclear; ~42% of exemestane is excreted via the biliary system and it is metabolized by CYP enzymes including CYP1A2 and CYP3A4. Two prior case reports: a 65-year-old woman with metastatic breast cancer with jaundice, conjunctival and skin jaundice, and generalized pruritis after eight weeks of therapy; and a 47-year-old postmenopausal woman hospitalized with grade 4 hyperbilirubinemia, pruritis, and grade 3 transaminitis three weeks after initiation. Total bilirubin peaked at 13.8 and 21.2 mg/dL and resolved ~4 months after discontinuation; management was symptomatic (antihistamines, or cholestyramine, phenobarbital, and lorazepam). Patient tolerated the non-steroidal AIs anastrozole and letrozole; drug resources report a higher incidence of bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase elevations with exemestane, though head-to-head clinical trials showed similar hepatotoxicity rates between steroidal and non-steroidal AIs.

raw_record.support_text: In the current phase I trial in healthy adults, CBD (cannabidiol, Epidiolex) treatment was associated with serum ALT elevations, with some participants exceeding 5× ULN; three participants developed signs and symptoms including eosinophilia, abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting, and two experienced fever within the same time frame as the ALT elevations. The paper characterizes these as CBD-related ALT elevations that are dose-dependent and resolve relatively rapidly after discontinuing treatment, and notes these symptoms are associated with hepatitis rather than benign ALT elevations.
raw_record.extra_details: Healthy adult volunteers in a phase I trial received 1500 mg CBD daily; five participants developed ALT elevations >5× ULN; symptoms included eosinophilia, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and fever, consistent with hepatitis. Liver events had >2-week latency after first dose and resolved rapidly after discontinuation; no correlation between mean CBD plasma concentrations and peak ALT elevations; no association with CYP2C19 metabolizer status. Mechanism not clarified: dose-dependence and rapid resolution considered most consistent with a direct effect, but eosinophilia/fever suggest immune activation; mouse transcriptomics showed oxidative-stress gene changes and CBD inhibited mitochondrial function in cultured cells; possible role of a minor metabolite or innate immune activation. Pivotal DS and LGS RCTs and an OLE also raised liver-safety concern. Caffeine was considered unlikely to contribute due to lack of hepatotoxic potential.

raw_record.support_text: In the late 1970s and early 1980s, reports surfaced of severe liver injury associated with unintentional acetaminophen (APAP) misuse, i.e., inadvertent overdoses in the setting of acute or chronic pain, often with alcohol use and without suicidal intent. A single-time-point APAP overdose of 12 to 15 g (24-30 extra-strength 500-mg tablets) carried approximately 50% mortality if untreated; ingestions of 6 to 7 g/day over several days (alcohol/starvation setting) could yield a similar hyperacute injury of great severity. By 1993, APAP was described as fast becoming the most frequent cause of acute liver failure (ALF) in the United States. The drug-related injury was described as dose-related hepatic injury manifested as centrilobular necrosis mediated by CYP2E1 metabolite binding after glutathione depletion.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose setting, including both single-time-point suicidal overdose and unintentional 'therapeutic misadventure' (several days' use of multiple APAP-containing products, often with alcohol use/starvation).
raw_record.extra_details: Mechanism: saturation of sulfation/glucuronidation leads to CYP (primarily CYP2E1) metabolism to N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine (NAPQI), which binds hepatic proteins via sulfhydryl linkage after glutathione (GSH) depletion, causing dose-related centrilobular necrosis. Parkland Hospital series: 71 hospital admissions over 40 months; suicidal group (N=50, single time-point ingestion, 10/50 had ALT >1000 IU/L, 1 death) vs unintentional group (N=21, several days' use of multiple APAP-containing products, virtually all ALT >1000 IU/L, 8 met ALF criteria, 6 died). NAC used as antidote; intravenous NAC licensed in the US in 2004. Brand names: Tylenol, including combinations such as Tylenol PM/Nyquil and opioid combinations.

raw_record.support_text: The phase I/II clinical study of mithramycin monotherapy in Ewing sarcoma (NCT01610570) was ceased due to hepatotoxicity. Approximately 75% of treated patients had dose-limited hepatotoxicity with acute injury starting within days of administration, noted at 25 µg/kg/dose and requiring dose de-escalation; notable transaminitis appeared within 72 h of treatment, reaching levels up to 500x the upper limit of normal, with resolution often taking 1-3 weeks. The hepatic injury was transient, rarely symptomatic, and did not require intervention, but significantly hampered the clinical utility of mithramycin. Investigations suggested the hepatotoxicity was related to inhibition of farnesoid-X receptor signaling and germline variants in bile acid flow/disposition genes (e.g., ABCB4, ABCB11).
raw_record.extra_details: Mithramycin (plicamycin) is an antineoplastic antibiotic; commercial production was discontinued in 2000 partly due to a narrow therapeutic window and severe toxicity. Hepatotoxicity was dose-limited in the Ewing sarcoma phase I/II monotherapy trial (NCT01610570), occurring at 25 µg/kg/dose and requiring dose de-escalation, with no efficacy demonstrated. ~75% of treated patients affected; acute injury within days; transaminitis up to 500x ULN within 72 h; resolution in 1-3 weeks; injury transient, rarely symptomatic, no intervention needed. Proposed mechanism: inhibition of farnesoid-X receptor signaling and germline variants in bile acid flow/disposition genes (ABCB4, ABCB11).

In a prospective cohort of 117 acetaminophen-poisoned patients receiving N-acetylcysteine, plasma procalcitonin on admission was associated with liver injury and its rise preceded alanine aminotransferase elevation, highlighting the need for better biomarkers to identify patients at higher or lower risk of acetaminophen-related acute liver injury.

Plasma procalcitonin (PCT) on admission predicted liver injury with excellent accuracy and negative predictive value, and its rise preceded alanine aminotransferase rise by a median of 33 h. Other candidate biomarkers mentioned: acetaminophen protein adducts, miR-122, HMGB1, keratin 18, GLDH. Predictive nomogram covers time-from-ingestion and dose scenarios.

The paper frames these as vascular drug-induced liver injury with drug-induced sinusoidal endothelial injury leading to non-cirrhotic portal hypertension, noting oxaliplatin among the causal drugs; EGV formation after oxaliplatin is described as a clinical feature of porto-sinusoidal vascular disease (PSVD) with portal hypertension.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients receiving first-line oxaliplatin-based chemotherapy for colorectal cancer; EGV formation developed only in cases of progressive splenomegaly and thrombocytopenia.
raw_record.extra_details: EGV formation presented as a clinical feature of porto-sinusoidal vascular disease (PSVD) with portal hypertension. EGV formation could be predicted by a decrease in platelet count of less than 10% and an increase in computed tomography spleen index (CT-SI) of more than 10% at the end of and 6 months after oxaliplatin administration; ROC-derived cut-offs for change in platelet count (62.5% end, 61.0% post 3 months, 64.0% post 6 months; AUC 0.65-0.81) and CT-SI (133%, 128%, 129%; AUC 0.77-0.89). Response at 3 or 6 months post-treatment was a better predictor of EGV formation.

raw_record.support_text: Bu (busulfan) is widely used as a chemotherapeutic drug for myeloablative or non-myeloablative conditioning before allo-HCT. The authors note that busulfan PK dosing with TDM introduced in the 2000s allowed an important reduction of hepatic toxicity and of sinusoidal obstruction syndrome (SOS), with SOS incidence reduced from about 15% to 3% in under 10 years, indicating busulfan is an established cause of hepatic toxicity and SOS in this setting.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients with myeloid malignancies receiving busulfan as part of myeloablative/non-myeloablative conditioning regimen before allogeneic stem cell transplantation (non-general population, transplant setting).
raw_record.extra_details: SOS (veno-occlusive disease) incidence reduced from about 15% to 3% after the introduction of busulfan PK-guided TDM. Andersson et al. set a target AUC of <1200 μmol/l to prevent significant hepatic toxicity, with a serious increase in SOS and neurological side effects at AUC >1500 μmol/l*min.

condition_text: Overdose exposure (paracetamol overdose, POD).

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that paracetamol overdose (POD) remains the commonest cause of acute liver failure (ALF) in the UK, and describes it as a defined liver insult resulting in acute liver injury (coagulopathy with INR > 1.5 and jaundice) that progresses to hepatic encephalopathy. The case of Mrs S is presented as a paracetamol-overdose ALF managed medically without meeting transplant criteria.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose exposure (paracetamol overdose, POD).
raw_record.extra_details: Mechanism: NAPQI, a hepatotoxic intermediate metabolite, accumulates after glutathione depletion, causing hepatonecrosis, liver dysfunction and hepatocyte enzyme release. Presentation in significant POD typically includes aminotransferases in the thousands, mildly elevated bilirubin and significant coagulopathy, with metabolic acidosis, hyperlactataemia and hypovolaemia. Patient Mrs S presented with ALT ~6000 U/L, INR 5.5, bilirubin 60 µmol/L, grade 3-4 hepatic encephalopathy and hyperammonemia (160 µmol/L at 24 h); paracetamol and salicylate levels were undetectable at presentation; treated with NAC, CVVH/CVVHDF, and supportive critical care; recovered and discharged after 3 weeks. Paracetamol levels are not reliable to exclude POD because many patients present late or with staggered overdose.

condition_atoms: reported_condition=accidental overdose (dosing error) of chloroquine; single-agent case with competing terminal factors (final fungal sepsis, pneumonia) and pronounced cerebral damage secondary to and accompanying the liver failure
condition_group: exposure=overdose_or_supratherapeutic+population=human+reported_condition=accidental overdose (dosing error) of chloroquine; single-agent case with competing terminal factors (final fungal sepsis, pneumonia) and pronounced cerebral damage secondary to and accompanying the liver failure
condition_text: Accidental overdose (dosing error) of chloroquine; single-agent case with competing terminal factors (final fungal sepsis, pneumonia) and pronounced cerebral damage secondary to and accompanying the liver failure.

raw_record.support_text: A female patient developed nausea, vomiting, hypotension, tachycardia and rising liver enzymes (serum GOT to ~2500 U/l, GPT to ~3500 U/l) beginning within the first days after an accidental chloroquine overdose (Dosierungsfehler). An acute liver failure (akuter Leberzerfall) was diagnosed and treated with plasmapheresis, but the patient progressed to coma and died 13 days after chloroquine ingestion. A blood chloroquine concentration of 0.83 mg/l was measured about 44 h after intake.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Accidental overdose (dosing error) of chloroquine; single-agent case with competing terminal factors (final fungal sepsis, pneumonia) and pronounced cerebral damage secondary to and accompanying the liver failure.
raw_record.extra_details: Serum GOT rose to ~2500 U/l and GPT to ~3500 U/l three days after intake; blood chloroquine 0.83 mg/l at ~44 h post-ingestion (HPLC). ICU admission with coma, intubation and ventilation; acute liver failure treated with plasmapheresis. Autopsy showed liver dystrophy with near-total hepatocellular necrosis, only few residual nuclei-containing hepatocytes with marked large-droplet steatosis, loss of lobular architecture, early annular-cirrhosis-like reparative fibrosis, and a pyrrole pigment consistent with intracellular storage liberated by necrosis; general icterus. Necrotic liver was held responsible for a secondary diffuse bleeding tendency; terminal complications included fungal sepsis with granulomas in brain, lungs and kidney, pulmonary abscess, and cerebral hypoxic damage. Patient died on day 13 from cerebral failure/cardiocirculatory arrest.

condition_text: Pediatric population; intentional self-poisoning (suicidal) in adolescents, with one accidental ingestion possibly reflecting negligent parental care; exposure was in the absence of medical recommendation.

raw_record.support_text: The paper describes dose-related acute hepatic failure attributed to acetaminophen (paracetamol), noting many cases of acute hepatic failure attributed to acetaminophen in children despite N-acetylcysteine treatment, with self-intoxication frequent among older children and adolescents. In the authors' pediatric DILI cohort, acetaminophen-related DILI cases were mostly adolescents over 12 years with voluntary ingestion for suicidal intent, presenting an increased incidence in adolescent girls. Liver injury secondary to acetaminophen toxicity was indicated by high liver enzymes (above 10 ULN) with no cholestasis and coagulopathy in 36% of children.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric population; intentional self-poisoning (suicidal) in adolescents, with one accidental ingestion possibly reflecting negligent parental care; exposure was in the absence of medical recommendation.
raw_record.extra_details: Mechanism of injury is dose-related (intrinsic). Acute intoxication onset is rapid, with marked ALT and AST elevation within 24-72 h after ingestion followed by clinical symptoms at 48-96 h; right upper quadrant pain, elevated liver enzymes, altered coagulation, and in severe cases nephrotoxicity or pancreatitis may appear after 24 h; liver failure and multi-organ failure common 72 h after ingestion, and death might occur in this stage; recovery when attained occurs in 4-14 days. 36% of children had coagulopathy; no cholestasis. Most frequent symptoms were abdominal pain (50%) and nausea/vomiting (45%). Treated with N-acetylcysteine. Acute hepatic failure is the reported clinical entity.

raw_record.extra_details: Acetaminophen-related DILI group: mean initial total bilirubin 1.28 mg/dL (range 0.3-4.2) and conjugated bilirubin 0.38 mg/dL (range 0.1-1.17); GGT elevated in intrinsic DILI (mean 44.3 UI/L, range 12-232) vs 80.2 UI/L (range 11-239) for idiosyncratic; coagulopathy (INR>1.5) in 12 cases (30%) and prothrombin activity <80% in 16 patients (40%), all in the acetaminophen-related group; median hospitalization 6.9 days (range 1-54). raw_record.support_text: In two Phase 1 studies, AB-506 (an HBV capsid inhibitor) was given at 160 mg or 400 mg daily for 28 days to subjects with chronic HBV infection. Four subjects (all Asian) had Grade 4 alanine aminotransferase (ALT) elevations during HBV DNA decline, with three events leading to treatment discontinuation; in a follow-up study, 2 Asian healthy subjects had serious transaminitis events leading to treatment and study termination. No subjects had bilirubin elevations or signs of hepatic decompensation. The authors conclude that these findings suggest AB-506 hepatotoxicity contributed to the ALT elevations, and the AB-506 development program was terminated because of these findings.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Findings restricted to Asian subjects; observed in both subjects with chronic HBV infection and healthy subjects; transient severe ALT flares with treatment/study discontinuation.
raw_record.extra_details: Phase 1 randomized double-blinded studies; AB-506 doses 160 mg or 400 mg daily for 28 days; Grade 4 ALT elevations in 4 CHB subjects (2 at each dose) plus 2 serious transaminitis events in Asian healthy subjects; no bilirubin elevations or hepatic decompensation; mean HBV-DNA declines 2.1 log10 IU/ml (160 mg) and 2.8 log10 IU/ml (400 mg); AB-506 development program terminated because of these hepatotoxicity findings.

condition_text: Intentional rat killer (yellow phosphorus) poison consumption; overdose/supratherapeutic exposure setting.

raw_record.support_text: In an observational study (n=48, mean age 29) of rat killer compound (yellow phosphorus) poison consumption, all patients developed acute liver failure; 29 (60%) underwent therapeutic plasma exchange based on the presence of acute liver failure and bone marrow toxicity. Despite plasma exchange, mortality was 18%. Factors associated with poor outcome included no gastric lavage within 2 hours, hemodynamic instability, hepatic encephalopathy, high toxin dose, higher admission lactate (>4), delayed presentation (>72 hours), and worsening liver/renal function despite plasma exchange. Case formulation of the toxin appeared less toxic than paste.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Intentional rat killer (yellow phosphorus) poison consumption; overdose/supratherapeutic exposure setting.
raw_record.extra_details: Rat killer compound (yellow phosphorus) is a protoplasmic poison causing multiorgan failure; dose >1 mg/kg is stated as nearly always fatal. Mean age 29; 50% (n=24) presented within 24 hours of consumption; 19% (n=9) had bone marrow toxicity at presentation (most commonly neutropenia with increased absolute monocyte count). 29 (60%) patients underwent therapeutic plasma exchange for acute liver failure and bone marrow toxicity; 3 developed hypotension during the procedure; number of sessions was based on LFT and coagulopathy. 18% mortality despite plasma exchange. Indication for exchange: acute liver failure and bone marrow toxicity; new-onset diabetes insipidus seen in 4 patients. Cake formulation appeared less toxic than paste.

raw_record.support_text: In this patient with COVID-19, liver enzymes were elevated only after 48 hours of remdesivir use; the known in vitro toxicity of remdesivir, the time relation, and automatic resolution after discontinuation of the drug together indicate a causal relation between elevated liver enzymes and remdesivir. No other drug in the patient's treatment could be related to hepatotoxicity, and viral, hypoxic, and autoimmune etiologies were excluded. The biochemical pattern of the injury was hepatocellular (R=ALT/ALP >= 5), and transaminases and INR declined starting 24 hours after remdesivir discontinuation, returning to normal nine days later.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of remdesivir-associated liver injury during treatment of COVID-19. Liver enzymes elevated 48 hours after remdesivir start; transaminases and INR (coagulopathy) declined within 24 hours of discontinuation and returned to normal nine days later. R ratio ALT/ALP >= 5 indicated hepatocellular injury. Patient remained ambulatory with no altered consciousness (EASL acute liver injury without encephalopathy). Viral, hypoxic (no hypotension), and autoimmune causes excluded; alcohol use ~2 units/week. No competing drug co-suspect in the regimen. Discharged on day eleven, recovered; course complicated by nonsevere Clostridium difficile infection treated with metronidazole and vancomycin.

raw_record.support_text: The case is described as APAP-induced acute liver injury with significant elevation in transaminases, in a patient who ingested large/unknown amounts of extra-strength acetaminophen (APAP) over days to weeks for chronic pain, with chronic alcoholism. Laboratory findings included an APAP level of 126.3 ug/ml, AST 2,175 U/l, ALT 896 U/l, total bilirubin 2.6 mg/dl, INR 1.6, and lactate 3.9 mmol/L; hepatic encephalopathy was present and King's College criteria were calculated daily. raw_record.extra_details: Case report of a 58-year-old female. Admission labs: APAP 126.3 ug/ml, ethanol <0.01 gm/dl%, AST 2,175 U/l, ALT 896 U/l, total bilirubin 2.6 mg/dl, INR 1.6, lactate 3.9 mmol/L, CK 151 U/L. Hepatic encephalopathy improved ~one day after admission; acute kidney injury occurred with differential diagnoses including APAP-induced hepatotoxicity, hepatorenal syndrome, and acute tubular necrosis; kidney function improved ~80 h post-admission without hemodialysis. N-acetylcysteine i.v. given (21-hour protocol, then dose increased to 12.5 mg/kg/h then 6.25 mg/kg/h until serum APAP undetectable at ~40 h); one-time fomepizole 15 mg/kg i.v. load then 10 mg/kg every 12 h x4, first dose ~30 h after admission (~36-48 h after last ingestion). King's College criteria did not indicate transplant evaluation. Liver and kidney function returned to baseline four weeks post-admission. Mechanism stated: CYP2E1 forms NAPQI, which depletes glutathione causing hepatocyte necrosis and hepatic failure in overdose.; confidence: 0.9; needs_more_context: False

Rise and fall of enzymes closely paralleled initiation and cessation of cefepime; competing causes ruled out; liver biopsy confirmed DILI. Female patient.

raw_record.support_text: Atazanavir (ATV), a protease inhibitor, is known to cause reversible increase in unconjugated bilirubin without liver injury due to UGT1A1 inhibition. raw_record.support_text: Based on the patient's clinical course and histological features, MTX (methotrexate) was considered the most likely cause of NASH-like liver injury. The authors presumed that obesity and T2DM could have worsened the liver damage. The patient had received a cumulative 4050 mg of MTX over 13 years (tapered from 8 to 4 mg); after MTX was discontinued the platelet count and FIB-4 index did not decrease/improve, and she subsequently developed chronic liver disease consistent with cirrhosis, esophageal varices, and eventually died of hepatic failure.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Chronic therapeutic use over 13 years to treat rheumatoid arthritis; concurrent obesity and type 2 diabetes mellitus, which were presumed to have worsened the liver damage; co-exposure to biologics (etanercept later replaced by tocilizumab and then golimumab).
raw_record.extra_details: Cumulative MTX dose 4050 mg over 13 years, tapered from 8 to 4 mg/week. Histology showed steatohepatitis with fibrosis, ballooning, and Mallory-Denk bodies, classified as Matteoni type 4 and NASH activity score 5, with interface hepatitis different from metabolic NASH. Disease progressed to cirrhosis, esophageal varices, splenomegaly, and hepatic failure (hyperbilirubinemia, elevated ammonia 151 microg/dL, prolonged PT 26.0%); patient died of hepatic failure 2 days after hospitalization. FIB-4 index did not improve after MTX discontinuation. Antinuclear and antimitochondrial antibodies negative.; additional_notes: None

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that the most serious side effect of isoniazid in adults is hepatitis, which can be fatal and is often difficult to distinguish from viral hepatitis. In a cohort analysis of nursing home residents in Arkansas treated for tuberculosis, hepatic toxicity occurred in 84 of 1935 (4.4%) residents who started isoniazid therapy; the table notes no death due to medication in this cohort.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Elderly nursing home residents (ages 50 and older) receiving isoniazid as chemoprophylaxis or treatment for tuberculosis; surveillance/recommendation context in an elderly population.
raw_record.extra_details: Isoniazid hepatitis described as often difficult to distinguish from viral hepatitis; in the Arkansas cohort hepatic toxicity was seen in 84/1935 (4.4%) residents (50-64 yrs: 12/339, 3.5%; 65-79 yrs: 36/788, 4.6%; ≥80 yrs: 36/808, 4.5%), with no death attributed to medication. Intolerance (nausea, anxiety, headache, somnolence, fever, skin rash) exceeded hepatitis incidence. Monitoring recommended based on symptoms (anorexia, nausea, vomiting); discontinue isoniazid if aspartate aminotransferase exceeds 500 U/L (8.34 µkat/L), with possible reinstitution if AST does not exceed 5 times normal in symptomatic patients. Rifampin 600 mg/day for 6-12 months suggested as alternative preventive therapy.

raw_record.support_text: In acute APAP (acetaminophen) poisonings, the CYP metabolite ratio APAP-Cys/APAP-Sul detects patients at risk of developing subsequent acute liver injury (defined as an increased serum ALT activity of 50% or more), with an AUC-ROC of 0.91 (0.83-0.98). The authors confirm this association for hepatotoxicity with a similarly high AUC-ROC, and note that a combination of traditional liver biomarkers, APAP body load, and APAP metabolites performs even better for predicting acute liver injury. The study reports that the number of patients with hepatotoxicity and fulminant hepatic failure was low, and further studies are needed to determine if metabolites aid in predicting outcomes such as liver transplant or death.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Acute APAP (acetaminophen) overdose (poisoning) setting, the studied exposure context.
raw_record.extra_details: Acute liver injury defined as an increase in serum ALT activity of 50% or more. The CYP-pathway metabolite ratio APAP-Cys/APAP-Sul (reflecting glutathione depletion, CYP metabolism, and sulfation balance) predicted subsequent acute liver injury with AUC-ROC 0.91 (0.83-0.98); a combination of traditional liver biomarkers, APAP body load (APAP ratio), and APAP metabolites predicted acute liver injury even better. Some patients received early acetylcysteine before the 4-hour APAP concentration, and acetylcysteine treatment may increase sulfation and/or CYP metabolites, though results remained similar when those patients were excluded. Fulminant hepatic failure and hepatotoxicity cases were few; further studies are needed to validate whether metabolites aid prediction of liver transplant or death. Fomepizole is noted as a newly proposed adjuvant to acetylcysteine.; confidence: 0.0
