raw_record.support_text: The timeline of levetiracetam (LEV) initiation 2 months before presentation with significant liver injury on initial presentation, in the setting of positive autoimmune serologic markers (ASMA and ANA at 1:80 titers) and classic biopsy findings (interface hepatitis with biliary change), was consistent with a diagnosis of drug-induced autoimmune hepatitis. The patient's IAIHG simplified score of 8 (>7 = definite AIH) further supported the AIH diagnosis based on serum globulins/IgG >1.1x ULN and negative hepatitis viral markers. Paragraph 12 states this is the first reported LEV-induced AIH that resolved with prompt discontinuation of LEV, suggesting that cessation of LEV may be sufficient to resolve the liver injury without corticosteroid treatment.
raw_record.extra_details: Single case report (first reported LEV-induced AIH). LEV initiated 2 months before presentation. ALT and AST elevations on presentation; positive ASMA and ANA at 1:80 titers; 'classic' biopsy findings of interface hepatitis and biliary change; negative hepatitis viral markers; serum globulins/IgG >1.1x upper limit of normal; IAIHG simplified score 8 (definite AIH). AIH type 1 phenotype (older onset, ASMA/ANA present, lack of extrahepatic autoimmune disease or inherited immune deficiency). Injury resolved with prompt discontinuation of LEV without corticosteroid treatment.

raw_record.support_text: The results of the BSP studies suggest that oral chenodeoxycholic acid (CDCA) is not hepatotoxic in man. In patients treated with CDCA, the 45-min BSP retention values were if anything lower than normal, and the more rapid late phase of BSP clearance supports this observation, possibly because bile acids increase the liver's capacity to excrete BSP in experimental animals.
raw_record.extra_details: Oral CDCA studied for gallstone treatment. BSP retention and clearance studies. Minor histological changes on liver biopsy occurred with the same frequency whether or not patients were treated with CDCA and were attributed to cholelithiasis itself rather than bile acid treatment; polymorphonuclear leucocyte infiltrates and hepatic cell necrosis on wedge biopsies in two CDCA-treated patients were attributed to possible biopsy artefacts. Raised serum bile acids and occasional GGT elevations during treatment were considered possibly due to other causes such as barbiturates or alcohol intake, not evidence of CDCA hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report clinical practice observations after changing from oral to IV busulfan (Bu) in high-dose therapy: a reduction in veno-occlusive disease/sinusoidal obstruction syndrome (VOD/SOS) of the liver but a change in its clinical presentation. Classic VOD/SOS had a rapid onset within the first 3-4 weeks after transplant and led to hepato-renal/multi-organ failure and death, while the IV Bu (DMA-PEG) formulation is now commonly followed by 'silent' transaminitis and hyperbilirubinemia occurring within 10-14 days in 30-40% of patients that typically resolves within 7-10 days. Serious treatment-related VOD/SOS may manifest early or later, with some patients developing liver failure up to at least 8-12 weeks after transplant, leading to decline and death. The authors hypothesize this change may involve an interaction between DMA and Bu in generating liver toxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: High-dose myeloablative conditioning before stem cell transplantation; observations made after switching from oral to IV Bu in a DMA-containing formulation; co-exposure with cyclophosphamide (Cy) or fludarabine (Flu) as part of the conditioning regimen.
raw_record.extra_details: IV Bu with DMA-PEG was reported safer and better tolerated than oral Bu, with a reduced incidence of VOD/SOS. Classic VOD/SOS onset within first 3-4 weeks post-transplant followed by gradual decline to hepato-renal/multi-organ failure and death. IV Bu-associated 'silent' transaminitis and hyperbilirubinemia occurred in 30-40% of patients within 10-14 days and resolved within 7-10 days; delayed serious VOD/SOS/liver failure could manifest up to 8-12 weeks post-transplant and lead to death.

raw_record.support_text: In pexidartinib registration trials, liver injury with jaundice developed in 5% of patients, with onset usually between 2 and 6 weeks and a pattern of liver enzyme elevations that was either mixed or solely cholestatic. Liver biopsy documented both bile duct injury and loss, and three patients treated for conditions other than tenosynovial giant cell tumors developed bile duct paucity and features of vanishing bile duct syndrome, leading to liver transplantation in one subject. The drug carries a boxed warning for hepatotoxicity requiring LIT monitoring, and should be avoided in patients with pre-existing elevations in ALT, bilirubin, or ALP or active liver/biliary disease.

raw_record.extra_details: ALT elevation common in 50-90% of patients (G3/4: 12-20%); ALP elevation in up to 20%; jaundice in 5% of registration-trial patients; onset 2-6 weeks; biopsy showed bile duct injury and loss; three patients developed bile duct paucity/vanishing bile duct syndrome, one requiring liver transplantation; boxed warning for hepatotoxicity with recommended LIT monitoring and dose-holding/reduction rules; rechallenge at reduced dose may cause recurrence of increased ALT, bilirubin or ALP. Indication: tenosynovial giant cell tumors.

Hepatic encephalopathy developed on the 7th day of follow-up, and a cadaveric liver transplant was performed on the 9th day, 44 days after initiation of Fingolimod treatment. Massive necrosis was detected in the pathological examination of the explanted liver.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of fingolimod (Gilenya)-treated MS patient. Duration of treatment 15 days; onset of symptoms on 12th day; laboratory abnormalities on 14th day; R ratio 11.4 (hepatocellular pattern) at first application; modified RUCAM +8 (Probable); severity grade 5+ (Fatal). Initial labs: ALT 517 U/L, AST 646 U/L, total bilirubin 36.7 mg/dL, INR 3.7, creatinine 0.66 mg/dL. Hepatic encephalopathy developed on day 7; cadaveric liver transplant on day 9 (44 days after therapy initiation); explant pathology showed massive necrosis with bile duct proliferation and perivascular connective tissue. Patient survived and complies with liver transplant outpatient follow-up. Therapeutic plasmapheresis was performed; patient had not received steroids before transplant.

raw_record.support_text: The AKRENDO1 trial assessed the dose–response relationship of five oral doses of the AKR1C3 inhibitor BAY1128688 relative to placebo for endometriosis-related pain. The trial was prematurely terminated after hepatocellular drug-induced liver injury was detected in two participants, one of whom fulfilled Hy's law criteria, indicating a safety profile that precludes further clinical development of BAY1128688.
raw_record.extra_details: Trial prematurely terminated after detection of hepatocellular DILI in two participants, one fulfilling Hy's law criteria. ALT increase >3xULN seen in 8 of 90 BAY1128688-treated participants, with increases observed relative to cessation of treatment in seven of these eight; no hepatotoxicity observed until after 8 weeks of exposure across dose groups, consistent with the preceding 4-week multiple-dose phase I trial. A separate, dose-related early elevation in total, direct, and indirect serum bilirubin (up to ~2xULN, peaking weeks 1-8, not associated with aminotransferase elevations) was described as 'isolated' and was not classified as DILI; the limited number of completers prevented inferential statistics, so no efficacy conclusions were drawn.

raw_record.extra_details: Incidence of voriconazole-related liver injury in hospitalized patients was 15.82% (217/1372) per CIOMS standard; liver injury defined as transaminase >3 ULN. Label-reported incidence was 18.04% (319/1768) in adults and 25.80% (73/283) in children. Injury spectrum spans mild abnormal liver biochemical indicators to fatal fulminant liver failure. Liver injury in transplant patients was higher and more likely to lead to premature drug withdrawal (e.g., 18.54% (28/151) lung transplant and 22.86% (48/210) allogeneic HCT cohorts). Disposal cost of voriconazole-related liver injury was higher than non-liver injury (median 101.90 vs 0.00 yuan, p<0.001); severe liver injury cost median 993.59 vs 0.00 yuan. Voriconazole-related liver injury was not associated with age, chronic liver disease, diabetes, tumors, heart disease, or fungal disease type; long treatment durations (anti-Candida ≥2 weeks, anti-Aspergillus ≥6 weeks, anti-Cryptococcus ≥6 months) may increase risk.

The incidence of hepatitis was high with isoniazid 400 mg daily, and the risk of hepatitis was appreciably higher in slow than in rapid acetylators (18% vs 2% in the spinal tuberculosis study with rifampicin and isoniazid; 21% vs 0% in a sample from the second pulmonary tuberculosis study), while incidence was low (1.3%) with isoniazid-containing regimens without rifampicin. The findings refute the hypothesis that isoniazid is more hepatotoxic for rapid rather than slow acetylators.

raw_record.support_text: The patient suffered acute liver failure attributable to acetaminophen (paracetamol) even though a dose below the recommended 4 g/day was administered. The paper notes liver damage from acetaminophen onsets in a dose-dependent manner and arises from its active metabolite N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone-imine (NAPQI), formed by cytochrome P450 and detoxified by glutathione conjugation; glutathione depletion increases NAPQI and causes liver damage. The authors attribute the case to patient background factors: undernutrition (reduced oral intake for about a week after postoperative-chemotherapy enteritis, with hypoalbuminemia and hypocholesterolemia), small body frame, and an intravenous route whose weight-equivalent dose of 68.5 mg/kg/day exceeded the 60 mg/kg/day guidance for adults under 50 kg. The maximum daily dose of 4,000 mg/day was adhered to.

raw_record.extra_details: Active metabolite N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone-imine (NAPQI) underlies the liver injury; acetaminophen undergoes sulfate conjugation and glucuronidation, with a fraction converted to NAPQI by cytochrome P450 and detoxified by glutathione conjugation, whose depletion increases NAPQI. Known risk factors for acetaminophen liver damage include undernutrition, drinking (alcohol), and a history of liver damage. Intravenous bioavailability (0.7-0.9) is higher than oral. The discussion also notes that acute liver failure from acetaminophen overdose is often fatal and that even recommended doses may act as an overdose in malnourished or underweight adults.

A preliminary diagnosis of DILI due to rivaroxaban was made; rivaroxaban was switched to apixaban on the sixth day of admission, and liver enzymes trended downward, further supporting the diagnosis.
raw_record.extra_details: RUCAM causality assessment score of 8 (probable). Hepatocellular pattern with calculated R-factor of 18.8. Patient on rivaroxaban for 13 days at presentation; median time to liver injury reported as 15 days. Elevated AST/ALT peaked around day 7 (ALT 1702 U/L, AST 810 U/L) then downtrended after discontinuation, normalizing by 2 months. Patient had malaise but no jaundice or vomiting. Competing causes (thyrotoxicosis, hepatitis B reactivation, ischemia) ruled out. Tenofovir already being taken for hepatitis B. Mechanism likely idiosyncratic and possibly immunologic; no CYP3A4 inhibitor co-medication present. Rivaroxaban has dual elimination (one-third renal, two-thirds hepatic, CYP3A4-dependent). raw_record.support_text: In this randomized controlled trial of preventive, preemptive, or placebo IV acetaminophen in pediatric and adolescent patients undergoing posterior spinal fusion, no patients experienced hepatic injury attributable to IV acetaminophen exposure, and there was no difference in the incidence of adverse events among the groups. The authors note that prior studies estimated the incidence of hepatic serious adverse events and drug-induced liver injury from IV acetaminophen at only 3.2 and 0.4 per million patients, respectively, with most cases related to other factors such as concomitant hepatotoxic medications, comorbid hepatic conditions, or medication errors.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric and adolescent patients undergoing posterior spinal fusion; IV acetaminophen given preventively or preemptively at 45 mg/kg or 3 g/day with systemic opioids (tramadol and PCA); analgesic-use setting in a randomized controlled trial.
raw_record.extra_details: No patients in the trial experienced hepatic injury due to IV acetaminophen exposure; prior estimates cited were 3.2 hepatic serious adverse events and 0.4 drug-induced liver injury cases per million patients, most related to concomitant hepatotoxic medications, comorbid hepatic conditions, or medication errors.

condition_atoms: reported_condition=massive overdose of 125 g apap (single-agent ingestion); no prior liver disease noted
condition_group: exposure=overdose_or_supratherapeutic+population=human+reported_condition=massive overdose of 125 g apap (single-agent ingestion); no prior liver disease noted
condition_text: Massive overdose of 125 g APAP (single-agent ingestion); no prior liver disease noted.

raw_record.support_text: An 18-year-old male presented 1 hour after consuming 125 grams of acetaminophen (APAP) with a peak APAP level of 738.6 µg/mL. He was treated with intravenous N-acetylcysteine, fomepizole, intermittent hemodialysis, and CVVH at a high replacement rate. His AST, ALT, and alkaline phosphatase remained low (AST 50 U/L, ALT 55 U/L, both <100 U/L during hospitalization), and no liver failure developed; the early NAC and fomepizole were credited with protecting him from APAP-induced hepatic injury.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Massive overdose of 125 g APAP (single-agent ingestion); no prior liver disease noted.
raw_record.extra_details: APAP level rose from 630.6 to 730 µg/mL despite 4 hours of intermittent hemodialysis, attributed to continued GI absorption and high tissue distribution. Treated with intravenous NAC (initially 150 mg/kg then 12.5 mg/kg/h, with oral NAC 70 mg/kg q4h) and fomepizole (15 mg/kg then 10 mg/kg q6h) during high-rate CVVH (replacement 90 mL/kg/h). Discussion notes APAP toxicity can be fatal if acute liver failure develops; prior massive tylenol ingestion cases delayed beyond the NAC effective window had AST/ALT in the thousands; this patient's AST and ALT remained <100 U/L throughout and liver enzymes returned to normal.

raw_record.support_text: The patient's liver injury was attributed to prednisolone use. Histopathological examination of a US-guided liver biopsy showed centrilobular necrosis with hemorrhage, and a drug-induced lymphocyte-stimulation test (DLST) with prednisolone was positive. Prednisolone was discontinued and AST and ALT returned to near-normal within one month, while all other medications except prednisolone were restarted without recurrence of hepatitis. The authors ultimately diagnosed the patient with prednisolone-induced DILI.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Low-dose maintenance prednisolone (5 mg every other day) used for IgA nephropathy treatment; a course of high-dose prednisolone approximately two years prior was noted as possibly relevant to the acute hepatitis; other suspect medications were concurrently withdrawn initially but were restarted without recurrence once prednisolone was stopped.
raw_record.extra_details: DLST with prednisolone was positive (stimulation index 244%; measured 386 cpm vs control 158 cpm). Liver biopsy showed centrilobular necrosis with hemorrhage and no fatty change, arguing against steatohepatitis. After withdrawal of other suspect medications ALT remained above 300 IU/L and AST continued to increase, resolving to near-normal within one month after prednisolone cessation. Peak labs near referral: AST 266 IU/L, ALT 472 IU/L, ALP 61 IU/L, T-Bil 0.6 mg/dL. Authors note no prior published report of low-dose oral steroid-induced liver injury; prior reports were mostly after high-dose methylprednisolone. Authors regard this as possibly the first documented acute DILI associated with low-dose oral prednisolone.

condition_text: Phase I clinical trial dosing in patients with established solid tumors; development was terminated for poor outcomes.

raw_record.support_text: Spisulosine (compound 21, ES-285), a deoxysphingosine-based marine mollusk natural product isolated from Spisula polynyma, was evaluated in Phase I clinical trials in patients with established solid tumors using various regimens (24 h IV infusion every three weeks, or 3 h IV infusion for five consecutive days every three weeks). Despite infrequent drug-induced grade 3 or 4 adverse effects and an encouraging pharmacokinetic profile, spisulosine's potential as an anticancer agent was impeded by dose-dependent hepatic and neurotoxicity, and further development was therefore terminated; the human trials were discontinued due to poor clinical outcomes, with the death of one patient attributed to drug-related central neurotoxicity rather than to the liver.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Phase I clinical trial dosing in patients with established solid tumors; development was terminated for poor outcomes.
raw_record.extra_details: Also known as ES-285 and spisulosine 21. Dose-dependent hepatic toxicity was reported. Dose-limiting/grade 3-4 drug-induced adverse effects were infrequent. Regimens included 24 h intravenous infusion every 3 weeks and 3 h intravenous infusion for 5 consecutive days every 3 weeks. The single reported patient death was due to drug-related central neurotoxicity, not hepatic injury. In vitro data (not human DILI) showed anti-proliferative/cytotoxic activity against prostate (PC-3, LNCaP), breast, colon, HeLa, and other tumor cell lines.

condition_text: Observed in Chinese adult psoriasis patients receiving MTX; significant fibrosis was correlated with obesity and diabetes and not with MTX cumulative dose or duration of use.

raw_record.support_text: Methotrexate (MTX) is effective for treating psoriasis and psoriatic arthritis, but its potential hepatotoxicity remains a concern. The paper frames liver biopsy as the gold standard for detecting MTX-induced liver injury, and the study investigated transient elastography for detecting MTX-induced liver fibrosis in Chinese psoriasis patients.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Observed in Chinese adult psoriasis patients receiving MTX; significant fibrosis was correlated with obesity and diabetes and not with MTX cumulative dose or duration of use.
raw_record.extra_details: Of 228 patients screened, 34 met inclusion criteria; 9 (26.5%) had significant liver fibrosis (Roenigk grade ≥3a). Transient elastography had an area under the ROC curve of 0.76 (95% CI 0.59-0.93; P=0.021); a cut-off of 7.1 kPa gave 100% sensitivity and 68% specificity. Liver biopsy was performed when liver stiffness was ≥7.1 kPa or total cumulative dose of MTX was ≥3.5 g. Fibrosis correlated with BMI ≥30 kg/m², waist circumference ≥138 cm, and glycated haemoglobin ≥7.8%.

raw_record.support_text: In this patient series, abemaciclib was one of the two CDK4/6 inhibitors mainly involved in CDK4/6 inhibitor-induced liver injury (alongside ribociclib). The predominant liver-injury type was hepatocellular, with autoimmune features (positive anti-nuclear antibodies and/or elevated serum IgG) present in 32% of patients. Corticosteroids were given in 40% of patients and permitted resolution of liver injury that had not improved spontaneously. No patient developed fulminant hepatitis or died from the anti-CDK4/6-induced liver damage.
raw_record.extra_details: Paper argues CDK4/6 inhibitors should be included in the drug-induced autoimmune-like hepatitis (DI-ALH) category given autoimmune features (ANA and/or elevated IgG in 1/3 of patients), consistent histology, and corticosteroid response without relapse after discontinuation. Corticosteroids started about 1 month after hepatitis onset and were given in 40% of patients; some patients resumed a different CDK4/6 inhibitor after resolution without relapse. Management: discontinue at hepatitis grade 3 or 4. No fulminant hepatitis or death.

raw_record.support_text: The paper concludes that neddylation is overrepresented in acetaminophen-induced liver injury (AILI) in patients and in preclinical animal models, and that MLN4924 (Pevonedistat) ameliorates this liver injury. It also states that MLN4924 treatment of DILI caused by APAP overdose even at 600 mg/kg induces a hepatic regenerative response. The study used paraffin-embedded liver samples from human AILI patients, confirming the human context of the APAP-overdose liver injury.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose setting (APAP overdose, up to 600 mg/kg in the animal experiments); human relevance is supported by paraffin-embedded liver samples from AILI patients, though the mechanistic study is largely carried out in mice.
raw_record.extra_details: The injury is termed acetaminophen-induced liver injury (AILI). Mechanism investigated: neddylation is overrepresented in AILI, impairing mitochondrial activity through PTM of TAM41, modulating cardiolipin (CL) levels; inhibiting neddylation with MLN4924 (Pevonedistat, an NAE-1 inhibitor) recovers hepatic mitochondrial complex I and II activities, increases mitochondrial membrane potential and ATP synthesis, and reduces mitochondrial ROS. At 600 mg/kg APAP overdose liver regeneration was compromised; MLN4924 treatment restored mitochondrial activity and induced a hepatic regenerative response.

condition_text: Kidney transplant recipients maintained on azathioprine with prednisone (10 mg) as second immunosuppressant; onset 16-24 months after grafting.

raw_record.support_text: Three patients who received a cadaveric kidney transplant and were maintained on the immunosuppressant azathioprine (2.0-2.3 mg/kg) plus prednisone (10 mg) developed liver disease 16-24 months after grafting. They had no previous hepatic disease, normal pre-transplant liver function, no alcohol use, and no hepatotoxic drug other than azathioprine; HBsAg/HBsAb remained negative and serologic tests (CMV, brucellosis, toxoplasmosis, mononucleosis, syphilis, hepatitis A and B) failed to show an infective cause. Liver biopsy showed sinusoidal dilatation progressing to cirrhosis, with improvement after azathioprine dose reduction, implicating azathioprine as the cause of the hepatic injury.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Kidney transplant recipients maintained on azathioprine with prednisone (10 mg) as second immunosuppressant; onset 16-24 months after grafting.
raw_record.extra_details: Case series of 3 transplant patients (patients 1-3: ages 48, 37, 33; azathioprine doses 2.3, 2.0, 2.1 mg/kg/day). Injury featured hepatic sinusoidal dilatation progressing to cirrhosis, with splenomegaly, ascites, esophageal varices, increased wedged hepatic pressure, and marked 99mTc uptake reduction. Laboratory findings of frank hemolysis (increased reticulocytes, no detectable serum haptoglobin, elevated LDH first fraction, elevated bilirubin), macrocytic anemia, leuco- and thrombocytopenia; SGPT/SGOT, alkaline phosphatase and gamma-GT only slightly elevated in patients 1 and 2 and normal in patient 3; serum albumin decreased. Congestive heart failure and infective causes excluded. Improvement after azathioprine dose reduction in all 3 patients.

raw_record.support_text: Liver injury from nitrofurantoin can cause either an acute or chronic active hepatitis-like syndrome and necrosis with or without jaundice; jaundice is associated with a 10% mortality rate. The chronic manifestation of DILI attributed to nitrofurantoin is more common and typically manifests after prophylactic treatment exceeding 6 months, with gradual progression, fatigue, weakness, dark-colored urine, and elevated liver enzymes, INR, and bilirubin. Cholestatic patterns may show elevated ALP and GGT. The prophylactic dosage is 50–100 mg once daily at bedtime for 6 months. In this case, the patient took the prophylactic dose for 2 years and presented with elevated bilirubin and liver enzymes.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Chronic prophylactic use; patient had taken the prophylactic dose for an extended 2-year period rather than the standard 6 months.
raw_record.extra_details: Prophylactic dosage 50–100 mg once daily at bedtime for 6 months. Jaundice is associated with a 10% mortality rate. Chronic form linked with positive antinuclear antibodies, smooth muscle antibodies, lupus erythematosus cells, hypoalbuminemia, and hypergammaglobulinemia and may resemble autoimmune hepatitis (AIH), though the patient's albumin/total protein stayed within range and autoimmune liver tests were negative. Cholestatic patterns may show elevated ALP and GGT. Discontinuation reverses the injury and biomarkers normalize within a few months if there is no preexisting fibrosis or cirrhosis; in this patient enzymes and bilirubin normalized after 5 months of follow-up.

raw_record.support_text: The case was diagnosed with a probable case of drug-induced liver injury (DILI). The patient had been self-medicating with tablet nitrofurantoin (initially 100 mg twice daily for 2 weeks as prescribed, then continued on her own at 100 mg once daily for the last 2 years) and presented with scleral icterus, pain, nausea, and loss of appetite. Nitrofurantoin was discontinued and LFTs trending downward after 1 month, while tests for HBsAg, HCV, HIV, and autoimmune liver disease were negative.

raw_record.extra_details: Initial prescribed dose 100 mg twice daily for 2 weeks; ongoing self-medicated dose 100 mg once daily for last 2 years for urinary discomfort. raw_record.extra_details: Clinically significant hepatotoxicity occurred in 14.7% of children with rheumatic fever. raw_record.support_text: Five patients with a prior history of halothane hepatitis were evaluated before emergency or elective surgery (2 weeks to 7 years after a previous episode). Two required emergency surgery during the recovery phase, when liver function tests were still abnormal, while the rest had resolved halothane hepatitis. Anesthesia was induced with intravenous agents and nitrous oxide-oxygen, and no halogenated agents were used; the anesthesia machine was never equipped with a vaporizer. Serial SGPT/ALT and other liver function tests showed no evidence of recurrent halothane hepatitis in any of the five patients.

raw_record.extra_details: The paper's case report strongly suggests that inapparent circuit contamination alone may lead to halothane hepatitis in patients with prior history of hepatitis following halothane anesthesia. The authors propose that NSAIDs may unmask latent BSEP dysfunction in genetically predisposed individuals, precipitating refractory cholestasis, and highlight ABCB11 polymorphisms as determinants of NSAID-related DILI susceptibility even at therapeutic doses.

raw_record.support_text: Emerging hepatotoxicity concerns have prompted regulatory action on epigallocatechin gallate (EGCG), particularly in concentrated supplement form. In 2023 the EU established a mandatory upper limit of 800 mg/day for EGCG in dietary supplements after safety evaluations revealed transaminase elevations in nearly a quarter of intervention trials at doses ≥800 mg/day; EFSA set an ADI of 322 mg/day. HLA-B*35:01 carriers accounted for 72% of reported liver injury cases versus 10-15% in the general population. The Minnesota Green Tea Trial showed a 6.7% incidence of ALT elevation in postmenopausal women consuming 843 mg/day EGCG, with COMT and UGT1A4 polymorphisms contributing to interindividual variability. Fasting-state ingestion markedly increases EGCG bioavailability and amplifies hepatotoxic risk, prompting warning-label mandates.

raw_record.support_text: In this phase 1 trial of the investigational agent REM127 in patients with mild-to-moderate Alzheimer's disease, adverse events in the hepatobiliary dysfunction system organ class were observed only in participants on active REM127 treatment and not in placebo recipients. One serious adverse event in the 350 mg dose group was considered related to study treatment and reported as toxic hepatitis. Drug-induced liver injury was reported in six participants leading to study discontinuation, and one case fulfilled Hy's Law criteria, led to hospitalization, and was reported as a suspected unexpected serious adverse reaction (SUSAR), prompting termination of the trial. Increased serum transaminases occurred in all 1400 mg (2/2) and 350 mg (2/2) participants and 1/5 in the 88 mg group versus none in placebo; increases typically started around the fourth week, peaked days to weeks after study discontinuation, and returned to normal in all participants over several weeks to months.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Investgational agent evaluated in a phase 1 clinical trial in patients with mild-to-moderate Alzheimer's disease at daily oral doses of 88, 350, and 1400 mg/day.
raw_record.extra_details: AE terms reported included drug-induced liver injury, toxic hepatitis, hepatitis toxic, hepatic enzyme increased, alanine aminotransferase increased, blood lactate dehydrogenase increased, and transaminases increased. Six participants had hepatobiliary dysfunction leading to study discontinuation; trial was terminated early for safety. One case fulfilled Hy's Law, required hospitalization, and was reported as SUSAR. Transaminase elevations typically began around the fourth week (at last study-drug day or follow-up), peaked days to weeks after discontinuation, and resolved over several weeks to months; an associated decrease in total cholesterol was noted. No deaths or liver transplantations occurred. REM127 is a septin 6 (SEPT6) modulator; one participant received the co-medication quetiapine from Day 21 to Day 23.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports on psoriasis patients with significant liver fibrosis and prior methotrexate (MTX) exposure, describing 'MTX-associated liver fibrosis' and hypothesizing that only a subset of patients developed fibrosis primarily due to MTX toxicity. One-third of patients showed liver fibrosis regression after MTX discontinuation, and MTX use for more than 4 years was associated with higher odds of regression (OR = 16.00, 95% CI 1.09–234.25; p = 0.043). The paper also notes obesity is a known risk factor for MTX-related liver injury (paragraph 37).
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Psoriasis patients with significant liver fibrosis and prior MTX exposure; study focused on fibrosis regression following MTX discontinuation.
raw_record.extra_details: Pilot cross-sectional study; MTX-associated liver fibrosis attributed to MTX toxicity, with postulated mechanisms including folate depletion, Nrf2 suppression, and mitochondrial dysfunction leading to oxidative stress and hepatic inflammation. MTX use duration >4 years OR 16.00 (1.09–234.25, p=0.043); MTX duration continuous OR 1.55 (0.92–2.63); cumulative MTX dose OR 2.25 (0.74–6.85); cumulative dose >2 grams OR 6.00 (0.56–63.98); MTX-free duration not significant (p=0.956). One-third of patients showed fibrosis regression after MTX cessation.

raw_record.support_text: The authors describe paracetamol (acetaminophen) overdose as a cause of severe hepatic damage and death. They note that in usual dosage paracetamol is a safe analgesic with no evidence of abnormal liver-function tests, but that in their series overdose patients had hepatic damage at doses as low as 13 g, and death occurred with 25 g, with a mortality rate of about 20% in their referred series.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose setting (suicidal ingestion); patients partly referred from other hospitals because of severe liver damage; many developed hepatic encephalopathy and coma. Doses ranged from 13 g (hepatic damage) to 25 g (death).
raw_record.extra_details: Nineteen patients had serum-bilirubin >4 mg per 100 ml on the 3rd-5th day with a prothrombin-time ratio of 2.2 or greater; with two exceptions they developed encephalopathy and twelve died. Liver biopsy showed massive and confluent necrosis of all lobules at necropsy and characteristic centrilobular necrosis/collapse with reticulin collapse during recovery; two coma survivors had increased fibrosis (no cirrhosis) that regressed by 6 months. SGOT was variable but generally higher in fulminant hepatic failure. Alleged doses as low as 13 g caused hepatic damage and 25 g caused death, consistent with Proudfoot and Wright. Hospital statistics for England and Wales show rising overdoses since 1966 with 29 deaths in 1970 (about 2-3% mortality); the study series mortality was about 20% due partly to referral of severe cases. Authors attributed lack of dose-injury correlation to unreliable tablet counts, vomiting, and gastric lavage.

raw_record.support_text: Chloroform intoxication produces hepatic injury seen after two to five days, which is the result of liver cell necrosis; prothrombin time and transaminase values are markedly elevated while bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase tend to be minimally abnormal. Alcohol or barbiturates that induce hepatic microsomal enzymes increase chloroform-induced liver cell damage, whereas enzyme inhibitors such as disulfiram prevent hepatotoxicity.

Hepatic injury is attributed to liver cell necrosis from toxic metabolites formed by hepatic enzymes rather than direct injury; alcohol/barbiturate enzyme induction worsens the injury and disulfiram prevents hepatotoxicity. raw_record.extra_details: Allopurinol given at 100 mg three times daily for hyperuricemia. Liver injury appeared ~3 weeks after starting allopurinol, with eosinophilia and worsening liver tests (SGOT, SGPT, alkaline phosphatase elevations; total bilirubin up to ~1.2 mg/100 ml). Liver biopsy revealed multiple non-caseating epithelioid granulomas chiefly in or adjacent to portal triads, focal necrosis, and mild fatty metamorphosis; a repeat biopsy ~1 month after stopping allopurinol showed complete absence of granulomas with occasional focal necrosis, mild fatty change, and portal fibrosis. Findings consistent with granulomatous hepatitis.

raw_record.support_text: Following a controlled halothane challenge (0.1 to 0.2 per cent halothane in oxygen given for 5 minutes on December 7), the patient's serum glutamic oxalacetic transaminase rose sharply from a normal baseline to 440 units on December 8 and 700 units on December 9, with total serum bilirubin rising transiently to 0.82 mg/100 ml, before returning toward normal. The patient had previously experienced halothane-related hepatitis, and the rechallenge reproduced the transaminase surge, supporting halothane as the cause of the liver injury.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Controlled rechallenge in a single patient with prior halothane-related hepatitis and moderately advanced inactive postnecrotic cirrhosis; halothane given as a brief 5-minute anesthetic at 0.1-0.2% via face mask without premedication.
raw_record.extra_details: Rechallenge produced a sharp rise in serum glutamic oxalacetic transaminase from normal to 440 units (day 1) and 700 units (day 2) after halothane, with transient total bilirubin rise to 0.82 mg/100 ml; serology subsequently returned toward normal. Liver biopsy before challenge showed inactive postnecrotic cirrhosis and fibrosis that had progressed from an earlier inflammatory picture. Mild leukopenia and thrombocytopenia were also present. The patient took prednisone (10-20 mg) during a prior period of malaise, unrelated to the halothane injury.

raw_record.support_text: Four hours after deliberate exposure to halothane, the patient began to experience severe leg aching, a symptom previously noted at the onset of his hepatitis relapses, followed by a chill, fever to 102.8°F, tachycardia, malaise, and a rise in serum glutamic oxalacetic transaminase with a slight increase in serum bilirubin. A liver biopsy 4 days after halothane challenge showed acute hepatitis with intense mononuclear inflammation, zones of recent collapse containing acidophilic bodies, and reticuloendothelial cell proliferation.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Rechallenge exposure in a patient with a history of repeated halothane hepatitis relapses over five and a half years; the patient had documented postnecrotic cirrhosis before this challenge.
raw_record.extra_details: Time course: leg aching and chill began 4 hours after halothane exposure; temperature rose to 102.2°F at 4 h and 102.8°F at 8 h, with pulse rise 80 to 108 and bilirubin/dark urine; SGOT continued to rise for 48 h after challenge then fell slowly and returned to normal about 2 weeks after exposure. Suggestive increase in eosinophils. Liver biopsy 4 days after challenge (December 11) showed acute hepatitis with small zones of recent collapse, numerous acidophilic bodies, proliferating reticuloendothelial cells, and monocytes, on top of pre-existing postnecrotic cirrhosis. Patient recovered clinically; splenomegaly noted during challenge resolved. The glutamic oxalacetic transaminase level was still elevated at discharge and took about 6 more days to return to normal.

condition_atoms: reported_condition=patients with leukemia or histiocytosis x in complete remission receiving methotrexate therapy; finding specifically that fibrosis can develop absent hepatosplenomegaly or abnormal liver function
condition_group: exposure=therapeutic_use+population=human+reported_condition=patients with leukemia or histiocytosis x in complete remission receiving methotrexate therapy; finding specifically that fibrosis can develop absent hepatosplenomegaly or abnormal liver function
condition_text: Patients with leukemia or histiocytosis X in complete remission receiving methotrexate therapy; finding specifically that fibrosis can develop absent hepatosplenomegaly or abnormal liver function.

raw_record.support_text: Liver toxicity was studied by sequential examination, liver function tests, and percutaneous liver biopsies (light and electron microscopy) during methotrexate treatment in patients whose leukemia or histiocytosis X remained in complete remission. Fibrosis was found even without hepatosplenomegaly or abnormal liver function and persisted despite normalization of physical findings and liver function. Initially hepatocellular changes were seen by light microscopy, progressing to portal inflammation and fibrosis with continued therapy. The authors conclude that the pathologic changes are secondary to methotrexate therapy, not the basic disease process, and stress the insidious nature of this hepatic toxicity in nonmalignant uses of the drug.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients with leukemia or histiocytosis X in complete remission receiving methotrexate therapy; finding specifically that fibrosis can develop absent hepatosplenomegaly or abnormal liver function.
raw_record.extra_details: 10 patients studied by sequential liver function tests and percutaneous biopsies (light and electron microscopy); hepatomegaly usually developed; fibrosis persisted despite normalization of physical findings and liver function; light microscopy initially showed hepatocellular changes progressing to portal inflammation and fibrosis; ultrastructural changes included double-nucleated hepatic cells with minor nucleolar changes and decreased perichromatin, varied cytoplasmic fat and glycogen, mitochondrial swelling, dilated endoplasmic reticulum, and sinusoidal slender filaments with collagen and basement membrane formation; authors state liver biopsy is the only accurate way to follow the extent of liver damage and discontinuation of therapy can result in return toward normal structure; toxicity also noted as concern for nonmalignant uses (skin disorders, immunologic diseases).

raw_record.support_text: Clinical, light, and electron microscopic observations suggest that the reactions to halothane and viral hepatitis are not identical, and the demonstration of antimitochondrial antibodies together with eosinophilia, granuloma formation, and an accelerated clinical syndrome after a second exposure suggests a hypersensitivity reaction as the cause of hepatic injury after halothane.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Hepatitis after halothane may be less frequent in children; mortality was higher after multiple exposures than after single ones; two patients had non-anesthetic occupational exposure (a halothane factory worker and an anesthetist repeatedly administering halothane) with findings not differing from the other patients.
raw_record.extra_details: Biopsy specimens resemble viral hepatitis with spotty necrosis, variation in size and cytoplasmic staining of hepatocytes, and acidophilic bodies; hepatic vein branch phlebitis and mononuclear inflammatory exudate; postmortem material shows more extensive hepatocellular necrosis. Ultrastructurally, halothane hepatitis mitochondria show segmental loss of the outer membrane and infolding of the inner one (absent in viral hepatitis); smooth ER increase may relate to prior drug exposure. Antimitochondrial antibodies, eosinophilia, and granuloma formation support a hypersensitivity mechanism. Sex or age did not influence susceptibility to hepatitis or mortality; nearly two thirds of patients were exposed more than once; a mortality rate could not be calculated owing to the selected nature of the collected material.

The patient became asymptomatic 36 hours after the drug was discontinued, and liver tests were normal 12 days after this rechallenge.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Deliberate rechallenge; prior sensitization from sulfamethoxazole-phenazopyridine (the initially administered drug); demonstrated cross-sensitization between sulfamethoxazole and sulfisoxazole.
raw_record.extra_details: Rechallenge at 500 mg 4 times daily (5 tablets) with onset ~30 h after first tablet; symptoms included malaise, restlessness, anorexia, arthralgia, dry mouth, temperature 100.6°F. Labs: SGOT 540 U, SGPT 390 U, alkaline phosphatase 16.9 King-Armstrong units, bilirubin 1.6 mg/100 ml, bromsulfalein 36% retention at 45 min; differential count, cholesterol, cephalin flocculation, thymol turbidity and serum proteins normal. Asymptomatic 36 h after discontinuation; liver tests normal 12 days later. The initial admission episode (earlier) had a percutaneous liver biopsy 'highly suggestive of drug-induced hepatitis' with SGOT 110 U, SGPT 360 U, alkaline phosphatase 28.0 King-Armstrong units, resolving within ~10 days of stopping medication. Authors attribute the onset, arthralgia and cross-reactivity to a hypersensitivity mechanism rather than direct toxicity.

condition_text: Restricted to patients with porphyria cutanea tarda (PCT) receiving chloroquine therapeutically.

raw_record.support_text: In all five patients with porphyria cutanea tarda treated with chloroquine, there was a 3.5- to 28-fold increase in urinary uroporphyrin excretion; serum transaminases were modestly increased in two patients (M.J., G.G.) and strikingly increased to up to 740, 810, and 670 units in three patients (C.W., C.K., W.C.). The transaminase elevation was transient, occurred during maximum uroporphyrin excretion, and in one patient (C.K.) serum bilirubin rose to 3.1 mg%. In patient W.C., liver biopsy at the time of maximum transaminase elevation showed distinct and rather marked centrilobular hepatic-cell necrosis, which had resolved 22 weeks later.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Restricted to patients with porphyria cutanea tarda (PCT) receiving chloroquine therapeutically.
raw_record.extra_details: Chloroquine doses of 0.5-1.0 g daily for 2-11 days increased urinary uroporphyrin excretion (up to 107.9 mg/24 hr, 3.5- to 28-fold) with transient SGOT/SGPT elevation; no change in serum bilirubin in two patients, but bilirubin rose to 3.1 mg% in C.K.; centrilobular hepatic-cell necrosis on biopsy in W.C. only, with normalization 22 weeks later. Patients experienced transient fever, malaise, nausea, and anorexia during initial treatment. Readministration of chloroquine to these patients after 1-26 weeks produced no effect (tachyphylaxis).; exact_agent_identity_note: Hepatotoxic transaminase elevation and hepatic necrosis attributed directly to chloroquine administration.

raw_record.support_text: The study demonstrated a clear relationship between methotrexate (MTX) therapy and chemically and histologically defined liver damage. The rapidity of onset and severity of abnormal liver function tests correlated with the intensity of therapy, with more hepatotoxicity observed in the group showing hematologic and gastrointestinal chemotherapy side effects. LFT abnormalities following intermittent MTX resolved completely within one month after cessation, and continued moderate-dose MTX therapy was associated with normal or near-normal liver function without progressive hepatic damage, including in patients with eye disease.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: One patient with pre-existing liver disease developed a somewhat more severe functional abnormality; his liver function returned to normal after cessation of therapy and repeated biopsies showed no further deterioration. Therapy was given for otherwise healthy ocular disease or as part of leukemia chemotherapy.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity included abnormal SGOT/SGPT and BSP retention, with histologic findings of portal fibrosis, fatty metamorphosis, mild toxic degeneration of hepatic parenchymal cells, and slight bile stasis. LFT abnormalities correlated with intensity of therapy and resolved within one month after cessation of intermittent MTX. Five patients received maintenance MTX 10-25 mg/m² IV once weekly for 3 months to 1.5 years; liver function returned to normal in 4 of 5, while one had persistent abnormalities (SGOT 30-60, SGPT 60-130, BSP 7-11%). Four intensive-therapy patients died of infectious complications of leukemia 4-6 months post-study with hepatic disease not involved; all showed leukemic portal infiltration, one with moderate fatty metamorphosis, one with slight portal fibrosis and moderate fatty metamorphosis.

raw_record.support_text: When the patient was challenged with the synthetic estrogen ethinyl estradiol (1 mg daily), the symptoms previously experienced during pregnancy developed promptly: jaundice with liver enlargement, hyperbilirubinemia (mainly direct-reacting), and bromsulfalein retention. Serum alkaline phosphatase remained normal after five days but serum 5-nucleotidase activity increased. On discontinuation the symptoms subsided within two days while abnormal liver function returned slowly to normal. Similar challenge studies in seven other patients with pruritus or jaundice of pregnancy reproduced their pregnancy abnormalities, whereas women asymptomatic during pregnancy remained asymptomatic. The paper concludes this observation strengthens the hypothesis that the episodes of jaundice during pregnancy were induced by hormones, and that the patient and other patients with intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy may be abnormally responsive to estrogens.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patient with prior pruritus and/or jaundice during pregnancy and abnormal menses who appears abnormally responsive to estrogens; challenge dose of ethinyl estradiol 1 mg daily (intended diagnostic challenge, not a therapeutic regimen); seven other patients with pregnancy cholestasis reproduced abnormalities while women asymptomatic during pregnancy stayed asymptomatic.
raw_record.extra_details: Ethinyl estradiol is a C-17 alkyl-substituted steroid; by analogy C-17 alkyl-substituted estrogens may be more likely to induce cholestasis than endogenous hormones. On challenge (1 mg daily): jaundice with liver enlargement, hyperbilirubinemia mainly direct-reacting, bromsulfalein retention, increased serum 5-nucleotidase activity after five days; serum alkaline phosphatase remained normal. Symptoms subsided within two days of stopping the hormone and liver function returned more slowly to normal.

condition_text: Very low therapeutic doses in a reportedly metabolically predisposed patient; simultaneous use of phenobarbital (potential enzyme induction) as a contributing co-exposure; sporadic non-A, non-B hepatitis could not be formally excluded.

raw_record.support_text: A diagnosis of acute type-A or B hepatitis was excluded by seronegativity for the relevant antibodies. The dramatic fall of serum transaminase levels to within the normal range 2 weeks after withdrawal of acetaminophen strongly supported drug-induced liver damage. The patient experienced hepatotoxicity at very low therapeutic doses of acetaminophen, suggesting a metabolic predisposition; simultaneous treatment with phenobarbital could have induced mixed-function oxidase activity and increased production of toxic metabolites in amounts exceeding normal glutathione binding capacity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Very low therapeutic doses in a reportedly metabolically predisposed patient; simultaneous use of phenobarbital (potential enzyme induction) as a contributing co-exposure; sporadic non-A, non-B hepatitis could not be formally excluded.
raw_record.extra_details: Only seven prior cases of hepatotoxicity from therapeutic doses of acetaminophen were cited; the striking feature here was the very low dose. Serum transaminase levels dramatically returned to normal within 2 weeks after acetaminophen withdrawal. Acute type-A/type-B hepatitis and cytomegalovirus, herpes virus, and Epstein-Barr virus infection were ruled out by antibody testing. Phenobarbital co-treatment was proposed to enhance mixed-function oxidase activity and toxic-metabolite production exceeding glutathione binding capacity.

raw_record.support_text: In this randomized trial of antidotes for paracetamol poisoning, patients who ingested paracetamol overdose (mean ingested amounts 25.5-29.3 g across groups) developed liver injury evidenced by elevated AST (geometric mean peak 1046 U/l in the supportive-therapy group), elevated bilirubin, and histological hepatic necrosis grades, with grade III (severe) necrosis occurring significantly less often with cysteamine or methionine treatment.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose exposure (accidental/deliberate paracetamol poisoning) treated with supportive therapy or an antidote (cysteamine or methionine).
raw_record.extra_details: Randomized trial of cysteamine vs methionine vs supportive therapy for paracetamol poisoning. Mean ingested paracetamol 25.5 g (S), 29.3 g (C), 28.4 g (M); mean delay to treatment ~7 h. One death (previously reported) occurred in the supportive-therapy group: a 24-year-old patient transferred 10 h after ingesting 15 g paracetamol and treated by charcoal haemoperfusion. Geometric mean peak AST 1046 U/l (S), 96 U/l (C), 139 U/l (M); significant AST reduction with cysteamine (p<0.002) and methionine (p<0.01); bilirubin significantly lower with cysteamine (p<0.05). Histology showed hepatic necrosis grades; grade III severe necrosis significantly reduced with cysteamine (p<0.01) and methionine (p<0.05). Peak plasma creatinine lower in treatment groups. Cysteamine and methionine were antidotes (treatments), not themselves causative. No randomized control group receiving placebo; supportive therapy served as comparator.

GTT results: 18 abnormal GTT among the cohort (8 with cirrhosis, 15 with fibrosis, 3 normal).

raw_record.support_text: The glucose-containing chloroethylnitrosourea chlorozotocin showed hepatic toxicity: a few patients in phase I trials had reversible elevations of serum liver enzymes, and Belt et al. described three cases of liver damage following chlorozotocin at a dose of 225 mg/m². Peak bilirubin elevations ranged 3.5-12.7 mg/100 ml (mostly conjugated/direct), alkaline phosphatase rose up to 20 times normal while SGOT rose only 3-4 times, and liver histology showed centrilobular cholestasis in two cases and cholestasis without lobular localization in the third.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: One of the three described cases had a history of alcohol ingestion; whether the cholestatic histologic pattern is entirely characteristic of chlorozotocin-induced liver damage was not known.
raw_record.extra_details: Presented as a glucose-containing chloroethylnitrosourea similar to other nitrosoureas. Phase I trials: a few patients with reversible serum liver-enzyme elevations. Belt et al.: three cases of liver damage at 225 mg/m², peak bilirubin 3.5-12.7 mg/100 ml mostly conjugated, marked alkaline phosphatase elevation up to 20 times normal, SGOT 3-4 times normal; histology showed centrilobular cholestasis (2 cases) and cholestasis without lobular localization (1 case). Treatment with acetylcysteine (N-acetylcysteine) was recommended for plasma levels above the nomogram line, most effective if begun within 16 hours of ingestion. Death rate was zero in this series. raw_record.support_text: The paper reports three patients in whom hepatitis developed in relation to halothane anesthesia. The authors conclude that the evidence supports the diagnosis of a halothane-induced sensitization reaction with hepatitis, based on the characteristic temporal relation between halothane exposure and fever/jaundice, onset with chills and high fever, significant eosinophilia, antecedent atopy and drug-hypersensitivity reactions, occurrence of the hepatitis after a second halothane exposure in two of the three cases, and histologic features consistent with drug-induced hepatitis. Biopsies showed severe hepatitis with bridging necrosis, and all three patients recovered fully.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Antecedent atopy and drug-hypersensitivity reactions; hepatitis occurred after a second (re)exposure to halothane in two of the three cases; one patient (Patient 3) was diabetic with a fish allergy.
raw_record.extra_details: Serial SGOT (normal 15–35 IU/ml) and serum bilirubin (normal 0.1–1.4 mg/dl) values were recorded after halothane exposure for each patient (e.g., Patient 1 SGOT 1600 IU/ml at 2 days, bilirubin 2.66 mg/dl at 7 days; Patient 2 SGOT 2480 IU/ml at 6 days, bilirubin 13.50 mg/dl at 13 days). Histology showed severe hepatitis with bridging necrosis and, in one case, granulomata and giant cells; Patient 3 had eosinophilia rising to 11%. The authors noted absence of epidemiologic or serologic evidence of type B hepatitis and excluded postoperative cholestasis or centrilobular necrosis attributable to shock/multiple transfusions. All patients recovered fully.

This case was described as illustrating the most serious and uncommon form of hepatic dysfunction associated with VPA, ending in death from uncontrolled intracranial hypertension.

raw_record.support_text: The paper concludes that the clinical, biochemical, and histologic observations in its group of patients support the view that enflurane-associated hepatic injury does occur and may be associated with a fatal outcome in some instances, although the incidence is lower than that of halothane jaundice. The character and presumably the mechanism of the injury are stated to be similar to those of halothane, and cross-reactivity/cross-sensitization may exist for enflurane, so the authors recommend not administering halothane, methoxyflurane, or enflurane to a patient who developed evidence of hepatic injury after prior exposure to any haloalkane anesthetic.
raw_record.extra_details: Enflurane-associated hepatic injury has a centrilobular type of necrosis similar to halothane and a lower incidence than (the rare) halothane jaundice; fatal outcome possible in some instances. Comparison table lists 7 accepted published cases/10 years in clinical use for enflurane. Enflurane has little intrinsic hepatotoxic potential: in >1800 volunteers/surgical patients few hepatic abnormalities seen, though transient mild elevations of AST, ALT, LDH or GGTP were recorded in up to 58% of subjects; multiple-exposure results were conflicting (Allen/Downing reported no significant enzyme changes; Dundee reported ALT/GGTP/LDH/cholinesterase elevations in almost 25%), but hepatic toxicity was never severe. Risk of cross-reactivity/cross-sensitization with halothane and methoxyflurane.

raw_record.support_text: Isoniazid (INH) is stated to be the only drug causing liver injury in normal doses that has received extensive research attention. The liver injury may be subclinical or, in a small proportion of patients, clinically indistinguishable from viral hepatitis, and very occasionally it is fatal. Onset may occur from one week to many months after initiation, most often within the first three months.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Therapeutic use in prophylaxis and treatment of tuberculosis.
raw_record.extra_details: Government-sponsored large-scale studies with several thousand patients. Injury may be subclinical or clinically indistinguishable from viral hepatitis, occasionally fatal. Onset ranges from 1 week to many months, most often within first 3 months; some patients asymptomatic until insidious jaundice; mild cases show only SGOT elevation. Mild disorder may persist without progression or resolve spontaneously even while therapy continues; improvement usually occurs shortly after stopping with complete recovery.

raw_record.support_text: The authors state that even if the patient survived the acute CNS depressant effects of propoxyphene, long-term survival appeared questionable because of the likelihood of severe liver damage by acetaminophen. Plasma-acetaminophen concentrations above 400 µg/mL at 4 h after ingestion are associated with very severe intoxication; the patient's concentration was 485 µg/mL at 22 h and probably over 1000 µg/mL at 4 h. Acetaminophen hepatotoxicity is increased by prior exposure to barbiturates and other enzyme-inducing drugs that enhance formation of its hepatotoxic reactive metabolite.

raw_record.extra_details: Ingestion of 58.5 g (1.22 g/kg) acetaminophen, among the largest known ingestions; back-extrapolated plasma concentration 1470 mg/L equivalent to 1.40 g/kg. Acetaminophen biologic half-life is 2-3 h at therapeutic doses but averages ~8 h in intoxicated patients, and long half-lives are usually associated with severe liver damage and a high fatality rate. Hepatotoxic reactive metabolite formed by mixed-function oxidase; toxicity increased by barbiturate-induced enzyme induction. Propoxyphene was attributed to coma, respiratory depression, and hypothermia rather than liver injury.

raw_record.support_text: Six women were diagnosed with halothane-induced hepatitis based on criteria of no pre-existing liver disease, hepatitis onset within two weeks of halothane exposure, and no alternative explanations. All had jaundice and high transaminase levels, all were female, and most were obese; the interval between anesthesia and hepatitis was two days in the one previously exposed patient and six to ten days in the others. Three patients died with autopsy findings consistent with post-halothane hepatitis, and no other causes such as prior hepatotoxin exposure, shock, or hepatitis B infection were found.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: All affected patients were women, markedly obese or at upper limits of normal weight, and from closely related families of common ethnic origin; only the patient with prior halothane exposure had a short (two-day) latency.
raw_record.extra_details: Halothane anesthesia exposure; all six cases satisfied the diagnostic criteria for hepatitis induced by halothane. Clinical features included jaundice, high transaminase levels, fever rising to 40°C (104°F) in five of six, peripheral eosinophil counts above 500/mm3 in three, and two-to-ten day interval from anesthesia to hepatitis. Three patients died; autopsy findings were consistent with post-halothane hepatitis, and alternative causes (prior hepatotoxin exposure, shock, hepatitis B virus) were excluded. Survivors remained healthy with no recurrence. Anti-HBs testing was performed on three surviving patients; a four-to-five-generation survey of 154 blood relatives revealed no additional cases of postoperative hepatic injury.

raw_record.support_text: The present observation demonstrates that cimetidine can induce mild forms of acute hepatitis without frank jaundice. Safety studies had shown substantial elevations of serum aminotransferases in 21 of 1816 cimetidine-treated patients, though most lacked collateral information for confident interpretation, and aminotransferase elevation was comparable in drug- and placebo-treated patients. Given cimetidine's wide use (~50 million tablets prescribed in Italy in 1979), cimetidine-induced symptomatic hepatitis appears to be a rare complication, whereas asymptomatic liver disturbances remain indefinite.

raw_record.extra_details: A 75-day interval occurred between drug administration and onset of hepatitis; liver biopsy showed acute hepatitis with spotty necrosis and iron-containing pigment in portal histiocytes and Kupffer cells; electron microscopy showed diffuse bile pigment accumulation in hepatocytes with otherwise normal smooth endoplasmic reticulum, mitochondria, and organelles. Rash and musculoskeletal pain suggested a hypersensitivity reaction; functional tests returned to normal 24 days after drug withdrawal; reexposure transiently reappeared most symptoms and signs of the hepatic reaction. Hepatitis was without frank jaundice. Safety studies reported substantial serum aminotransferase elevations in 21/1816 treated patients.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports the proportion of patients developing significant liver dysfunction from isoniazid (INH) therapy, attributed on the basis of a multiple logistic regression analysis of a prospective cohort. Age over 35 years and slow acetylation phenotype were the primary risk factors: in those ≥35 with slow acetylation 37.5% developed significant liver dysfunction versus 3.7% in rapid acetylators under 35. The discussion further states that INH is associated with overt hepatocellular disease, subclinical and overt hepatitis, with historical fatalities from INH-induced liver damage.

raw_record.extra_details: Multiple logistic regression equation: log_e(theta/(1-theta)) = -1.90434 + 1.37376X1 - 1.35344X2, where X1=1 if age >35 and X2=1 if rapid acetylation (chi^2=10.5, d.f.=3, p=0.015). Observed rates of significant liver dysfunction: age<35 rapid 4.2% (1/24), age<35 slow 12.5% (3/24), age≥35 rapid 12.5% (2/16), age≥35 slow 37.5% (9/24). Historic evidence cited: Garibaldi et al. 2321 patients, 19 overt hepatocellular disease with 2 deaths; Bailey et al. 471 patients, 8.7% subclinical and 1% overt hepatitis, no deaths; Maddrey & Boitnott 14 overt biopsy-documented hepatitis cases ascribed to hypersensitivity; Black et al. 13,838 patients, 114 (0.82%) overt liver damage with 13 fatalities (11.4%). Discussion of proposed mechanism via acetylisoniazid, acetylhydrazine, and hydrazine metabolites (mainly animal evidence) that the paper notes is not clearly documented in humans prospectively.

Features of chronic active hepatitis with hypergammaglobulinemia, high titers of antinuclear and smooth muscle antibodies, and biopsy showing chronic aggressive hepatitis suggestive of the lupoid form. Case 1 biopsy: moderate hepatocellular unrest, spotty centrilobular necrosis, focal acidophilic degeneration, portal/periportal inflammation and piecemeal necrosis with prominent plasma cells, minimal fibrosis. Repeat biopsy showed progression possibly evolving into cirrhosis. Case 2 showed marked enhancement of lymphocyte transformation by nitrofurantoin (ratio 13.8) at first study, gone in follow-up (ratio 1.4); Case 1 showed no enhancement. Discontinuation led to clinical improvement.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report three new patients with cholestasis probably related to disopyramide (Norpace). The patients had no hepatosplenomegaly, fever, abdominal pain, or heart failure; tests for hepatitis B surface antigen, alpha-fetoprotein, and antimitochondrial antibodies were negative.
raw_record.extra_details: Three patients: a 63-year-old man on digoxin, isosorbide dinitrate, and disopyramide 400 mg/d who became jaundiced 10 days after starting, with cholestasis lasting 4 months; a 60-year-old man on dipyridamole, K-strophanthin, and disopyramide 300 mg/d with jaundice 10 days later clearing after 7 months; and a 79-year-old woman on K-strophanthin, oxazepam, furosemide, and pentaerythritol tetranitrate who developed pruritus (without jaundice) 15 days after adding disopyramide 300 mg/d. Surgical exploration/IV cholangiography confirmed a normal biliary system in each. The authors attribute the cholestasis to disopyramide because no cholestatic reactions have been reported for the concurrent drugs, patients were on different drugs except disopyramide, there was a fixed 10-15 day interval between starting the drug and onset of cholestasis, and doses were within the normal therapeutic range.

raw_record.support_text: A case of self-limited hepatitis with an influenza-like reaction to hydroxyurea therapy is presented. The association was strongly supported by recurrence on rechallenge with the drug. The patient presented with biochemical evidence of acute hepatocellular damage along with fever, malaise, drowsiness and delirium; symptoms and transaminase/bilirubin elevations settled within 36 hours of ceasing hydroxyurea, and a 1 g oral rechallenge on day seven re-triggered rigors, malaise, tachycardia (130 beats/minute), fever (40°C), drowsiness, delirium and mild re-elevation of hepatic enzymes within 5 hours, with liver function normal two weeks later.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Single case report; low-dose hydroxyurea used for severe psoriasis in a patient for whom methotrexate was contraindicated.
raw_record.extra_details: Influenza-like reaction with fever, rigors/chills, malaise, drowsiness and delirium accompanying biochemical acute hepatocellular damage. Onset within 5 hours of ingestion and resolution within 36 hours of drug cessation; positive rechallenge with 1 g oral hydroxyurea on day seven re-triggered symptoms plus mild re-elevation of hepatic enzymes (resolved within 36 hours; liver function normal two weeks later). Self-limited hepatitis. The paper notes only one prior report of hepatic dysfunction caused by hydroxyurea, giving no details, and that Moschella reported an influenza-like reaction (fever, chills, malaise) in 6 of 60 psoriasis patients on hydroxyurea with no hepatic problems noted.

raw_record.support_text: The authors state this case provides corroborative evidence of an acute hepatitis-like reaction caused by hydrallazine, in this instance without symptoms. Liver function tests may not routinely be performed during follow-up of patients taking hydrallazine.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patient was a rapid acetylator; concurrent oxprenolol and bendrofluazide continued during hydrallazine rechallenge.
raw_record.extra_details: Hydrallazine 25 mg twice daily (later increased to 150 mg daily) for hypertension. A mixed hepatocellular-cholestatic picture of liver function abnormality with normal serum total bilirubin (<17 µmol/l) appeared 3 days after drug reintroduction; LFTs remained grossly abnormal for ~2 weeks and returned to normal within 5 weeks of stopping. The patient was asymptomatic; gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase, alanine transferase and alkaline phosphatase were raised. No viral or autoimmune cause found and no pre-existing liver disease. Rechallenge reproduced the abnormality within 3 days. Citation to Bartoli et al.: a patient with acute hepatic necrosis 2 days after hydrallazine 50 mg daily, jaundiced with right-upper-quadrant pain, nausea and vomiting, diagnosis supported by biopsy and rechallenge. Authors propose unrecognised hydrazine/acetylhydrazine metabolites as possible aetiology via microsomal oxidation, with rapid acetylator status possibly increasing risk of acetylhydrazine-induced hepatic necrosis.

raw_record.extra_details: Fourteen autopsy cases of paraquat poisoning. Laboratory: five of twelve patients had elevated serum bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase (cholestasis); all but one patient showed laboratory evidence of liver cell damage, most marked in patients surviving more than 8 days. raw_record.support_text: The correspondence discusses a case of overdose with an extended-release acetaminophen product. Because of the delay between the overdose and arrival, the pattern of acetaminophen elimination in the case could not be timed to peak level or assessed with the Rumack-Matthew nomogram, but the observed elimination pattern is 'similar to that seen with acute acetaminophen overdose when hepatotoxicity has developed.' The text frames acetaminophen overdose as leading to hepatotoxicity and gives management and nomogram guidance for extended-release acetaminophen overdoses.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose of an extended-release acetaminophen formulation; severe overdose context in which the delay between ingestion and arrival precluded timing of peak level or application of the Rumack-Matthew nomogram.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of extended-release acetaminophen overdose; elimination pattern consistent with acute acetaminophen overdose hepatitis. Management discussion: measure plasma acetaminophen at least 4 h post-ingestion and again 4-6 h later; if either exceeds the Rumack-Matthew nomogram line, complete acetylcysteine antidotal therapy; if the specific product is unknown, manage as an extended-release overdose. Refers to Poisindex Information System for management.

raw_record.extra_details: Cohort of acetaminophen overdose admissions 1987-1993 with acute liver failure. Among the 112 patients fulfilling transplant criteria, 62 (55%) were not listed for transplantation (28 due to untreatable sepsis, hypotension, or cerebral edema; 24 due to alcohol/drug/psychiatric history; 10 due to clinical improvement). Among the 50 listed, 21 (42%) died before a donor organ became available and 6 recovered without transplant. Mortality of the 394 patients not fulfilling transplant criteria was 8% (32 patients): 17 died of unresponsive cerebral edema, 11 of sepsis, 4 of cardiovascular failure. Survival of non-transplanted medically managed patients improved from 23% in 1987 to 42% in 1993. Some patients in the low-dose group possibly had genetically determined increased susceptibility; a cited case of chronic 15-20 g/day use with heavy alcohol intake but no hepatotoxicity illustrates variable susceptibility.

raw_record.support_text: The hepatotoxic effects of tacrine occur in nearly half the patients treated with it. Although some patients have had increases in serum ALT as high as 20 times the upper limit of normal, no deaths have been associated with tacrine hepatotoxicity. Tacrine is described as a relatively pure hepatocellular toxin, with ALT increases usually without concomitant increases in alkaline phosphatase or bilirubin, and hepatotoxicity does not seem to be dose related.

raw_record.extra_details: 47% of permanently withdrawn patients were withdrawn due to pronounced ALT increases; 49% of controlled-trial patients had at least one increased ALT, 25% had ALT >3x ULN, and 2% had ALT >20x ULN; no deaths from tacrine hepatotoxicity; raised ALT was delayed with peak incidence at 6-8 weeks of exposure and 90% of increases by week 12; not dose related; age, weight, and concomitant drug/alcohol/nicotine use did not predict risk; ALT increases usually without alkaline phosphatase or bilirubin rises; jaundice indicates severe liver injury and mandates drug withdrawal and supportive therapy; some patients have malaise or nausea/vomiting, many are symptom-free; data from controlled clinical trials (n=634 tacrine, n=342 placebo) and Cognex package insert.

raw_record.support_text: The most important side effect of isoniazid administration is hepatitis, which can be fatal. By 1969 it had been established that isoniazid frequently caused asymptomatic hepatocellular injury, and fatal isoniazid hepatitis during preventive therapy was recognized in 1970. In a US Public Health Service surveillance study of isoniazid preventive therapy, the risk of isoniazid-associated hepatitis was age-related, being rare in persons aged <20 years and increasing to over 2% in those aged >50 years, with deaths recognized; an estimated mortality rate of 14 per 100,000 persons starting IPT and 23.2 per 100,000 completing a full course was reported.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Preventive therapy for latent tuberculosis infection; hepatitis risk varies directly with age and is potentiated by alcohol and possibly concomitant acetaminophen; hepatitis deaths clustered with possible cofactor potentiation; increased hepatitis-mortality risk suggested in women especially post-partum.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatitis most frequent during the initial 3 months of treatment. Less important side effects include polyneuropathy, sedation, gastrointestinal symptoms and rash. Isoniazid-associated hepatitis mortality estimated at 14 per 100,000 persons starting IPT and 23.2 per 100,000 completing a full course. Similar age relationship found in the Eastern Europe trial but with lower incidence than the US study.

raw_record.support_text: A six-month phase 2 trial of fialuridine in patients with chronic hepatitis B was terminated on an emergency basis 13 weeks after it was begun when hepatic failure and lactic acidosis suddenly occurred in one patient. Despite immediate discontinuation of the medication, the toxicity eventually led to hepatic failure, lactic acidosis, and pancreatitis in seven patients, of whom five died; the other two survived after emergency liver transplantation.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients had pre-existing chronic hepatitis B (the trial's therapeutic indication).
raw_record.extra_details: Phase 2 trial, 24 patients with chronic hepatitis B, randomized to 0.10 or 0.25 mg/kg/day fialuridine orally in two or three divided doses; seven patients developed severe hepatotoxicity (five died, two survived after liver transplantation); three other patients had mild hepatotoxicity; several patients also had pancreatitis, neuropathy, or myopathy; lactic acidosis also occurred. Liver histology showed marked accumulation of microvesicular and macrovesicular fat with minimal hepatocyte necrosis or architectural change; electron microscopy showed abnormal mitochondria and fat accumulation in hepatocytes. The trial was terminated on an emergency basis after 13 weeks.

raw_record.support_text: Treatment with fialuridine (FIAU) was stopped at week 11 because of paresthesias; two weeks later the patient developed nausea, vomiting, weakness, jaundice, lactic acidosis, and shock, and died two days after orthotopic liver transplantation. Seven patients in the study developed severe hepatotoxicity attributed to fialuridine, with hepatic failure and lactic acidosis that resulted in multiple deaths and liver transplantations.

raw_record.extra_details: Fialuridine was given at 0.10 or 0.25 mg/kg/day for 9.5-13 weeks; 7 patients had severe hepatotoxicity with hepatic failure and lactic acidosis, and 5 patients died (one per patient numbers 1-7, deaths in patients 1,2,4,6,7). All seven patients with severe hepatotoxicity also had biochemical evidence of pancreatitis (progressive serum lipase increases up to 50-fold); five had gross and microscopic pancreatitis at autopsy. Five patients with severe hepatotoxicity had peripheral-nerve injury and muscle findings similar to zidovudine-induced myopathy. Three patients (patients 5,8,9) with comparable cumulative doses had mild hepatotoxicity (nausea, abdominal discomfort, aminotransferase elevations, mild hypoalbuminemia and hypofibrinogenemia) that resolved. Five patients treated less than 4 weeks (total <200 mg) had no evidence of fialuridine-induced toxicity.

In a randomised study, FUDR with dexamethasone versus FUDR alone showed a trend toward decreased bilirubin elevation (9% versus 30%, P = 0.07).

raw_record.support_text: In a study by Davis and coworkers, one patient who took 50 g of acetaminophen (based on urinary recovery) developed only moderate liver damage, excreting more glucuronide and sulfate conjugates and less reactive-metabolite-derived cysteine and mercapturic acid conjugates than predicted by the kinetic model. The paper notes that 25 mmoles of reactive metabolite appears to be the amount above which most adult patients become severely intoxicated, and that oxidation of acetaminophen forms a reactive metabolite thought to be responsible for hepatic and other tissue injury in overdose.

raw_record.extra_details: In human overdose, a patient taking 50 g acetaminophen developed moderate liver damage and survived (urinary recovery 331 mmoles). Reports describe 17 patients who developed liver damage vs 13 who did not following a dose, and the paper states ~25 mmoles of reactive metabolite is the amount above which most adult patients become severely intoxicated. Hepatic injury is attributed to an oxidative reactive metabolite (thought to be the N-hydroxy/reactive pathway) formed more than proportionately with increasing dose. Doses modeled were 15 g and 50 g; predicted effect of infusion rate on urinary metabolite composition (glucuronide, sulfate, cysteine/mercapturic acid conjugates) on rapid injection and constant-rate infusions was simulated.

raw_record.support_text: A previously healthy 13-year-old girl arrived at the hospital 19 hours after ingesting two handfuls of Tylenol Extended Relief (McNeil Pharmaceuticals), a new extended-release formulation of acetaminophen containing 650 mg per caplet. After the overdose she developed epigastric and right upper quadrant tenderness, and laboratory testing showed an elevated serum acetaminophen level (89 µg/mL), alanine aminotransferase 180 IU/L, bilirubin 1.7 mg/dL, and an INR of 1.5. The alanine aminotransferase (7459 U/L) and INR (4.2) peaked 59 hours after ingestion, and the patient was sent home on day 4 with resolving liver-function values after acetylcysteine therapy. The paper discusses the risk of hepatotoxicity from this acetaminophen overdose.

raw_record.support_text: Jones et al demonstrated that hypophosphataemia was a feature of paracetamol poisoning whether hepatotoxicity was present or not; the degree of hypophosphataemia correlated with the degree of hepatic damage. The surrounding discussion covers fulminant hepatic failure developing after paracetamol overdose, including survival statistics, treatment (NAC) and management of its complications.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose setting (paracetamol poisoning); fulminant hepatic failure cases presenting to a specialist treatment unit.
raw_record.extra_details: Discussion of fulminant hepatic failure after paracetamol poisoning including survival by plasma creatinine (<100 µmol/L: 65%; 100-300 µmol/L: ~40%; >300 µmol/L: 23%), survival by age (37% for 15-30 years vs 24% for >50 years) and by encephalopathy grade (grade 0: 50% vs grade 4: 24%). Hypophosphataemia and phosphaturia feature in paracetamol poisoning whether or not hepatotoxicity is present, correlating with severity of hepatic damage. Treatment of fulminant hepatic failure includes a course of NAC.
