raw_record.support_text: Table 3 reports hepatic damage (ALT/AST>1000 IU/L) and mortality from hepatic failure in patients treated with intravenous NAC after paracetamol overdose. Among patients given 20 h NAC within 10 h after a paracetamol concentration above the 200 line, 1 of 62 (1.6%) developed hepatic damage and none died from hepatic failure, whereas in the supportive-care group (paracetamol above the 200 line) 33 of 57 (58%) developed hepatic damage and 3 (5.3%) died from hepatic failure. Elsewhere the paper describes patients with paracetamol-induced fulminant hepatic failure whose survival improves with prolonged NAC administration, and cites mortality of 37% with NAC versus 58% without the antidote.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Paracetamol overdose (supratherapeutic ingestion) as the exposure; patients also received intravenous NAC treatment and the paper focuses on antidote effects.
raw_record.extra_details: Fulminant hepatic failure (FHF) attributed to paracetamol overdose; hepatic damage defined as ALT/AST>1000 IU/L. Table 3 gives hepatic damage and mortality across 20 h vs 48 h NAC and supportive care, stratified by plasma paracetamol concentration (200 line = >200 mg/L at 4 h and 30 mg/L at 15 h; 300 line = >300 mg/L at 4 h and 45 mg/L at 15 h) and treatment delay (<10 h, 10-24 h, <24 h). Mortality in FHF patients: 37% with a 20.25 h NAC course vs 58% without (p<0.05); NAC reduced grade 3/4 coma (51% vs 75%). Prognostic factors include prothrombin time >37 s at 48 h (peak <90 s ~80% survival vs >180 s ~8%), factor V <10% (91% sensitivity), and factor VIII:V ratio >30. NAC adverse effects (nausea, flushing, urticaria, pruritus, angio-oedema, wheezing, respiratory distress, hypotension, hypertension) are anaphylactoid/histamine-related rather than hepatic.

raw_record.support_text: Busulfan, a standard component of high-dose chemotherapy regimens, is metabolized by the liver and exhibits concentration-related hepatic toxicity in the form of veno-occlusive disease of the liver. A retrospective analysis of children treated with dosage regimens extrapolated from adult data found a 65% lower incidence of this concentration-related hepatic toxicity (veno-occlusive disease) and a suggestively lower response rate than adults.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patients treated as part of high-dose chemotherapy regimens using dosage schedules based on adult data; finding reported in children specifically.
raw_record.extra_details: Busulfan clearance was 8.4 mL/min/kg in children under age 4 years, 4.4 mL/min/kg in older children, and 2.5 mL/min/kg in adults (ref 19). Retrospective analysis (ref 20) found 65% lower incidence of concentration-related hepatic toxicity (veno-occlusive disease of the liver) in children and a suggestively lower response rate than in adults, illustrating that simple adult-dose body-size adjustment was insufficient.

raw_record.support_text: A female patient with Graves' disease on propylthiouracil (PTU) therapy presented with severe vomiting, fatigue, and anorexia; PTU was discontinued for suspected PTU-induced hepatic damage after markedly elevated liver enzymes (AST 1884 U/L, ALT 2610 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 357 U/L, total bilirubin 2.4 mg/dl), and liver scintigraphy revealed findings attributable to PTU-induced submassive hepatic necrosis (SHN). Viral hepatitis markers were negative, and enzymes declined after PTU withdrawal, with eventual normalization.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patient had Graves' disease; SHN believed to be an idiosyncratic reaction; PTU dose up to 1200 mg/day, stated to be within acceptable therapeutic practice.
raw_record.extra_details: SHN developed approximately 7 months after initiation of PTU therapy. Lab values: AST peaked 1884 U/L (N 0-41), ALT 2610 U/L (N 0-45), alkaline phosphatase 357 U/L (N 30-115), total bilirubin 2.4 mg/dl, direct bilirubin 1.2 mg/dl, ammonia 70 µm/L (N 11-35), prolonged PT 13.7 s; anti-smooth muscle antibody 1:80, ANA 1:1280 consistent with autoimmune process known to accompany PTU-induced hepatic necrosis. Hepatitis B/C markers negative. Two days after PTU discontinuation AST fell to 1153 U/L and ALT to 1716 U/L; symptoms resolved by end of third week. Tc-99m SC planar and SPECT imaging showed focal photopenic defects (no colloid shift) consistent with SHN; repeat imaging 4.5 months later showed marked resolution and normal planar images; liver biopsy denied. SHN can be potentially fatal; the paper notes virtual hepatitis may occur in up to 30% of PTU patients and clinical hepatotoxicity is rare, usually appearing within 0.5-3.5 months.

raw_record.support_text: The authors describe a patient who presented with acute hepatitis and, after ruling out all other causes, determined her illness was due to therapy with penicillin V (phenoxymethyl penicillin), which she had taken for 15 days before admission. They note penicillin V-induced hepatotoxicity had not been reported within the last decade.
raw_record.extra_details: Single case report of a 67-year-old woman with facial actinomycosis. Admission labs: AST 2,590 IU/L, ALT 3,073 IU/L, GGT 240 IU/L, total bilirubin 1.3 mg/dL, normal alkaline phosphatase; negative serology for viral and Toxoplasma etiologies. raw_record.support_text: In 107 acetaminophen-poisoned patients, all who developed hepatotoxicity (elevated transaminases) recovered and none developed hepatic encephalopathy; the study compared standard N-acetylcysteine therapy with N-acetylcysteine plus cimetidine, and found no statistically significant difference in mean peak transaminase levels, AST category distributions, or bilirubin between the cimetidine and control groups. One patient in the cimetidine group died from esophageal carcinoma 2 weeks after recovering, not from liver injury.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Acetaminophen poisoning (overdose) treated with N-acetylcysteine, with or without cimetidine co-administration.
raw_record.extra_details: All 107 poisoned patients who developed hepatotoxicity recovered; none developed hepatic encephalopathy. Peak AST up to 11,925 IU/L and AST >1000 IU/L occurred in 22% (NAC only) and 20% (NAC + cimetidine) of 105 analyzed patients; mean peak AST 1,259 ± 330 vs 1,301 ± 451 IU/L (p=0.94), mean peak ALT 1,724 ± 452 vs 1,212 ± 435 IU/L (p=0.42), mean total bilirubin 1.38 ± 0.19 vs 1.33 ± 0.25 mg/dL (p=0.86). Adding 300 mg IV cimetidine every 6 h throughout NAC treatment did not alter hepatotoxicity. One death was due to esophageal carcinoma, occurring 2 weeks after recovering from the acetaminophen ingestion.

raw_record.support_text: A previously healthy 13-year-old girl presented 19 hours after ingesting two handfuls of Tylenol Extended Relief (extended-release acetaminophen, 650 mg per caplet) with vomiting, abdominal pain, and epigastric and right-upper-quadrant tenderness. Serum acetaminophen was 89 µg/mL with ALT 180 IU/L, bilirubin 1.7 mg/dL, and INR 1.5; ALT (7459 IU/L) and INR (4.2) peaked 59 hours after ingestion. She was treated with acetylcysteine, remained clinically well, and was sent home on day 4 with resolving liver-function values. The author notes that unless acetaminophen levels after such an overdose are in the potentially toxic range, the nomogram is of doubtful value, and even elevated nontoxic levels do not exclude subsequent hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric (13-year-old) patient; overdose of the extended-release formulation Tylenol Extended Relief; delayed presentation 19 hours after ingestion.
raw_record.extra_details: Vomiting and abdominal pain began 6 hours after ingestion; serum acetaminophen 89 µg/mL on arrival; ALT peaked at 7459 IU/L and INR at 4.2 at 59 hours post-ingestion; bilirubin 1.7 mg/dL initially; apparent elimination half-life 11.08 hours with linear decline in drug concentrations; treated with oral acetylcysteine (140 mg/kg loading, then 6 doses of 70 mg/kg and 11 doses of 100 mg/kg); patient remained clinically well and was discharged on day 4 with resolving liver-function values. Authors discuss uncertainty over whether slowed elimination reflected prolonged absorption or hepatic dysfunction and question the value of the immediate-release acetaminophen nomogram for sustained-release overdoses.

raw_record.support_text: This paper reports the first case of liver injury ascribed to tianeptine, a patient with a cholangitis-like hepatitis showing jaundice, pruritus, and preceding abdominal pain, fever and chills, with histological microvesicular steatosis. The authors note the patient developed hepatitis at therapeutic doses with fever, chills, blood hypereosinophilia and anti-smooth muscle antibodies, all features commonly observed in amineptine-induced hepatitis and suggestive of an immunoallergic mechanism (paragraphs 15 and 17).
raw_record.extra_details: First report of tianeptine hepatotoxicity, predicted 2 years earlier from rodent/human experimental reactive-metabolite data. Clinical features: jaundice, pruritus, abdominal pain, fever, chills mimicking acute cholangitis; blood hypereosinophilia; anti-smooth muscle antibodies. Liver biopsy showed microvesicular steatosis (macrovesicular/microvesicular type); cholestasis absent, attributed to biopsy 3 weeks after onset when jaundice had almost completely disappeared. Mechanism: immunoallergic response with microvesicular steatosis from inhibition of mitochondrial fatty acid beta-oxidation via the acyl chain; metabolic activation mainly mediated by glucocorticoid-inducible CYP3A. Therapeutic-dose exposure; no formal causality instrument reported.

Across 61 untreated and treated patients, 11 (18%) had bilirubin >3 mg/dL by 3 months, increasing to 28 (46%) beyond 6 months, with 3% developing biliary sclerosis. In the prior FUDR+LV trial, 70% of patients had bilirubin >3 mg/dL by 6 months and 21% developed biliary sclerosis at any time. condition_text: Paracetamol overdose exposure

raw_record.support_text: Liver-cell necrosis after paracetamol overdose is mediated by a chemically active intermediate metabolite of the drug, which combines irreversibly with hepatic macromolecules. After therapeutic doses of paracetamol (0.5 to 1 g orally up to five times daily) the metabolite is conjugated with hepatic glutathione to form nontoxic mercapturates; only when the dose is large enough to deplete hepatic glutathione reserves does the excess metabolite remain free to exert harmful effects leading to cell death.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Paracetamol overdose exposure
raw_record.extra_details: Five patients died in acute hepatic failure, all showing subtotal lobular necrosis with only small islets of altered hepatocytes surviving periportally. In survivors, grade III (severe) centrilobular necrotic zones were reconstituted by 3 months with only minor residual changes, including one patient with mild centrilobular fibrosis and reticulin scarring. Injury mechanism: a chemically active metabolite depletes hepatic glutathione, releasing the reactive metabolite to cause cell death; experimental animal data showed a dose threshold for paracetamol-induced centrilobular necrosis. No close dose-damage relationship could be established from stated/estimated overdose size, but plasma paracetamol levels above 400 g/l at 2 h to 30 g/l at 18 h were frequently associated with severe (grade III) damage, while lower admission levels were usually associated with mild (grade I) damage.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report four cases of niacin-induced hepatotoxicity in patients using sustained-release niacin preparations; symptoms and laboratory abnormalities resolved after the patients stopped taking niacin. Two patients had focal fatty infiltration of the liver on imaging, and one patient had a coagulopathy despite only mildly elevated aminotransferase levels. The authors recommend periodic liver-enzyme monitoring and discontinuation if abnormalities develop.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Sustained-release niacin formulation for treatment of hyperlipidemia.
raw_record.extra_details: Four patients; all used sustained-release niacin preparations; symptoms and laboratory abnormalities resolved on discontinuation (dechallenge). Focal fatty infiltration of the liver seen on imaging in two patients, presented as a not previously described presentation of niacin hepatotoxicity. One patient had a coagulopathy despite only mildly elevated aminotransferases (prothrombin time 16.6 s, AST 86 U/L, ALT 86 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 136 U/L, total bilirubin 1.7 mg/dL, albumin 3.3 g/dL) and a factor VII deficiency attributed to liver disease. Niacin is a water-soluble B vitamin used for hyperlipidemia therapy.

raw_record.support_text: A prospective study by Zaric and colleagues found clinically significant liver damage in 4 of 1166 patients anesthetized with halothane for minor orthopedic procedures; all four were obese women, three of whom had previously received halothane anesthesia, whereas no serious liver damage was found in a comparison group of 1443 patients (enflurane, neuroleptic, or regional anesthesia). The authors conclude that halothane-induced liver damage is by no means a rare event, and add that two patients with fulminant liver failure after halothane anesthesia (obese women about 50 years old with multiple prior halothane anesthesias) were treated at Klinikum Großhadern.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Predisposing factors emphasized in the paper: female sex, obesity, and repeated (multiple) halothane anesthesias, sometimes at short intervals; most reported cases occurred after repeat anesthesia.
raw_record.extra_details: Halothane hepatitis is characterized by nonspecific symptoms (anorexia, nausea, vomiting, headache, arthralgia, upper-abdominal complaints); fever starting with a latency of 6-14 days up to 40 degrees C (shorter free interval, sometimes only hours, after repeat anesthesia); icterus that often follows fever but is not obligatory. Laboratory: pronounced serum transaminase elevations predominate; gamma-GT, alkaline phosphatase, and bilirubin may or may not be elevated; eosinophilia and antinuclear/antimitochondrial antibodies may be present. Histology cannot reliably distinguish halothane hepatitis from hepatitis of other origin; diagnosis is typically one of exclusion (after excluding hepatitis A/B/C, EBV, CMV, herpes, varicella-zoster, coxsackievirus, other drug-induced liver injury, extrahepatic cholestasis). Halothane-associated antibodies against trifluoroacetylated proteins detectable by ELISA in only about 70% of suspected patients; a negative result does not exclude halothane liver damage. Prospective study: 4/1166 halothane patients (0.34%) with clinically significant liver damage; comparison 1443 patients with no serious liver damage.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report a case of drug-induced hypersensitivity reaction to allopurinol in a patient who presented with fever, skin rash, arthralgias, acute hepatitis, and acute renal failure, temporally related to initiation of allopurinol therapy 5 weeks earlier. The patient was also receiving diuretics and had mild renal insufficiency, both reported risk factors for allopurinol hypersensitivity. Rapid improvement on withdrawal of allopurinol and lack of recurrence of hepatitis after re-exposure to all prior medications except allopurinol led the authors to conclude that allopurinol caused the hypersensitivity syndrome in this patient.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patient also receiving diuretics and had mild pre-existing renal insufficiency (risk factors for allopurinol hypersensitivity); indication was gout.
raw_record.extra_details: Latency ~5 weeks from allopurinol initiation; syndrome included fever, skin rash, arthralgias, and acute renal failure. Renal insufficiency decreases renal clearance of the metabolite oxypurinol, potentially yielding toxic serum levels. Liver biopsy showed primarily T lymphocyte infiltration. Peripheral blood immunophenotyping showed increased activated and CD8 lymphocytes returning to normal after resolution; similar in vitro changes with 1.2 x 10^-3 M oxypurinol were not seen in normal controls. Allopurinol and oxypurinol did not induce cell lysis of Hep-G2 cells in vitro.

raw_record.support_text: Aspirin administered early in the patient's disease (juvenile rheumatoid arthritis) ameliorated symptoms, but a subsequent liver biopsy showed hepatocyte cytoplasmic vacuolation and focal cell necrosis with inflammation. The authors describe 'aspirin hepatotoxicity,' noting LDH is the first liver enzyme to rise, followed in 7 to 10 days by the transaminases. On aspirin rechallenge, at an aspirin level of 9.1 mg/dl about 30 h after onset, marked liver function abnormalities developed with alarming rapidity, along with a slightly prolonged prothrombin time, increased fibrin split products, and microangiopathy with falling hematocrit, responsive to high-dose steroid therapy.

Liver biopsy showed hepatocyte cytoplasmic vacuolation and a focal area of cell necrosis and inflammation. LDH was the first enzyme to rise, followed by transaminases in 7-10 days. Aspirin discontinued and high-dose corticosteroid reinstituted; no recurrence of hepatic dysfunction during 8-month follow-up.

raw_record.support_text: In a second operation on the same patient (in an orthopedic hospital, under N2O/O2/halothane anesthesia), the patient with suspected hereditary fructose intolerance (HFI) received a total of 175 g sorbitol and 50 g fructose IV in two-thirds electrolyte solutions intraoperatively and on postoperative days 1 and 2. A few hours after surgery, the Quick prothrombin time was 19%, serum transaminase activity was increased, and renal retention values rose. The patient was transferred to a medical intensive care unit on postoperative day 2; the discharge diagnosis was again 'transient postoperative liver failure of unclear cause.'
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patient with hereditary fructose intolerance (HFI); perioperative IV parenteral nutrition setting; co-exposure to fructose infusions.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report: a 49-year-old woman with HFI who had experienced a similar transient postoperative liver failure two years earlier during a first orthopedic operation where sorbitol (125/50/75/50 g) and fructose (25/25/50 g) were infused IV. In the second episode, liver and coagulation values normalized within a few days after stopping glucose-exchange substances (sorbitol/fructose) and substituting coagulation factors, and the patient was discharged with the diagnosis of transient postoperative liver failure; she was later referred for metabolic diagnostics of HFI after her sister refused elective surgery due to prior experience. Laboratory values at peak included SGOT 726 U/l, SGPT 984 U/l, total bilirubin 4.6 mg/dl, Quick 9%, with renal retention (urea up to 84 mg/dl, creatinine 1.9 mg/dl). Sorbitol is metabolized to fructose and exerts its toxicity in HFI by this pathway.

raw_record.support_text: In children with acute lymphoblastic leukemia receiving maintenance therapy that included daily oral 6-mercaptopurine (6MP), a group of patients developed gastrointestinal symptoms and 6MP-induced hepatotoxicity with elevated aminotransferases and jaundice. Other potential causes (viral hepatitis, sepsis, leukemic infiltration of the liver, and other hepatotoxic drugs such as methotrexate) were ruled out as far as possible: when 6MP was held, the symptoms and signs of hepatitis resolved despite continuation of methotrexate, and rechallenge with 6MP resulted in similar adverse effects. The paper states that 6MP has been reported to be toxic to the liver as well as to the bone marrow and intestine.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patients (ages 3-17 years) with ALL on maintenance chemotherapy; received combination therapy including methotrexate, vincristine, and prednisone; small case series of 4 symptomatic children compared with asymptomatic children.
raw_record.extra_details: Symptomatic patients had AST 174-385 IU/L, ALT 204-558 IU/L, bilirubin up to 243 µmol/L (elevated direct bilirubin up to 213 µmol/L); doses 52-100 mg/m². Lower 6MP peak concentrations and AUC, longer time to peak in symptomatic patients suggested impaired absorption and/or hepatic accumulation. TPMT activity 10-27 units/ml pRBC consistent with homozygous wild-type genotype, ruling out low-TPMT-related hematologic toxicity as the mechanism. Possible proposed mechanisms include selective hepatic toxicity of methylated nucleotide (meMPN) metabolites or a hypersensitivity reaction developing after weeks to months of sensitization; rechallenge reproduced the adverse effects.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports cases of severe liver damage after administration of cyproterone acetate (CPA) to male patients with prostate cancer and to postmenopausal women with advanced breast cancer. Signs of hepatitis included jaundice, fatigue, nausea, elevated serum liver enzymes, and different types of necrosis (bridging, confluent, and centrilobular) with inflammation. After withdrawal of CPA, some patients slowly recovered within 2-3 months, but in some cases the incurred liver damage was too severe to allow recovery. The abstract additionally states that cases of liver damage and liver tumors have been reported after treatment of prostate cancer patients with CPA.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Reported in prostate cancer patients and postmenopausal women with advanced breast cancer (indication-restricted population); reported together with flutamide in the same set of cases.
raw_record.extra_details: Signs of hepatitis included jaundice, fatigue, nausea, elevated serum liver enzymes, and bridging/confluent/centrilobular necrosis with inflammation; some patients recovered within 2-3 months of drug withdrawal, while in others the liver damage was too severe to allow recovery. CPA is an antiandrogen used for hirsutism, acne, prostatic cancer, and breast cancer. Liver tumors also described in CPA-treated patients (separate from non-neoplastic DILI).

raw_record.support_text: Letters to the Editor note the tragic outcome of the fialuridine trial described by McKenzie and colleagues, in which delayed mitochondrial toxicity of the nucleoside analogue was the probable cause of the lactic acidosis and hepatic failure that killed five patients during experimental treatment of chronic hepatitis B infection. A follow-up report states that after 10 to 12 weeks of fialuridine (1.5 mg/kg/day orally), virus-carrier and uninfected woodchucks had levels of lactic acidosis and hepatic failure much like those seen in humans, with the dose only slightly higher than the 0.1 and 0.25 mg/kg/day used in the 1993 trial.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients with chronic hepatitis B infection treated in an experimental clinical trial; outcomes include hepatic failure with lactic acidosis leading to five deaths.
raw_record.extra_details: Nucleoside analogue used as experimental treatment for chronic hepatitis B. Delayed mitochondrial toxicity was considered the probable cause; in vitro, the inhibition constant (Ki) of fialuridine triphosphate against DNA polymerase gamma was lower than that found with other eukaryotic DNA polymerases. 1993 trial used 0.1 and 0.25 mg/kg/day orally; woodchuck studies at 1.5 mg/kg/day orally produced similar lactic acidosis and hepatic failure after 10 to 12 weeks. Subtext: patients' hepatitis was examined as a possible exacerbating factor but viral infection was not considered to produce or exacerbate the toxicity.

raw_record.support_text: Ten children in this pediatric phase I/II trial were withdrawn because of presumed toxicity related to administration of the study drug lamivudine. Three children developed increased serum transaminases (>10 times the upper limit of normal, or grade 4 toxicity on the NCI Common Toxicity Criteria), and one of these continues to have hepatic dysfunction 10 months after stopping the drug. These events resolved with supportive care and discontinuation of lamivudine except for the episode of persistent hepatitis.

raw_record.extra_details: Three of 89 children developed increased transaminases >10x ULN (NCI grade 4 toxicity); one child had persistent hepatitis with hepatic dysfunction for 10 months after stopping lamivudine. Events otherwise resolved with supportive care and drug discontinuation. Attribution was as presumed drug-related toxicity in the trial.

This attributes human hepatotoxicity to an accidental CsA overdose.

raw_record.extra_details: Presenting illness was valproate-associated hepatic encephalopathy with hyperammonaemia (serum ammonia rising from 43 to 215 umol/l, normal <33 umol/l) and low carnitine (free 7.6, total 15.4 umol/l) despite normal routine liver function tests; delirium and asterixis resolved within three days after valproate reduction (3 g to 2.75 g/day) and oral L-carnitine 330 mg four times daily. raw_record.support_text: In the index patient, three separate exposures to Distalgesic were each followed by jaundice (onset 10 days, 4 days and 24 hours after exposure respectively), with dark urine, pale stools and yellow sclerae. After a normal cholangiogram and a liver biopsy showing minor portal fibrosis but no liver cell necrosis or bile stasis, he was rechallenged with 130 mg dextropropoxyphene alone and developed the same abdominal pain and unwell feeling as after Distalgesic; subsequent exposure to paracetamol was uneventful, and he remained well after stopping Distalgesic. This implicates dextropropoxyphene, rather than paracetamol, as the cause of the cholestatic jaundice.

raw_record.support_text: The paper concludes that this observation strongly supports the hypothesis that carbimazole can induce fulminant hepatitis, hypothetically through an immunoallergic mechanism, which broadens the spectrum of liver lesions induced by this drug, and suggests careful monitoring of serum liver enzymes during carbimazole therapy for hyperthyroidism.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Co-exposure to propranolol in the reported case; whether propranolol contributed to hepatitis is explicitly unresolved. Patient had hyperthyroidism (treated with carbimazole).
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of a patient treated with carbimazole for hyperthyroidism who developed fulminant hepatitis. An immunoallergic mechanism is supported by hepatitis at recommended doses, short delay between re-exposure and hepatitis relapse (rechallenge), and lobular eosinophilic infiltration on pathology. The carbimazole dosage was not excessive and the drug was discontinued at onset of first hepatitis manifestation. Propranolol is not a potent inducer/inhibitor of drug-metabolizing enzymes and is not known to promote hepatotoxicity of other drugs. Recommended careful serum liver enzyme monitoring during carbimazole therapy.

raw_record.support_text: The paper discusses severe paracetamol (acetaminophen) overdose causing hepatic damage and hepatic failure. It notes that continued paracetamol conversion to metabolites damages the liver for days after overdose, and that in patients vulnerable by virtue of hepatic glutathione deficiency as little as 4 g paracetamol can precipitate hepatic failure. The text also describes hepatic necrosis measured on liver biopsy as correlating with clinical grade of hepatic encephalopathy, indicating paracetamol overdose produces liver injury.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose context; patients vulnerable to paracetamol by virtue of hepatic glutathione deficiency (as little as 4 g paracetamol can precipitate hepatic failure).
raw_record.extra_details: Severe paracetamol overdose treated with charcoal haemoperfusion and/or high-flux dialysis. Continued conversion of paracetamol to metabolites damages the liver for several days after overdose; a blood level of ~100 mg/l in a 70 kg patient represents roughly 5 g body load (assumed volume of distribution 0.7 g/l). Extent of hepatic necrosis on liver biopsy correlated with clinical grade of hepatic encephalopathy. Prognostic markers included venous bicarbonate and serial factor V and VII levels; patients with later arrival had significantly higher prothrombin times on days 2-5. Plasma selenium was lower in the treated group than the good-prognosis group (42.9 vs 54.8 µg/l).

raw_record.support_text: Paracetamol is the most common drug used for self-poisoning in the UK and is associated with potentially fatal liver damage. This is an overdose context: patients admitted to hospital because of paracetamol overdoses were studied to determine characteristics and factors that might have deterred them or reduced overdose dangers.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Self-poisoning/overdose exposure setting; patients admitted to hospital following deliberate paracetamol overdose.
raw_record.extra_details: Acute liver dysfunction occurred in 25 of the 80 studied patients and was associated with consumption of more than 25 tablets (OR 4.46, 95% CI 1.31-17.41, P=0.014). More patients using loose preparations consumed 25+ tablets (69%) than those using blister packs (40%). Only 20 patients thought any warning label would have deterred them. Paracetamol liver damage accounts for over half of cases referred to liver units for fulminant liver failure, is the definite cause of at least 150 deaths per year in the UK, and has become a common reason for liver transplantation.

raw_record.support_text: In a 7-month-old infant presenting with a Reye's syndrome-like picture (hyperventilation, metabolic acidosis, respiratory alkalosis, hyperammonaemia, raised transaminases, hepatomegaly), salicylic acid and metabolites were found in the urine. The mother admitted giving the child 'Angiers' tablets (Bristol-Myers), each containing 81 mg acetylsalicylic acid (aspirin), at about 20 mg/kg/day for several days. The paper states that the biochemical changes and hepatomegaly almost certainly resulted from salicylate ingestion, supported by spontaneous clinical improvement when salicylate ingestion ceased.

raw_record.extra_details: Salicylate given as 'Angiers' tablets, each containing 81 mg acetylsalicylic acid. Serum-salicylate level was 2 mmol/l (27.6 mg/dl) 12 h after admission. Alanine transaminase rose from 169 to 543 U/l; total bilirubin from 12 to 147 µmol/l; plasma ammonia 91 µmol/l. Urine positive for salicylate breakdown products by mass spectrometry. No disturbance of sensorium or hypoglycaemia argued against Reye's syndrome. Spontaneous improvement occurred when salicylate ingestion ceased (positive dechallenge). Presentation title: salicylate hepatitis with acidosis.

raw_record.support_text: Methotrexate is reported to cause hepatic toxicity in rheumatoid arthritis patients: three of eight patients with adverse events in Weinblatt et al.'s study had hepatic toxicity, one with biopsy-proven cirrhosis and repeated transaminase elevations. A separate Australian group reported three male RA patients who developed cirrhosis after methotrexate therapy, with risk factors including advanced age (average 69 years), total methotrexate dose above 3900 mg, and alcohol intake in one case, and estimated a 5-year cumulative cirrhosis incidence of 9.4 per 1000 treated patients. Another cirrhosis case was reported in a male RA patient heterozygous for alpha-1-antitrypsin (PiMZ) deficiency.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Rheumatoid arthritis indication; cirrhosis cases occurred in elderly patients (average age 69), after high cumulative methotrexate dose (>3900 mg), with alcohol intake in one case, and in one patient with heterozygous alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency (PiMZ phenotype); subjects with pre-existing risk factors or liver susceptibility.
raw_record.extra_details: Includes biopsy-proven cirrhosis, repeated transaminase elevations (marker of toxicity in ACR guidelines), 5-year cumulative cirrhosis incidence of 9.4 per 1000 treated patients; authors suggest screening methotrexate-treated patients with abnormal liver function tests for alpha-1-antitrypsin levels/phenotype. In a separate long-term prospective biopsy study (Kremer et al., 27 RA patients, mean 6.3 biopsies over 8.2 years, AST checked every 4-6 weeks, dose reduced by 2.5 mg/wk for abnormal AST), Roenigk score increased significantly with time but changes were not clinically relevant and other histologic/ultrastructural scores did not progress; this was deemed reassuring on methotrexate safety in a carefully monitored low-alcohol population.

raw_record.support_text: This case reports chronic acetaminophen intoxication in a child, the youngest fatal outcome among four reported fatalities from chronic acetaminophen poisoning. Hepatic injury resulted from doubling the recommended therapeutic dose (60–90 mg/kg/day); the toxic threshold for repeated pediatric overdosing was reported as roughly 150 mg/kg/day for two to four days.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patient; chronic excessive dosing by a caregiver (about double the therapeutic 60–90 mg/kg/day dose).
raw_record.extra_details: Autopsy revealed massive centrilobular necrosis consistent with acetaminophen intoxication. Serum aminotransferases were markedly elevated at >10,000 IU/L. Acetaminophen levels were 91.7 and 60.2 µg/ml at 12 and 24 hours after the last dose; elimination half-life was 19.8 hours (hepatic coma associated with half-life >12 h). The Rumack nomogram was deemed not appropriate for chronic poisoning. Patient expired despite hemodialysis, plasmapheresis, enteral lactulose, and inotropic support.

raw_record.support_text: The discussion explicitly attributes liver injury to acute arsenic poisoning: 'Hepatic injury due to acute arsenic poisoning is uncommon,' noting that large doses may induce massive hepatic necrosis or Milian's syndrome (a hypersensitivity reaction with fever, lymphadenopathy, rash, arthralgia, eosinophilia and hepatitis), that arsphenamine-related damage shows intrahepatic cholestasis, and that hepatic veno-occlusive disease has been related to acute arsenic poisoning. In both reported cases, liver biopsy after acute arsenic poisoning showed hepatocytic alterations with increased mitotic activity.

raw_record.extra_details: Case 1 (37-year-old man, day 1 1978): acute poisoning suspected via urinary arsenic 10 mg/24 h; liver biopsy on day 11 showed preserved architecture, portal infiltration, hepatocytic ballooning, granular cytoplasm, acidophilic bodies, enlarged nuclei, cholestasis and increased mitotic activity; PC10 positive in 18% (0.3% control), Ki 67 in 15% (0.1% control); AST peaked ~278-234 IU/l, ALT ~368 IU/l, prothrombin fell to 30%; treated with dopamine, haemodialysis and BAL; recovered and discharged day 26. Case 2 (26-year-old man, day 1 1990): abdominal pain/vomiting, liver biopsy on day 8 suggested acute arsenic intoxication confirmed day 9 by urinary arsenic 867 µg/ml (normal <25 µg/ml); biopsy showed granular hepatocytic cytoplasm, vesicular nuclei, multiple mitotic figures, acidophilic bodies, periportal cholestasis; PC10 8.4%, Ki 67 6%; treated with BAL and 2,3-dimercaptosuccinic acid; died on day 25 from cerebral oedema due to meningeal bleeding. Discussion also notes large-dose arsenic may cause massive hepatic necrosis, Milian's syndrome (hypersensitivity hepatitis), and hepatic veno-occlusive disease.

Many residents had to discontinue tacrine because of adverse drug reactions, with a higher incidence of weight loss and poor appetite in this elderly sample. The authors note a larger study and control group would be needed to confirm whether weight loss and anorexia are truly associated with tacrine.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Elderly nursing home residents with Alzheimer's disease; comparison drawn to younger populations treated with tacrine.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxic effects comparable to previous findings (Watkins et al.); many discontinued tacrine due to adverse drug reactions. Weight loss and poor appetite were noted but their association with tacrine was considered unconfirmed without a larger study and control group. Doses up to 80, 120, or 160 mg/day were considered; authors suggested 80 or 120 mg/day may be preferable. Some improved on ADAS cognitive, MMSE, and PSMS assessments.

Serological tests for hepatitis A, B, C, CMV and EBV were negative; flutamide was discontinued on admission and UDCA 12 mg/kg/day was started, followed by progressive clinical and biochemical improvement with full recovery. The authors conclude the hepatitis is likely to have been caused by flutamide administration.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report a child who developed a Dilantin (phenytoin)-induced hypersensitivity reaction. Clinical signs included fever, exfoliative dermatitis, interstitial nephritis, hepatitis with jaundice, hepatosplenomegaly, generalized lymphadenopathy, eosinophilia, and hemolytic anemia. This explicitly attributes hepatitis with jaundice to phenytoin exposure in a human case.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patient (6-year-old child) with hepatitis as part of a multisystem hypersensitivity reaction; prior phenobarbital had been discontinued 3 weeks before Dilantin was started.
raw_record.extra_details: A 6-year-old black male developed a hypersensitivity reaction after about one month of Dilantin (phenytoin) 50 mg three times a day for a grand mal seizure. Jaundice became evident on the third hospital day (total serum bilirubin 4.4 mg/dl, later rising to 9.2 mg/dl), with SGOT 254 SF units (later 320), SGPT 250 SF units, and alkaline phosphatase 12 Bodansky units (later 24); plasma Dilantin concentration was 3 µg/ml. Hepatitis worsened after Dilantin was discontinued. Associated features included fever, maculopapular rash, lymphadenopathy, liver (12 cm) and spleen (6 cm) enlargement, eosinophilia (4,500 cells, 22% of WBC), interstitial nephritis with some renal impairment, and Coombs-negative hemolytic anemia. Liver and skin biopsies showed portal triaditis with lymphocytic, plasma cell, and eosinophilic infiltrates. Treatment with prednisone improved the eosinophilia, lymphadenopathy, and hepatosplenomegaly and laboratory values returned to normal.

raw_record.support_text: The letter discusses valproate-associated hepatotoxicity, noting that most victims are in the young age group and that hepatotoxicity is very rare in patients over 10 years on monotherapy, though with polytherapy it may occur at any age. Status epilepticus and febrile illness were frequently time-related to the onset of hepatic impairment, and the authors propose an occult metabolic abnormality that is unmasked when mitochondrial mechanisms are stressed, such as by administration of the mitochondrial toxin valproate.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Polytherapy (valproate given with other antiepileptics), young age, occult metabolic abnormality, and a preceding hepatic challenge (status epilepticus-damaged liver); onset linked to status epilepticus or febrile illness.
raw_record.extra_details: Valproate framed as a mitochondrial toxin; proposed mechanism involves unmasking of an occult metabolic disorder (e.g., urea cycle enzyme defects, Alpers disease/Huttenlocher variant, altered fatty acid metabolism). The patient under discussion died of a terminally fatal metabolic cascade after valproate was given following status epilepticus-induced hepatic enzyme elevations, with liver synthetic function (fibrinogen, prothrombin time) not documented as recovered.

raw_record.support_text: Hepatotoxicity is the major adverse effect of pyrazinamide. At daily doses of 40-50 mg/kg introduced in the 1950s, elevations of serum transaminase levels and symptomatic hepatitis were observed in 20% and 10% of treated patients, respectively; some patients exhibited a fulminant course and several deaths occurred. It was concluded that pyrazinamide was a major hepatotoxin.

raw_record.extra_details: Serum transaminase elevations in 20% and symptomatic hepatitis in 10% of treated patients; some affected patients had a fulminant course with several deaths. Authors concluded pyrazinamide was a major hepatotoxin and the drug transiently fell into disrepute.

raw_record.support_text: Isoniazid, a major antitubercular agent introduced in 1952, has been given alone as a prophylactic agent, permitting a precise assessment of its intrinsic hepatotoxicity. The paper establishes that about 10% of patients receiving isoniazid monotherapy develop serum transaminase increases, about 1% develop symptomatic hepatitis (with jaundice, marked transaminase rises possibly exceeding 10x ULN and bilirubin possibly exceeding 200 µmol/L), and a fulminant, encephalopathic course is observed in 5-10% of symptomatic patients (0.05-0.1% of treated patients). Histology shows liver cell necrosis and hepatocellular ballooning with portal inflammatory infiltrates and occasional cholestasis.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Therapeutic isoniazid monotherapy or prophylactic use in general adults; age above 50 years, female gender, delayed onset (≥2 months), continued isoniazid administration after symptom onset, and serum bilirubin above 350 µmol/L associated with higher mortality; daily doses of 10 mg/kg or more (markedly above the usual 5 mg/kg/day) possibly at higher risk of fulminant hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: About 10% of treated patients develop serum transaminase increases, mainly within the first 10 weeks, usually resolving spontaneously even with continued therapy. About 1% develop symptomatic hepatitis, typically within the first 3 months but occasionally from 1 week to 12 months; jaundice is the main sign with anorexia, nausea and vomiting, fever/arthralgia/rash usually absent. Fulminant course in 5-10% of symptomatic hepatitis (0.05-0.1% of treated patients) heralded by prolonged prothrombin time and encephalopathy. Histology: liver cell necrosis and hepatocellular degeneration (ballooning), portal inflammatory infiltrates, occasional cholestasis. In large series injury was independent of isoniazid dosage; in 2 series of multidrug-regimen patients with probable isoniazid-induced fulminant liver failure the mean daily dose was markedly above recommended.

raw_record.support_text: The report describes cases of severe liver damage and toxic hepatitis in patients who chronically ingested moderately excessive amounts of acetaminophen. The first patient's severe liver damage from chronic ingestion of moderately excessive acetaminophen was attributed to concurrent chronic alcohol abuse (which presumably induced his cytochrome P-450 enzyme system, increasing susceptibility), and a second patient developed toxic hepatitis after ingesting excessive acetaminophen doses on two occasions, with negative nitrogen balance/cachexia and low serum albumin possibly lowering hepatic glutathione stores.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Chronic abuse of moderately excessive acetaminophen doses in metabolically susceptible patients; concurrent chronic alcohol abuse (case 1) or cachexia with low serum albumin and suspected reduced hepatic glutathione stores (case 2).
raw_record.extra_details: Cases of serious liver damage from chronic abuse of acetaminophen in susceptible patients. Reported post-cessation serum acetaminophen levels of 37 and 15 µg/ml more than 24 h after stopping ingestion, described as in the toxic range (normal therapeutic 4-h level <9 µg/ml). In supporting animal work, alcohol and glutathione-depleting agents (diethylmaleate) potentiate acetaminophen-induced hepatic necrosis in mice, and protein restriction depletes glutathione in rats; diethylstilbestrol and ethacrynic acid also deplete glutathione in animals.

raw_record.extra_details: Three patients (Patients 1-3) described. Patient 1 showed very severe pericentral necrosis on liver biopsy; Patient 2 had improved liver tests after initial withdrawal, but rechallenge with 5.2-6.5 g/day for 7 days raised SGOT to 121 IU and total bilirubin to 2.4 mg/dl with biopsy showing moderately severe pericentral necrosis and increased lipofuscin pigment (serum acetaminophen 37 µg/ml 24 h after stopping; SGOT fell to 27 IU in 2 days); Patient 3 had SGOT 400 IU, total bilirubin 0.6 mg/dl, mild pericentral necrosis with lipofuscin, improving after withdrawal and normalizing within 4 weeks. Mechanism attributed to saturation of sulfate/glucuronide conjugation and cytochrome P450-dependent reactive electrophilic metabolite with glutathione depletion and covalent binding to hepatocyte membranes; alcohol/barbiturates may induce this pathway (Wright & Prescott retrospective overdose data cited).

raw_record.support_text: In an eight-week evaluation of mycophenolate mofetil (500 mg to 3 g/day) as rescue therapy for mild acute rejection in 30 heart transplant patients on unchanged prednisone and cyclosporine, hepatotoxicity and nephrotoxicity were explicitly not observed during the initial eight-week trial period. A second similar trial in 17 heart transplant patients at 3 g/day also reported that clinically significant alterations in hepatic and renal function were not observed.

raw_record.support_text: Previous reports of ampicillin-associated acute liver injury included isolated cases of acute cytolytic hepatitis, cholestatic hepatitis, and acalculous cholecystitis. A probable case of reversible acute cytolytic hepatitis was reported within 4 days after reexposure to ampicillin. Another ampicillin-treated patient developed severe Stevens-Johnson syndrome and jaundice after 2 days of treatment, with a persisting cholestatic syndrome, biopsy showing severe intracanalicular cholestasis, ductopenia, and portal inflammation, progressing to features of chronic cholestasis and primary biliary cirrhosis over more than 3.5 years. A patient with clindamycin-associated acute vanishing bile duct syndrome had a recurrence of similar prolonged cholestasis after 10 days of ampicillin treatment, with ampicillin-clindamycin cross-reactivity suggested though not conclusive.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: One case followed reexposure to ampicillin; cross-reactivity between ampicillin and clindamycin was suggested but not conclusive.
raw_record.extra_details: Reported ampicillin-associated injury included acute cytolytic hepatitis, cholestatic hepatitis, and acalculous cholecystitis. Probable reversible cytolytic hepatitis within 4 days of reexposure. A severe case with Stevens-Johnson syndrome and jaundice after 2 days of ampicillin showed persistent cholestatic syndrome despite corticosteroids; biopsy at 1 month showed severe intracanalicular cholestasis, ductopenia, and portal inflammatory infiltration, later complicated by pure red cell aplasia and histologic features of chronic cholestasis and primary biliary cirrhosis, with improvement over >3.5 years and persistent paucity of bile ducts on the last biopsy. A patient with prior clindamycin-associated vanishing bile duct syndrome had recurrence of prolonged cholestatic symptoms and lesions after 10 days of ampicillin.

raw_record.support_text: Norfloxacin hepatotoxicity was documented in two women treated for urinary tract infection, including one with a history of hepatitis C who had received higher dosages than currently recommended. Laboratory analysis showed a similar hepatocellular type of liver injury after only 2 and 7 days of treatment. Histopathology revealed preserved architecture, moderate steatosis, centrilobular necrosis, and eosinophilic infiltrates. In both patients no other possible cause was found, and prompt improvement occurred within 1-1.5 months after treatment was discontinued.

raw_record.support_text: A boy with delayed psychomotor development, attention deficit disorder, and therapy-resistant epilepsy was treated with valproate. The patient died of liver failure after 4 months of valproate treatment. Postmortem investigation of cultured fibroblasts suggested medium chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency, an unexpected finding since the boy had not presented typical manifestations of this disease. Because MCAD is important in fatty acid beta-oxidation, the patient probably had a genetically reduced tolerance to valproate, and the drug should be omitted in treating seizures in patients with possible MCAD deficiency.

The patient had prior/ concurrent antiepileptic polypharmacy (phenobarbital, phenytoin, carbamazepine) and therapy-resistant epilepsy.
raw_record.extra_details: Fatal fulminant hepatic failure occurred after 4 months of valproate treatment. Valproate-induced fatal hepatotoxicity has been regarded as an idiosyncratic reaction; risk factors noted include young age, polypharmacy, high valproate serum levels, and inborn errors of metabolism. Reduced MCAD activity was detected postmortem in cultured skin fibroblasts. Authors recommend omitting valproate in patients with possible MCAD deficiency.

In another case a mother developed severe liver damage after an overdose of aspirin and paracetamol (maternal plasma paracetamol 160 mg/l at 16 h after ingestion). These passages attribute acute maternal liver damage to paracetamol overdose.

raw_record.extra_details: Paracetamol (acetaminophen) overdose hepatotoxicity can be fatal: muscle necrosis was found histologically in all of 26 patients with fatal hepatic failure, including six who had taken a paracetamol overdose. Includes cases of transient mild maternal liver damage and severe liver damage with recovery.

raw_record.support_text: O'Malley et al. conducted a 12-week, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of naltrexone 50 mg/day as an adjunct to coping-skills training or supportive therapy in 72 male and 25 female alcohol-dependent patients. Compared with placebo, the naltrexone group had significantly lower SGOT and a non-significant trend toward lower SGPT, with both groups' enzyme levels remaining within normal limits; no hepatotoxicity was attributed to naltrexone.

At 36-48 h both mother and fetus were markedly deteriorating, supportive therapy for liver failure was started, and maternal liver transplantation was considered. After a prostaglandin-induced delivery at 84 h, the maternal liver function improved the next day, the liver transplant was not required, and both mother and infant made a full recovery, with the infant developing normally at 18 months.

Gilbert et al (ref 19) reported three patients who required liver transplantation for MTX-induced cirrhosis. raw_record.support_text: The authors report an unusual case of liver disease in a patient treated with glibenclamide whose clinical and laboratory findings from a liver biopsy support the diagnosis of glibenclamide liver toxicity. Sulfonylureas are described as causing rare liver injury expressing as intrahepatic cholestasis or hepatitis, attributable to drug hypersensitivity or dosage.
raw_record.extra_details: A 64-year-old man with type II diabetes treated with glibenclamide 10 mg/day for 2 months developed muscle pain, fatigue, jaundice, dark urine, and mild pruritus. Laboratory values during hospitalization: total bilirubin up to 10.3 mg/dl, direct bilirubin up to 5.9 mg/dl, ALT (SGOT) up to 310 U/l, AST (SGPT) up to 265 U/l, GGT up to 590 U/l, and alkaline phosphatase (SAP) up to 147 U/l. Serology for hepatitis A/B/C, EBV, CMV, and autoantibodies (smooth muscle, mitochondrial, antinuclear) negative; ultrasound, ERCP, and CT normal. Liver biopsy 10 days after stopping glibenclamide showed necrosis of liver cells, mild intrahepatic cholestasis in central areas with several bile infarcts, portal infiltration by eosinophils and lymphocytes, and bile duct proliferation. Liver function improved after drug withdrawal, with complete clinical and laboratory recovery by 4 months. No rechallenge reported; no competing causes identified.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report a case of cholestatic hepatitis induced by the oral fungicidal drug terbinafine, characterized by a prolonged course and mild reduction in the number of interlobular bile ducts (ILBD). In the discussion they explicitly conclude terbinafine is the offending agent, noting its four-week latency to jaundice, normalization of bilirubin and aminotransferases within three months of cessation, and exclusion of other causes of liver disease, while concurrent medications (nicergoline, fenofibrate) taken for four years were considered unlikely to be responsible.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: 75-year-old female patient treated for cutaneous candidiasis; concurrent nicergoline (5 mg daily) and fenofibrate (100 mg daily) were deemed unlikely offending agents because both had been taken for four years before terbinafine.
raw_record.extra_details: Oral terbinafine 250 mg/day for three weeks; onset of asthenia, anorexia, weight loss a few days after discontinuation, jaundice within ~4 weeks of start, followed by pruritus. Laboratory values ~2 weeks after discontinuation: total bilirubin 89 µmol/L (conjugated 70), ALT 277 IU/L, AST 242 IU/L, γGT 321 IU/L, alkaline phosphatase 375 IU/L; normal eosinophil count and prothrombin time. Cholestyramine relieved pruritus; bilirubin normalized 10 weeks after stopping terbinafine, but anicteric cholestasis persisted, with γGT still elevated 17 months later. Percutaneous liver biopsy 6 months after withdrawal showed reduction of interlobular bile ducts (visible in 16 of 23, 70%, portal tracts; ILBD/portal tract ratio 0.7 vs 0.9-1.8 in normal liver), occasional lymphocytes between biliary cells, minimal portal/periportal fibrosis, mild mononuclear infiltration, mild centrilobular canalicular cholestasis and minimal hepatocyte necrosis; negative copper stains. The authors note terbinafine-induced hepatitis is considered uncommon (five prior self-limited cases; liver tests showed cholestatic and cytolytic features resolving within 2-6 months, with cholangitis and centrilobular cholestasis in two biopsied cases), and asymptomatic transaminase elevations occur at an estimated incidence of 1/120,000.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report a case of recurrent severe acute hepatitis induced by omeprazole, noting that isolated reports of fulminant hepatic failure exist but that their described patient's injury recurred with rechallenge.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: 30-year-old man with advanced renal failure secondary to diabetic nephropathy; omeprazole was the only new medication after ranitidine was stopped; prior co-medications included ranitidine, calcium carbonate, furosemide, and nifedipine.
raw_record.extra_details: Omeprazole 20 mg once daily. Nine days after starting, acute liver injury developed (AST 1788 U/L, ALT 1294 U/L) with prothrombin time normal; liver tests normalized within 4 weeks of discontinuation. Six months later a rechallenge produced acute liver injury within 1 week (AST 954 U/L, ALT 762 U/L), again resolving on discontinuation. Viral (hepatitis A/B/C, EBV, HSV, CMV), immunologic, ferritin, ceruloplasmin, and alpha-1-antitrypsin evaluations were negative/normal. Authors state the time association plus positive rechallenge strongly suggests a cause-and-effect relation, and that the mechanism is probably idiosyncratic because an allergic or direct toxic reaction is unlikely.

raw_record.support_text: An 83-year-old man treated with 0·2 mg moxonidine daily for moderate hypertension, with no other medication and an uneventful past history, developed itching, nausea, painless jaundice and a maculopapular rash 9 months after starting moxonidine.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Elderly patient (83-year-old man); hypertension indication; single-agent therapeutic exposure.
raw_record.extra_details: Dose 0.2 mg/day; latency 9 months after treatment start; symptoms of itching, nausea, painless jaundice, maculopapular rash. Bilirubin rose to 173 µmol/L then 412 µmol/L, transaminases >1000 U/L (ASAT 1005, ALAT 1560) with only slight elevation of GGT and alkaline phosphatase. Liver biopsy showed severe localised intralobular and intraportal lymphoplasmocellular infiltrates with some neutrophils, intracytoplasmatic intracanalicular cholestasis, mild small-duct proliferation and considerable localised pericellular fibrosis. ANA, AMA, ANCA negative; α-1-antitrypsin, caeruloplasmin, copper normal; hepatitis B and C excluded, hepatitis A IgM negative. Patient recovered after drug discontinuation (vitamin K, albumin, diuretics), discharged within 4 weeks, liver indices normal 8 weeks after stopping and 1 year later. Authors note this is the first reported case and that in a manufacturer postmarketing surveillance programme none of >20,000 patients developed cholestatic hepatitis; they judge the case as drug-induced inflammatory intrahepatic cholestasis compatible with a causative role for moxonidine.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report a case of cholestatic hepatitis during treatment with moxonidine in an 83-year-old man treated with 0.2 mg moxonidine daily for moderate hypertension, and conclude there is convincing evidence of a causative role of moxonidine in this case. No other drug was given to this previously healthy patient, a liver biopsy showed features compatible with drug-induced inflammatory intrahepatic cholestasis, other diseases of the liver and bile ducts were excluded, and the patient recovered after stopping the drug.
raw_record.extra_details: 83-year-old man, previously healthy, no other prescribed or non-prescribed medication (single-agent attribution). Dose 0.2 mg moxonidine daily for hypertension; jaundice, itching, nausea and maculopapular rash developed 9 months after drug start. Liver tests rose to bilirubin 173 uM/L (peak 412 uM/L), ASAT >1000 U/L, ALAT 1560 U/L, with slight elevation of gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase and alkaline phosphatase; coagulation disorder, hypoalbuminaemia 17 g/L and generalized oedema led to hospital admission. Liver biopsy: severe localized intralobular and intraportal lymphoplasmocellular infiltrates with neutrophils and intracytoplasmatic intracanalicular cholestasis, mild small bile-duct proliferation, and focal pericellular fibrosis. Clinical phenotype is cholestatic hepatitis (drug-induced inflammatory intrahepatic cholestasis). Negative hepatitis B/C serology, negative ANA/AMA/ANCA, normal alpha-1-antitrypsin, caeruloplasmin and copper; no biliary dilatation or stones on ultrasound (2 cm hepatic cyst). Dechallenge with recovery: laboratory indices normal 8 weeks after stopping, patient well 1 year later. Postmarketing surveillance by the manufacturer reported no cholestatic hepatitis in more than 20,000 patients treated.

raw_record.support_text: This paper addresses acetaminophen-associated hepatotoxicity from multiple accidental overdoses in children. It describes markedly elevated serum ALT and AST levels in children with fulminant hepatic failure together with serum acetaminophen levels exceeding the toxic range defined by the Rumack-Matthews nomogram as highly suggestive of acetaminophen toxicity, and notes that plasma 3-(cystein-S-yl) acetaminophen may be a relatively sensitive and presumed specific marker of acetaminophen-associated hepatotoxicity.

Suggested mechanisms: reduced sulfation/glucuronidation and hepatic glutathione with fasting, increased CYP2E1-related turnover.

raw_record.support_text: The study compared a 52-hour regimen of IV-NAC with standard therapy with O-NAC for reducing the incidence of hepatotoxicity after acetaminophen (paracetamol) overdose in a pediatric cohort (mean age 15.6 ± 3.2 years). In this cohort, no patients treated within 10 hours and only 9.8% treated between 10 and 24 hours after ingestion experienced hepatotoxicity, whereas other series reported 6.1%/26.4% (oral NAC) and 10%/27.1% (IV-NAC) depending on treatment timing. The hepatic injury is attributed to acetaminophen overdose, with the toxic metabolite N-acetyl-p-benzoquinoneimine (elaborated by CYP1A2 and CYP2E1) discussed as mechanism.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric population (mean age 15.6 years); overdose setting; one patient with hepatic encephalopathy reportedly abused ethanol (unresolved co-exposure).
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity incidence in acetaminophen overdose: 0% when NAC begun within 10 hours and 9.8% when begun 10-24 hours after ingestion in this cohort; compared to Smilkstein et al. reports of 6.1%/26.4% (oral NAC) and 10%/27.1% (IV-NAC). One patient developed hepatic encephalopathy: ALT/AST >3000 IU/L by 32 h, peak ALT/AST 10,600/9840 IU/L at 58 h, peak ammonia 138 µg/dl at 106 h, improved by day 6 and discharged without sequelae; O-NAC attempt at 11 h with multiple episodes of emesis. Coagulopathy was clinically apparent in two patients (epistaxis, menorrhagia), neither requiring fresh frozen plasma. Mechanism discussion: N-acetyl-p-benzoquinoneimine (initially reported as N-acetyl-p-benzoquinoneimine) produced via CYP2E1/CYP1A2; ethanol induced CYP2E1 and reduced glutathione may increase susceptibility; pediatric sulfation more prominent and possibly greater glutathione regeneration.

raw_record.support_text: In two patients treated with prednisolone and azathioprine (one for chronic aggressive hepatitis, the other for Wegener's granulomatosis) a severe cholestatic jaundice occurred. The dominant feature was a reversible functional disturbance of the liver affecting elimination and synthesis, with only moderate signs of parenchymal cell damage. After azathioprine was discontinued, the pathological parameters gradually normalized over 6-8 weeks, and the paper concludes that azathioprine must be regarded as an indirect, facultative hepatotoxin and recommends regular liver function checks during long-term azathioprine therapy.

raw_record.support_text: The authors present a pediatric epilepsy patient who developed fulminant hepatic failure attributed to lamotrigine. On admission the lamotrigine level was 30.2 µg/ml (normal 1.0-3.0 µg/ml); the drug was discontinued and the patient recovered. The authors state that lamotrigine was the most likely cause of the fulminant hepatic failure, noting that valproic acid given 2 weeks earlier could only have had a short-term effect on lamotrigine metabolism. The paper also cites two prior adult case reports of lamotrigine-induced hepatic failure (Schaub et al., 3 weeks after addition; Makin et al.).
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric epilepsy patient; valproic acid administered 2 weeks before the episode was considered a possible (but dismissed as short-lived) effect on lamotrigine elimination.
raw_record.extra_details: Antiepileptic; inhibits excitatory amino acid release. Admission lamotrigine level 30.2 µg/ml (normal 1.0-3.0 µg/ml); parents insisted appropriate dose was given. Presented with jaundice/hepatic compromise and fulminant hepatic failure; recovered uneventfully after lamotrigine discontinuation plus supportive care, intravenous fluids, and 5 mg vitamin K; discharge labs showed normal renal function and coagulation, normalized ammonia, mildly elevated liver enzymes (AST 121 U/L, ALT 932 U/L). Patient had normal liver function tests 3 weeks prior and negative workup for metabolic disorders. Two prior adult case reports of lamotrigine-induced hepatic failure cited (Schaub et al., 2 weeks after addition to carbamazepine/clonazepam; Makin et al., 3 weeks after addition to valproic acid, carbamazepine, and vigabatrin). Authors recommend monitoring hepatic function in all lamotrigine-treated patients.

The paper also notes that in human patients with FIAU-induced hepatic failure, serum transaminase activities were not characteristically elevated, and that moderate to severe microvesicular or mixed microvesicular and macrovesicular hepatic steatosis found in woodchucks was essentially identical to that reported in human patients.

raw_record.extra_details: Hepatic failure and lactic acidosis developed in 7 of 10 clinical patients after more than 9 weeks of FIAU treatment and continued even after treatment was suspended; serum transaminase activities were not characteristically elevated in these patients. Microvesicular (and mixed microvesicular/macrovesicular) hepatic steatosis in humans was essentially identical to the moderate-to-severe steatosis found in FIAU-treated woodchucks, and mitochondrial ultrastructural findings (swelling, dissolution of cristae, decreased matrix density) reported in humans were similar to those in woodchucks. FIAU (fluoro-arabinosyl uracil) is a nucleoside analogue under evaluation for chronic HBV.

raw_record.support_text: In a patient who became jaundiced and febrile during malaria chemoprophylaxis, chloroguanide (proguanil) was stopped; a toxic reaction to chloroguanide was considered the most likely cause of the clinical presentation. Because liver enzymes and bilirubin remained elevated, a liver biopsy was performed 3 weeks after admission and showed hepatitis with periportal infiltrates consisting mainly of lymphocytes and eosinophils, indicative of drug-induced hepatitis. Other causes (hepatitis A/B/C, CMV, EBV, leptospirosis, malaria, Salmonella, parasites) were excluded.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of a patient presenting with fever to 39.0 °C, chills, vomiting, mild abdominal cramp, anorexia and jaundice (total bilirubin 4.4 mg/dL, conjugated 3.1 mg/dL; ALT 58 rising to 183 U/L, AST 33 to 45 U/L, GGT 96 U/L, ALP 158 U/L). Differential diagnosis initially considered either a toxic reaction to chloroguanide or a bile-duct infection (e.g., Salmonella); infection was excluded by negative blood/stool cultures, parasite examination, and serology (hepatitis A/B/C, CMV, EBV, leptospirosis, malaria). Chloroguanide was stopped and ciprofloxacin 500 mg twice daily given for 6 days; patient became afebrile within 3 days, bilirubin normalized after 2 months and aminotransferases after 4 months. Liver biopsy (3 weeks after admission) showed hepatitis with periportal lymphocytic and eosinophilic infiltrates indicative of drug-induced hepatitis. Reported as an adverse effect not previously described. Systemic involvement (fever, chills, eosinophilic infiltrate) fits the idiosyncratic pattern discussed in the paper. Patient had a history of hepatitis in 1980 probably due to ketoconazole and consumed 2-4 glasses of beer/wine weekly.

raw_record.support_text: Actinomycin D (administered with vincristine) is reported as a cause of hepatopathy in children receiving chemotherapy for Wilms' tumour. In NWTS 4, 5 of 37 children receiving a single 60 µg/kg dose per 3-week course developed hepatic toxicity, while none of 63 children on the divided-dose regimen did; dose reduction to 45 µg/kg followed. In SIOP 9, 64 children suffered at least one episode of hepatotoxicity, with 41 of 511 (8%) classed as 'H-VOD', supporting a steep dose/toxicity relationship between 1.5 and 1.8 mg/m².
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Children with Wilms' tumour; administered together with vincristine (and in some cohorts with abdominal radiation, which increases risk); infants and younger/lower-weight children appear more vulnerable, and right-sided tumours are associated with higher risk; dose and scheduling varied across study protocols.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatic veno-occlusive disease ('H-VOD') was the reported syndrome. Dose/schedule data: NWTS 4 single dose 60 µg/kg per 3 weeks (approx 1.8 mg/m²) versus same total fractionated over 5 days; dose later reduced to 45 µg/kg. UKW1/UKW2 used pulsed 1.5 mg/m² 3-weekly, with 6/355 (1.7%) developing hepatopathy. SIOP 9 used 0.45 mg/m²/day x 3 days (later 15 µg/kg/day x 3) in weeks 1-2, repeated in weeks 4-5 for the 8-week arm; infants received 66% of doses; 64 children had at least one episode, 41/511 (8%) H-VOD. SIOP series: abdominal irradiation produced hepatopathy in 11/68 (16%) versus 30/443 (6.7%), multivariable P=0.001. Right-sided Wilms' tumour associated with more hepatopathy (5.6% vs 1.2%, P=0.0002); of 33 H-VOD cases from four series, 27 were right-sided. A newborn with fatal hepatopathy after 75 µg/day x 5 days (approx 100 µg/kg if ~3 kg) and one fatal hepatopathy in 5/9 infants on UKW3 new dosing were reported. A convincing case in a 3.8-year-old with rhabdomyosarcoma after 2.25 mg/m² in divided doses is also cited.

raw_record.support_text: The authors describe a case of fatal hepatitis associated with troglitazone in an 85-year-old man with type 2 diabetes. Troglitazone therapy had been started 5 months before presentation and increased to 400 mg/day after 15 weeks; abdominal pain, malaise, and jaundice developed. A diagnosis of troglitazone-induced hepatitis was made, liver biopsy showed submassive hepatic necrosis, and the patient died 8 weeks after presentation. The paper notes that troglitazone use is in rare cases associated with fatal hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Elderly (85-year-old) male patient with type 2 diabetes treated with insulin; troglitazone added for glycemic control.
raw_record.extra_details: Dose increased to 400 mg/day after 15 weeks of therapy; fatal case. Symptoms included abdominal pain, malaise, and jaundice; ALT 608 U/L initially then 287 U/L at presentation, total bilirubin 15.6 mg/dL, albumin 2.5 g/dL, normal prothrombin time, glycosylated hemoglobin 5.2%; serology negative for hepatitis A, B, and C; normal hepatic ultrasonogram. Liver biopsy showed lobular cholestatic hepatitis with areas of confluent necrosis (submassive hepatic necrosis); patient died 8 weeks after presentation despite aggressive therapy. Concomitant medications included metoprolol (50 mg) and levothyroxine (0.05 mg daily). Author note that postmarketing reports of troglitazone-related death and transplantation led to withdrawal from the British market.

raw_record.support_text: In this US multicenter ALF study, acetaminophen overdose was the most frequent cause of acute liver failure (ALF), accounting for about 20% of cases, though less frequent than in the United Kingdom where it accounts for 50%–75% of cases. The paper frames acetaminophen as the leading attributable cause of drug-induced ALF.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose exposure; findings from the US Acute Liver Failure Study Group registry of 295 ALF patients from 13 US centers, where outcome was spontaneous survival, death, or transplantation.
raw_record.extra_details: Acetaminophen overdose accounted for ~20% of ALF cases in this US cohort, versus 50%–75% in the United Kingdom. In the acetaminophen subgroup (n=51), mean age was 33±13 years; spontaneous survival 28, death 17, transplantation 6, with no age difference among survival/death/transplant (P=.52). Acetaminophen patients with deep coma (grade III/IV) on admission had lower survival than those with mild coma (27% vs 68%, P=.020). From the US Acute Liver Failure Study Group; acetaminophen hepatotoxicity may have been underestimated because some centers included only transplant-listed cases.
